word_study.meaning: Servant, slave, one who serves; used in relation to both human servants and those who serve God. The word carries connotations of loyalty and obedience.
word_study.significance: Here, the Servant is referred to in the third person, suggesting the speaker is a prophetic voice commenting on the Servant's role. The word eved emphasizes the Servant's function as God's chosen agent.

word_study.meaning: Darkness, obscurity, lack of light; figuratively, a condition of confusion, trials, or spiritual perplexity.
word_study.significance: Walking in darkness is the condition of faith tested, where external circumstances offer no reassurance. It parallels the Servant's suffering in verse 6 and calls believers to identify with the Servant's willingness to proceed without comfort or proof.

word_study.meaning: To trust, rely on, put confidence in; to make something one's security or refuge.
word_study.significance: This verb is the active response to walking in darkness. When sight fails, trust becomes the only resource. It is the counterpart to the Servant's resolve in verse 7.

word_study.meaning: To lean on, rely on, support oneself by; to depend upon as one's foundation.
word_study.significance: The image is physical: to lean one's full weight on something or someone. To stay upon God is to transfer one's weight—all one's burdens, uncertainties, fears—onto God's shoulders.

cross_references.connection: Faith is 'the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.' The verse calls for exactly this kind of faith—trust when darkness obscures and no light appears. Like Abraham, those who fear the Lord must walk in darkness trusting in God's promises.

Trust in the Lord with all thine heart...and he shall direct thy paths.' Walking in darkness without visible light requires trusting God's direction over our own understanding, precisely the posture verse 10 calls for.

God is light; those who walk in darkness are not yet in covenant. Yet verse 10 calls believers to walk in darkness as a test of faith—a tension resolved by understanding that walking in darkness (uncertainty, trial) while trusting God is how one's faith is perfected.

The Lord teaches Joseph Smith: 'Let thy bowels also be full of charity...and then shall thy confidence wax strong in the presence of God.' The verse anticipates this: those who trust in God's name while walking in darkness will find their confidence strengthened.

Nephi teaches: 'Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men.' The Servant's call is to press forward in darkness while maintaining faith—the Nephite parallel emphasizes pressing forward despite uncertainty.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Hebrew thought, darkness (choshek) was often associated with chaos, judgment, and the realm of death. To walk in darkness was to be in a place of danger and disorientation. Yet the prophetic voice reframes darkness not as a place of hopelessness but as a testing ground of faith. The command to 'trust in the name of the LORD' appeals to God's revealed character (His name, shem, encompasses His nature and covenant reliability). The phrase 'stay upon his God' draws on ancient images of shepherding and physical support—the idea that God is a staff or staff upon which one leans.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains multiple accounts of walking in spiritual darkness while trusting God. Alma's conversion experience (Alma 36) involves darkness and despair followed by trust in Christ's redemption. The passage from Alma 37:33-34 teaches: 'see that ye are not lifted up unto pride; yea, see that ye do not boast in your own strength, nor your own wisdom...trust in God even in the darkest of times.'
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 112:10 contains this promise: 'Therefore, be faithful; stand in the office which I have appointed unto you; succor the weak, lift up the hands which hang down, and strengthen the feeble knees.' The verse calls covenant members to support one another while walking in darkness—the Servant's path becomes a communal covenant.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment ritual involves literal passage through darkness (the premortal and telestial realms) requiring faith and trust. Verse 10's call to walk in darkness while trusting God is enacted in the temple drama, where candidates must proceed without knowing the end, trusting in the covenants and God's guidance.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is simultaneously the Servant (whose suffering is invoked as a model) and the one through whom faith in darkness is made possible. Hebrews 12:2 describes Jesus as 'the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God'—He walked in darkness (Gethsemane, the cross) trusting in His Father's purposes. The verse calls believers to follow Christ through darkness into resurrection.
commentary.application: This verse speaks directly to members in seasons of spiritual trial—loss of certainty, unanswered prayers, delayed blessings, or dark nights of the soul. The prophet does not promise these seasons will pass quickly. Instead, it calls for a specific posture: fear the Lord (maintain reverent faith), listen to the Servant's voice (trust Christ's witness and example), and lean entirely on God without demanding light. The verse teaches that darkness itself—properly endured through faith—is a place of spiritual maturation. We do not graduate from darkness by gaining all answers; we graduate by learning to trust God when answers are withheld. This is the faith the Servant exemplifies: proceeding with set face like flint, knowing God's help, without demanding proof.

text_kjv: Behold, all ye that kindle a fire, that compass yourselves about with sparks: walk in the light of your fire, and in the sparks that ye have kindled. This shall ye have of mine hand; ye shall lie down in sorrow.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 11 concludes Isaiah 50 with a sharp and sobering warning that directly contrasts verse 10. Where verse 10 calls the faithful to trust in God's name while walking in darkness, verse 11 addresses those who reject that path and instead manufacture their own light. The image of 'kindling a fire' and 'encompassing themselves about with sparks' is vivid and intentional. These are people who refuse to wait in darkness trusting God; instead, they take matters into their own hands, creating their own illumination. This fire is not the warm glow of God's guidance but the frantic, self-generated heat of human effort and rebellion.

The prophet's voice becomes God's voice: 'This shall ye have of mine hand; ye shall lie down in sorrow' (ma'atsevah). The self-made fire appears to solve the problem of darkness—it provides light and warmth. But the verdict is stark: those who rely on their own fire will lie down in torment. The word ma'atsevah (sorrow, pain) echoes Genesis 3:16-17, where pain is decreed as a consequence of disobedience. The image suggests that while the fire one kindles may provide temporary illumination, it ultimately leaves the person consumed by the very flames they thought would save them. The contrast between verses 10 and 11 is Isaiah's final theological statement in this chapter: there are two paths—trust in God through darkness, or trust in self-generated light. One leads to vindication; the other leads to torment. There is no middle ground and no neutral choice.

word_study.meaning: To kindle, light a fire, strike sparks; to ignite or set aflame. Used literally for fire-starting and metaphorically for causing conflict or rebellion.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests active, deliberate effort to create fire—not a gift from God but a human accomplishment. This reflects the prideful choice to rely on one's own resources rather than God's.

word_study.meaning: To gird about, encircle, arm oneself with; to surround oneself. Often used for preparing for battle or equipping oneself for action.
word_study.significance: The image is of people surrounded by, indeed armed with, their own fires and sparks. They have made rebellion their defensive and offensive strategy, believing their self-generated light will protect and guide them.

word_study.meaning: Sparks, flashes of flame; the bright bits of fire that fly upward from a burning fire. Often used metaphorically for sudden, temporary illuminations.
word_study.significance: Sparks are the most transient part of fire—they fly upward briefly then vanish. They provide momentary light but no lasting warmth or guidance. The term suggests that human efforts to self-illuminate are inherently temporary and unreliable.

word_study.meaning: Pain, sorrow, suffering, torment; literally 'a place of pain or affliction.' The root connects to idolatry and fashioning false gods.
word_study.significance: The word deliberately echoes Genesis 3:16-17, where Eve is told her childbearing will bring forth 'itsavon' (sorrow) and Adam's work will bring 'itsavon' (toil and pain) as consequences of sin. To lie down in ma'atsevah is to experience the pain that results from disobedience to God's word.

cross_references.connection: Jesus teaches: 'if therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness!' The self-kindled fire of verse 11 is a false light—what appears to be illumination is actually darkness that leads away from God.

There is a way that seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.' The self-kindled fire seems to provide guidance and protection, but it leads to torment—seeming wisdom that ends in destruction.

The Book of Mormon describes how Satan 'saith: Be blind and astonished; wonder; for he performeth not a work, and a work shall come by the power of the devil.' Those who kindle their own fire are deceived into believing their self-effort will accomplish God's work—it will not.

The Lord declares: 'And the arm of the Lord shall be revealed; and the day cometh when they who will not hear the voice of the Lord...shall be cut off from among the people.' The self-kindled fire is the choice to not hear God's voice and rely instead on self.

The word ma'atsevah (sorrow) in verse 11 directly echoes the consequence language of Genesis, suggesting that reliance on self-generated light is a recapitulation of the Fall—the human attempt to be autonomous from God.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern texts, fire often symbolizes divine judgment, purification, or human rebellion and pride. The image of someone surrounded by their own fires, relying on sparks they have kindled, would strike an ancient audience as a picture of someone utterly self-deluded—kindling a fire in the darkness only to be consumed by it. The contrast with verse 10's call to trust in darkness would have been stark: the faithful walk in darkness trusting God; the foolish attempt to banish darkness through their own effort and are burned by their own flames. The warning is not gentle; it is prophetic judgment on those who reject the Servant's path.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly warns against self-deception and self-reliance apart from God. Alma 5:40-41 describes those 'separated from the Spirit of the Lord' as those who kindle their own light, metaphorically speaking. 2 Nephi 9:28 teaches: 'O that cunning plan of the evil one!...to lead astray the children of men...' by convincing them their own light is sufficient.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 50:23-24 teaches: 'And that which doth not edify is not of God...Wherefore, by this ye may know if a spirit is of God; every spirit that telleth unto you that you must worship the Father in spirit and in truth; or, every spirit that guideth you to do good is of God.' The self-kindled fire is a spirit that does not edify and does not guide toward God's truth.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment contrasts the true light of God's covenant (the veil, the final room, the presence of God) with false lights offered along the journey. Those who accept the false lights of the world and do not complete the covenant are left in darkness despite their effort. Verse 11 is a warning to those who think their own efforts (their kindled fire) will substitute for genuine covenantal progression.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the true light (John 1:4-5, 8:12). The contrast in verses 10-11 is ultimately a contrast between trusting in Christ as the light (walking in darkness while faithful to Him) versus trusting in human alternatives to Christ (self-kindled fires that lead only to torment). Revelation 21:23 describes the New Jerusalem where 'the Lamb is the light thereof'—there is no self-generated light in the fully redeemed cosmos. The Servant's path, modeled by Christ, requires abandoning the false fires of self-reliance.
commentary.application: This verse addresses a temptation every member faces: the desire to solve problems, find certainty, or achieve spiritual security through our own efforts, our own understanding, our own wisdom. It could be reliance on reason alone (rejecting revelation), on personal interpretation (rejecting prophetic guidance), on pride in accomplishment (rejecting humble dependence on God), or on any system we construct to replace trust in God. The verse does not say these self-constructed systems won't provide light—they do, temporarily. It says that ultimately, anyone who trusts in their own fire will 'lie down in sorrow.' The word is specific: ma'atsevah—not just sadness but the deep pain of realizing too late that one's foundation was false. The application is urgent: examine where you are kindling your own fire instead of trusting God in darkness. Lay down the sparks you have struck and learn to trust in God's name.

text_kjv: Hearken to me, ye that follow after righteousness, ye that seek the LORD: look unto the rock whence ye are hewn, and to the hole of the pit whence ye are digged.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah opens chapter 51 with a summons to the faithful remnant—those actively pursuing righteousness and seeking the Lord. The metaphor shifts immediately from listening to seeing: they must 'look unto the rock' and 'the hole of the pit.' This is not poetic decoration but theological instruction. The 'rock' (tsur) and 'quarry' represent their origins, their foundational identity as a people carved and shaped by God's hand. In the ancient Near East, stone quarrying was a rigorous, intentional process; the mason selected the stone, split it, refined it into useful form. Isaiah uses this image to remind Israel that their formation as a covenant people was deliberate, purposeful, and authored by God—not accidental or arbitrary. The parallel verse that follows will identify this 'rock' explicitly as Abraham, but here the image stands alone: you are not random, you are hewn, you are quarried by divine intention.
commentary.narrative_continued: The Covenant Rendering captures a subtle layer the KJV somewhat flattens: the 'rock whence ye are hewn' speaks to the permanence and solidity of one's origin, while 'the hole of the pit whence ye are digged' emphasizes the removal from raw, formless material. These two images—the extracted stone and the empty quarry—frame Israel's journey from raw potential to shaped nation. This is the opening move of the Comfort Section: before offering promises of future restoration, Isaiah calls the people to remember their past formation. Memory precedes hope.

word_study.meaning: to listen, hear, obey; implies not merely passive hearing but attentive response
word_study.significance: This is a covenant language formula, used throughout the Torah and prophets to summon Israel to covenant awareness. The call to 'hear' is the call to enter into relationship.

word_study.meaning: literally 'pursuers of righteousness'—those actively chasing, pursuing, seeking out right relationship and just action
word_study.significance: The verb radaf (pursue) carries active engagement, not passive membership. These are the spiritually alert, the ones who refuse to settle for comfortable compromise. This echoes Psalm 23:6 ('Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me') but inverts it—here the righteous pursue righteousness, not vice versa.

word_study.meaning: rock, stone, cliff; metaphorically, foundation, strength, refuge, God Himself (Psalm 18:2)
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that tsur here represents Abraham—Israel's ancestral bedrock. But the term tsur itself carries immense weight in Israelite theology as a standard epithet for God (Deuteronomy 32:4, 15; Psalm 89:26). The layering is intentional: Abraham is your rock in the sense that he is your foundation, but he himself points to the Rock of Israel, God Himself. This is a multi-layered call to remember both ancestral heritage and divine origin.

word_study.meaning: hewn, quarried, carved out (from the verb chatzab, to hew, split, cut stone)
word_study.significance: The passive voice is essential: you are hewn, not by yourselves. God is the mason. This emphasizes divine agency in Israel's formation and denies any notion that Israel shaped itself or achieved its status through its own strength. The image is violent and intentional—like a chisel striking stone—underscoring that covenant formation is not gentle or incidental.

word_study.meaning: literally 'quarry of the pit,' the excavation site where stone is extracted
word_study.significance: The doubled image (rock + quarry, hewn + digged) emphasizes thorough formation. Just as a quarry is not left half-finished, Israel's formation as a people was complete and intentional. The Covenant Rendering's choice of 'quarry' clarifies the image for modern readers who may not immediately picture stone extraction.

cross_references.connection: The original call to Abraham to leave his homeland and become the father of a great nation; Isaiah's call to 'look unto Abraham your father' in verse 2 directly echoes this covenant foundation.
Moses' Song: 'He is the Rock, his work is perfect' — the same Hebrew word (tsur) used for God's foundational character; Isaiah links Abraham to this divine stability.

David declares 'He shall cry unto me, Thou art my father, my God, and the rock of my salvation' — the same tsur metaphor, showing how Israel understood both God and ancestral fathers as foundational 'rocks.'
Nephi explains that the 'rock' upon which the Church is built is revelation from Jesus Christ; the LDS reading connects tsur to foundational truth itself.
The principle that what is of God must be understood by the Spirit; Isaiah's summons to 'listen' and 'look' frames understanding as a spiritual act, not mere intellectual reception.

commentary.historical_context: In the 6th century BCE context of Babylonian exile, this memory work was radical and countercultural. The exiles had lost their land, their temple, their visible signs of covenant status. By calling them to 'look unto the rock whence ye are hewn,' Isaiah anchors their identity not in geography or current circumstances but in ancestral memory and divine intention. Stone quarrying was well-known throughout the ancient Near East—Phoenician and Egyptian quarries produced the massive blocks for temples and palaces. The image would have been visually immediate to Isaiah's audience. Moreover, the call to remember Abraham at a moment of national catastrophe parallels how covenant communities have always renewed themselves in crisis: by returning to founding narratives and ancestral models.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 22, Nephi interprets Isaiah 51-52 as applying to the Restoration and the gathering of Israel in the latter days. The Book of Mormon repeatedly returns to the theme of covenant roots and ancestral memory (see 1 Nephi 5, where Nephi retrieves the brass plates and reads the genealogy of his fathers). 2 Nephi 30:5-6 promises that scattered Israel will be 'brought again into the true fold of God' — precisely the restoration theme Isaiah introduces here.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 113 directly quotes Isaiah 52:1-2 and provides revelation on these verses, explaining that 'Zion' refers to the Church, and that those who seek righteousness are called to 'awake and put on thy strength.' The restoration principle of recovering lost truth parallels Isaiah's call to remember lost identity. D&C 84:33 teaches that all who receive the priesthood covenant are bound to God 'with an everlasting covenant' — the same covenantal consciousness Isaiah summons here.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The image of being 'hewn' and 'quarried' parallels temple imagery: the temple is built of hewn stone (1 Kings 6:7), and Latter-day Saints understand the temple as the place where covenant identity is renewed and refined. The metaphor of shaping and refining stone connects to the temple as a place of spiritual formation and endowment.

commentary.christological_typology: While this verse does not explicitly name Christ, the 'rock' metaphor carries christological weight in LDS interpretation. In D&C 50:23-24 and throughout the New Testament, Christ is identified as the 'Rock.' By calling Israel to look to the rock whence they are hewn, Isaiah points forward to the Rock of Israel who would become the foundation of the Church. Abraham himself is presented in scripture as a type of Christ: he was willing to offer his son as a sacrifice, and through his seed all nations would be blessed. The formation of Israel through Abraham foreshadows the formation of the Church through Christ's atonement.
commentary.application: Members of the Church facing trials or doubts are often counseled to 'look back' to their conversion, their baptism, their personal covenant moments—just as Isaiah calls Israel to look back to Abraham. The verse teaches that identity grounded in divine intention and ancestral covenant is more stable than identity based on current circumstances. In an era of rapid social change, the call to 'look unto the rock' invites modern members to anchor their identity in eternal covenant rather than in passing cultural trends. The Covenant Rendering's emphasis on being 'hewn' rather than self-made challenges the modern American instinct toward self-invention: you are not the author of your own formation; you are shaped by covenant and divine intention.

text_kjv: Look unto Abraham your father, and unto Sarah that bare you: for I called him alone, and blessed him, and increased him.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah now identifies the 'rock' explicitly: Abraham, your father. But notice what is remarkable here—Sarah is also named. In covenant language, women are often rendered invisible, yet Isaiah summons Israel to 'look unto Sarah that bare you.' The Covenant Rendering's phrase 'who bore you' reminds the reader that Sarah was not merely Abraham's wife but the actual biological source of the covenant line (Isaac). This dual invocation of patriarch and matriarch is rare and theologically significant: God's covenant with Israel flows through both the male and female ancestors. The promise depends on Sarah's miraculous conception and birth as much as on Abraham's faith. This is a correction, subtle but firm, to any reading that renders the women of scripture merely instrumental or secondary.
commentary.narrative_continued: The substance of the verse is a promise rooted in comparison: Abraham was 'one' (echad) when God called him—childless, aged, apparently barren of any future. Yet God blessed him, and out of that one man came a multitude. The logic is intentional: if God could multiply one into many in the past, God can now restore the exiled many back to fullness and blessing. This is not mere nostalgia; it is a theological argument from analogy. The exiles are told: you are like the seed of Abraham—many but currently scattered and diminished. Just as God brought Abraham from one to many, God will gather the scattered many and restore them. The promise is built on precedent and pattern.

word_study.meaning: 'Abraham [your] father' — the possessive suffix makes Abraham the ancestor of Israel, the patriarch through whom covenant flows
word_study.significance: This is covenantal genealogy language. To call someone 'father' is to claim kinship and to inherit the covenant made with that ancestor. In exile, the Israelites risked losing this familial identity; Isaiah re-establishes it.

word_study.meaning: literally 'Sarah who gave birth to you' (from cholel, to writhe, bring forth in labor)
word_study.significance: The verb tcholel emphasizes the physical, bodily act of birth. Sarah is not a symbolic or spiritual figure but the actual biological mother of the covenant line. The Covenant Rendering uses 'bore' to preserve this embodied reality. This is theologically significant because it insists on the woman's role in producing the covenant community.

word_study.meaning: 'one I called him' — the word echad (one) emphasizes singularity, loneliness, absolute solitude in the moment of calling
word_study.significance: Abraham was alone, without heir, without visible promise of a future—yet God called him. The Covenant Rendering's rendering 'he was but one when I called him' emphasizes the improbability and miracle of the promise. This echoes the power language of Isaiah 40:26 ('He calleth them all by names by the greatness of his might')—God's call creates reality out of nothing.

word_study.meaning: and I blessed him (from barak, to bless, to bestow favor, to grant fertility and prosperity)
word_study.significance: The verb barak carries a sense of abundant conferral—blessings multiply and overflow (as in the threefold blessing of Numbers 6:24-26). God did not merely promise Abraham a blessing; God actively bestowed blessing upon him.

word_study.meaning: and I multiplied him, made him many (from the verb rabah, to be great, numerous, to increase)
word_study.significance: The verb rabah shows the miracle completed: not merely promised but realized. Abraham's descendants became 'as the stars of the heaven' and 'as the sand of the seashore' (Genesis 22:17). The exiles hearing this were promised the same multiplication in their restoration.

cross_references.connection: After the binding of Isaac, God promises Abraham: 'thy seed shall possess the gate of his enemies; And in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed' — this is the foundational promise Isaiah appeals to.
God's initial call to Abraham: 'I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great' — Isaiah echoes this exact promise structure (I called, I blessed, I increased).

Paul cites Abraham as the archetype of faith: 'God, who quickeneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were' — the same logic of miraculous multiplication from nothingness that Isaiah invokes.

Hebrews honors both Abraham and Sarah: 'through faith also Sara herself received strength to conceive seed...Therefore sprang there even of one man...a multitude as the stars of the sky' — this New Testament passage directly parallels Isaiah's dual naming of patriarch and matriarch.
Nephi interprets Isaiah's promise to the scattered remnant of Israel, explaining that the gathering of Judah and Israel fulfills the Abrahamic covenant through the Restoration.

commentary.historical_context: The historical irony cannot be missed: in 586 BCE, Judah's exiles sat in Babylon, seemingly cut off from the land of Abraham, bereft of the visible markers of their covenantal identity. The temple was destroyed, the king was deposed, the priesthood's sacrificial office was suspended. To call them to remember Abraham—a man without a land who was promised a covenant through faith alone—was to anchor their identity in the very thing exile could not take: faith in the promises of their fathers. Ancient Near Eastern literature often invoked ancestors as models (we see this in Mesopotamian hymnic literature and Egyptian biographical inscriptions), but few texts achieve the theological depth of Isaiah's move: Abraham is not merely a model but a guarantee. If God's promises held for Abraham in his complete solitude, they will hold for the exiles in theirs. Importantly, the naming of Sarah reflects a strand of Israelite piety that refused to render women invisible; the Targum (Aramaic paraphrase) also names Sarah, suggesting this dual invocation was a known interpretive tradition.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly emphasizes that the covenant made to Abraham extends to the Gentiles and to Israel in the latter days. 1 Nephi 15:12-18 and 2 Nephi 30:3-6 both interpret Isaiah as a promise that Israel will be gathered from all nations and restored to their lands. Alma 36:2-3 teaches that Alma, in repentance, called upon the name of Jesus Christ and received mercy, in the spirit of Abraham's faith. The parallel is important: just as Abraham was justified by faith before the law, so the exiles are justified by faith in God's promises even when circumstances seem hopeless.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 84:33-34 teaches that all who receive the priesthood covenant are bound to God with an everlasting covenant—precisely echoing the Abrahamic covenant language. D&C 132:29-31 teaches that the marriage covenant is eternal and produces 'seeds' (spiritual posterity), directly paralleling Abraham and Sarah's promise. The Restoration doctrine of eternal marriage is grounded in the Abrahamic model.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In LDS temple theology, the promise to Abraham and Sarah is renewed in every endowment session. The sealing ordinance for husband and wife directly echoes the covenant made to Abraham and Sarah, promising that their offspring will be numberless. The phrase 'multiplied' (arebbehu) appears in temple covenants and in the endowment narrative itself.

commentary.christological_typology: Abraham is a type of Christ in the willingness to offer a son as a sacrifice (Genesis 22). Sarah is a type of the Church (the bride of Christ who bears spiritual children). The promise that from one man and one woman come many is ultimately fulfilled in Christ and His Church: Christ is the 'one man' through whose redemption 'the many' are justified (Romans 5:15-19). The Covenant Rendering's emphasis on Sarah's role as the actual bearer of the promise points to the Church's role in bearing the witness of Christ to the world.
commentary.application: The modern covenant member facing disappointment or delay in promised blessings can draw courage from this verse. Abraham was 'alone' when called; he waited decades for Isaac; Sarah herself doubted (Genesis 18:12). The verse teaches that faith is not faith when circumstances are clear and easy; faith is faith when the promise seems impossible. The modern application is personal: When you feel alone in your faith, when promised blessings seem delayed, remember that you are descended from Abraham and Sarah, whose entire covenant was built on the principle of multiplying what seems barren. The promise to Abraham and Sarah is not merely historical; it is personal: you, the covenant member, are their seed, and the promises made to them extend to you. The dual naming of Abraham and Sarah also invites modern members to see themselves reflected in both—whether male or female, you are part of the Abrahamic covenant. Sarah's naming corrects the modern tendency to see the patriarchs as male-only history; the covenant belongs equally to men and women.

text_kjv: For the LORD shall comfort Zion: he will comfort all her waste places; and he will make her wilderness like Eden, and her desert like the garden of the LORD; joy and gladness shall be found therein, thanksgiving, and the voice of melody.

commentary.narrative: This verse shifts from memory to promise, and the tone shifts from instruction to assurance. The opening 'For' (ki) links back to verse 1: because Israel is rooted in the rock of Abraham, therefore the Lord will comfort Zion. The double use of 'comfort' (nicham) echoes Isaiah 40:1 ('Comfort ye, comfort ye my people'), establishing continuity between the opening of the Comfort Section and its development here. But 'comfort' here is not merely emotional solace; it is active restoration and transformation. God will comfort 'all her waste places'—every ruin, every destruction becomes subject to divine reversal. The cascade of images that follows—wilderness becoming Eden, desert becoming the garden of the Lord—represents the complete reversal of exile and judgment.
commentary.narrative_continued: The parallel structure of 'wilderness like Eden' and 'desert like the garden of the LORD' is intentional; they are two ways of saying the same restoration, but each adds depth. Eden is the primordial paradise (Genesis 2-3), where God walked with humanity in direct presence. The garden of the Lord (gan-YHWH) echoes Ezekiel 28:13 and refers to the archetype of divine proximity and beauty. By equating Zion's restored state with both Eden and gan-YHWH, Isaiah claims that restoration is not mere return to pre-exile normalcy but a return to paradise itself—to the condition of primal intimacy with God. The final line overwhelms us with four words of celebration: joy, gladness, thanksgiving, song. The Covenant Rendering notes that these four words overflow the poetic line, suggesting abundance and surplus of emotion. The wilderness will not merely survive; it will sing.

word_study.meaning: to comfort, console, show mercy; can also mean to have pity, to repent (God 'repents' of judgment when He withdraws it)
word_study.significance: The verb nicham is doubled ('comfort...comfort'), emphasizing urgency and totality. This is the opening word of Isaiah 40:1 ('Comfort ye, comfort ye my people'). In Hebrew thought, doubling a verb intensifies its force. God will not merely touch Zion's wounds but will saturate her with comfort. The Covenant Rendering uses 'comforts,' shifting to the present tense, suggesting that this comfort is already in motion, not merely future.

word_study.meaning: ruins, desolations, devastated places (from charab, to destroy, desolate)
word_study.significance: The word charabim refers to the literal ruins of destroyed cities and temples (see Isaiah 49:19, 52:9). This is not abstract or metaphorical; the exiles know these ruins firsthand. God's comfort will address the concrete, visible destruction of exile.

word_study.meaning: wilderness, desert, desolate place; often symbolizes the place of trial, testing, and wandering (Exodus 15:22, Numbers 14:33)
word_study.significance: Midbar (wilderness) is the primary symbol of Israel's testing and transition in the Torah. By transforming midbarah into Eden, Isaiah promises that the wilderness of exile will become the place of spiritual renewal, not merely punishment. The wilderness that bred idolatry will become the garden where God walks again with His people.

word_study.meaning: Eden, the garden of God where humanity was placed before the fall (Genesis 2:8-9, 15); represents primal innocence, abundance, and divine presence
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that the scroll equates Eden with gan-YHWH, the garden of the Lord (Ezekiel 28:13). By promising a return to Eden, Isaiah claims that restoration reverses not merely political exile but also the theological exile from God's immediate presence caused by human sin. This is eschatological language: the end state is a return to the beginning state, but now without the possibility of fall.

word_study.meaning: the garden of the Lord, an archetype of divine beauty and order, often identified with Eden or with the divine throne room
word_study.significance: The phrase gan-YHWH appears in Ezekiel 28:13 and 31:8-9 to describe the original creation in its perfection. To say Zion will become gan-YHWH is to say Zion will become the meeting place of heaven and earth, where God's order and beauty prevail. This is the language of cosmic restoration.

word_study.meaning: joy (sason: gladness, exultation) and gladness (simchah: joy, happiness, festivity)
word_study.significance: These are not mere synonyms; sason carries a sense of exultation and shout of joy (see Isaiah 48:20), while simchah denotes the quieter, deeper contentment of satisfaction. Together they frame joy from every dimension—the outward and the inward.

word_study.meaning: thanksgiving, gratitude, a thanksgiving sacrifice or psalm (Psalm 100:1); implies acknowledgment of God's salvation
word_study.significance: Todah is not merely emotional gratitude but covenantal response—the recognition that God has acted and the response of the people in worship. The Covenant Rendering includes this, showing that restored Zion will not merely be joyful but will be a place of active worship and acknowledgment of God.

word_study.meaning: voice of song, voice of singing; zimrah refers to musical praise or vocal music
word_study.significance: The wilderness will not merely be silent or peaceful; it will resound with song. This is the language of Psalm 100 and of the Temple worship—the restored Zion will be a place of musical praise. The Covenant Rendering's 'sound of song' conveys the auditory vividness of the promise.

cross_references.connection: The original creation of Eden, 'the garden of the LORD'; Isaiah promises that Zion's restoration will return to this state of primal beauty and divine presence.

An earlier Isaiah passage promises that 'the wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad for them; and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose' — this verse is a near-identical parallel, showing the consistency of Isaiah's restoration vision.
The opening of the Comfort Section: 'Comfort ye, comfort ye my people' — the doubled 'comfort' (nicham) connects this verse to that opening promise and shows the development of the comfort theme.
Ezekiel refers to the archetype of the garden of God (gan-YHWH): 'thou hast been in Eden the garden of God' — Isaiah's language directly echoes this cosmic geography.

A thanksgiving psalm that calls for joy, gladness, and singing in God's presence: 'Serve the LORD with gladness: come before his presence with singing' — Isaiah's promise of joy, thanksgiving, and song draws on this liturgical tradition.
Modern revelation promises that after the Millennium, the earth will be restored to its 'former glory' — this is the LDS understanding of Isaiah's promise that the wilderness will become Eden.

commentary.historical_context: In the 6th century BCE, the exiles sat among the ruins of Jerusalem. The temple that had stood for nearly 400 years was a charred ruin. Fields lay fallow. The city gates hung open to emptiness. To speak of 'comfort' in this context was not sentimentality; it was a direct challenge to the theology of desolation that exile bred. The promise that wilderness would become a garden was not merely poetic but was a claim about God's power and will to reverse historical catastrophe. In ancient Near Eastern thought, the garden (particularly the royal garden) was a symbol of order, fertility, and divine favor. Mesopotamian kings built processional gardens as symbols of their cosmic authority. By promising that desolate Zion would become a garden of the Lord, Isaiah asserted that God's authority exceeded that of Nebuchadnezzar and all earthly powers.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 30:7-8 parallels Isaiah's promise with the Restoration promise: 'And the Lord will surely prepare a way for his people...And I am confident that all things which have been written hath been written for our profit and learning.' The restoration of Zion in Isaiah is tied to the restoration of all things in the latter days (1 Nephi 1:19-20). Alma 41:3 teaches that 'restored means to bring back again; therefore that which has been lost shall be restored.' This is exactly Isaiah's promise: what was lost in exile will be restored to a state even more glorious than before.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:23-24 promises: 'And verily, verily, I say unto you that when the thousand years are ended, and Satan shall be loosed, and shall go forth to deceive the nations...the earth shall be renewed and receive its paradisiacal glory.' This is the Restoration understanding of Isaiah's promise. Additionally, D&C 64:10 teaches that 'I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive, but of you it is required to forgive all men' — the comfort of restoration is grounded in divine mercy and human willingness to be transformed.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The imagery of Zion as a garden, as a place where God's presence dwells, and as a place of joy and singing is central to temple theology. The temple is Zion in miniature — the place where fallen creation is transformed and where humans encounter divine order and beauty. The promise of Zion becoming a garden is fulfilled in the temple, where members pass through different realms (like the different areas of Eden) and ascend toward God's presence.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the gardener (John 20:15)—the one who tends, restores, and cultivates. Isaiah's promise that the wilderness will become a garden is a promise of Christ's redemptive work. The fall was a expulsion from the garden (Genesis 3); Christ's atonement makes possible the return to the garden (Luke 23:43, 'This day shalt thou be with me in paradise'). The promise of restored joy, thanksgiving, and song is the promise of the resurrection, when all tears are wiped away and sorrow and sighing flee away (Revelation 21:4, Isaiah 35:10).
commentary.application: For the modern member, this verse offers a vision of spiritual restoration. Just as Zion's ruins will become a garden, so the ruins of a broken heart, a failed marriage, a life of addiction, or years of spiritual drought can become fertile ground for God's work. The promise of transformed wilderness is not a promise of escape from difficulty but of transformation through difficulty. Specifically, the verse teaches that comfort is not passive but active: God will comfort all waste places, will actively transform the desert. This invites modern members to cooperate with God's comfort by opening themselves to His reshaping work. The four words—joy, gladness, thanksgiving, song—describe the marks of restored life: not mere survival but celebration, not merely getting through but singing through.

text_kjv: Hearken unto me, my people; and give ear unto me, O my nation: for a law shall proceed from me, and I will make my judgment to rest for a light of the people.

commentary.narrative: The second summons in this section opens with the same command as verse 1: 'Hearken unto me.' But now the audience is expanded and redefined: 'my people' and 'my nation.' The repetition of the dual address ('Give heed' and 'listen') mirrors verse 1 but adds emotional weight—God is not merely making an announcement but calling for personal, intimate attention. The substance of the summons is theological instruction about the future: a law (torah) will proceed from God, and this law will become 'a light to the peoples.' The Covenant Rendering's phrase 'law will go out from me' captures the active emanation: torah is not merely promulgated but flows out from God's being. The key theological move is the shift from 'people' (am) in the opening address to 'peoples' (ammim) in the promise. The modern reader might miss this shift, but the Dead Sea Scrolls variant here is significant: 1QIsaᵃ reads 'peoples' (ammim, plural) in the opening phrase as well, universalizing the address. Whether the original reads 'my people' or 'peoples,' the result is the same: God's law will become universal, extending beyond Israel to illuminate all nations.
commentary.narrative_continued: This verse anticipates the universal scope developed in Isaiah 49:6 ('I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles'). The exile itself is being reframed: it is not merely judgment but a prelude to a mission. Israel, in exile among the nations, will become the bearer of God's justice to those nations. This is the opening note of the Suffering Servant theme that dominates chapters 52-53. The Servant will be a 'light to the nations' precisely by bearing the suffering that brings them restoration.

word_study.meaning: listen, pay attention, give heed; implies not merely hearing but focused, intentional attention
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'give heed' captures the sense better than the KJV's 'hearken unto me.' Hakshibu appears in Isaiah 42:4 ('the isles shall wait for his law') and carries a sense of anticipatory waiting. The exiles are not merely told to listen but to listen with expectation.

word_study.meaning: ami: my people (collective noun for a group bound by kinship or covenant); leumi: my nation (from leum, a people or ethnic group as a political entity)
word_study.significance: The doubling (people, nation) emphasizes completeness: every member, at every level of community, is addressed. The Covenant Rendering captures the intensity of this dual address. The Dead Sea Scrolls variant that reads 'peoples' instead of 'my people' would universalize this address from the start, opening it to all nations.

word_study.meaning: law, teaching, instruction, revelation; the Mosaic law and, more broadly, God's revealed will and direction
word_study.significance: Torah here is not merely legal code (mishpat) but holistic instruction/teaching. The Covenant Rendering notes that torah means not merely the Mosaic law but God's instruction that will illuminate the nations — anticipating the universal scope of the Servant's mission. This is torah in the sense of prophetic revelation, not merely legal statute.

word_study.meaning: from me will go out, emanate, proceed; the verb yatza means to go out, emerge, proceed forth
word_study.significance: The verb yatza captures active emanation: torah flows out from God's being like light from the sun (Isaiah 2:3 parallels this: 'the word of the LORD shall go out from Zion'). This is not torah as static text but as living, moving revelation.

word_study.meaning: judgment, justice, righteous decision, proper order; often paired with sedek (righteousness) to indicate both the act of judging and the quality of what is judged
word_study.significance: Mishpat in Isaiah often refers to God's saving justice—not merely punishment but the restoration of right order (see Isaiah 42:1-4, where the Servant brings mishpat to the nations). The Covenant Rendering shifts 'my judgment' to 'my justice,' capturing this sense that God's judgment is restorative, not merely punitive.

word_study.meaning: I will set at rest, establish, cause to rest (argiya: from root nua, to rest, settle, endure); the sense is of making stable and permanent, not merely temporary
word_study.significance: The verb argiya means to settle, establish, make enduring (see Deuteronomy 28:11, 'the Lord shall make thee plenteous in goods'). God's justice will not be a fleeting gift but will be established as a lasting light. The Covenant Rendering's 'set my justice as a light' captures this sense of establishment.

word_study.meaning: for a light to the peoples; or (with the DSS variant 'ammim' in verse 4 opening): 'a light to the peoples' extends the Servant motif
word_study.significance: This exact phrase appears in Isaiah 49:6 in reference to the Servant. The light-metaphor for God's revelation and justice is central to Isaiah (42:6, 49:6, 60:1-3). By promising that God's justice will become 'a light to the peoples,' Isaiah positions Israel (and particularly the Suffering Servant) as the bearer of divine revelation to all nations. This is the foundation of the universal mission that motivates the Servant's suffering.

cross_references.connection: The Servant is promised: 'it is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant...I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles' — verse 4 here anticipates this Servant designation and universal mission.
God's first servant song: 'Behold my servant...I have put my spirit upon him: he shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles' — the same language of bringing justice/mishpat to the nations.
In the eschaton, 'the word of the LORD shall go out from Zion, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem' — echoing the image of torah proceeding from God to illumine all peoples.

Jesus tells His disciples: 'Ye are the light of the world...Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works' — this is the fulfillment and universalization of Isaiah's promise that Israel would become a light to the nations.

Modern revelation echoes Isaiah: 'And that the testimony which ye shall bear shall be sent forth among all nations, kindreds, tongues, and people. And as I said unto mine apostles...I say unto you again, that the day speedily cometh that ye shall see me and know that I am.'

commentary.historical_context: The promise that Israel's torah will become 'a light to the peoples' would have sounded revolutionary to 6th-century exiles. They had been conquered, displaced, and were living under Babylonian authority and pagan religious practices all around them. To tell them that they were about to become the teachers and spiritual light of the nations would have seemed absurd. Yet this is precisely the function the Jewish people took on after the Babylonian exile: the Torah became a portable, universal text that could be studied anywhere. The Babylonian Talmud itself (compiled in Babylon itself) became the central text of Jewish learning for centuries. Moreover, the Christian New Testament emerges from the Jewish claim that God's law has been universalized and opened to the Gentiles. The historical reality is that the exiled, defeated people became the bearers of a spiritual tradition that has shaped billions of lives across continents and centuries.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 13:39-41 teaches that through the Book of Mormon and other latter-day scriptures, 'the Lord shall make bare his arm in the eyes of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of the Lord.' The missionary work of the Restoration fulfills Isaiah's promise that God's word will proceed forth to illuminate all peoples. 2 Nephi 3:12 promises that Joseph Smith will bring forth words that will 'convince them of the truth of the first,' i.e., the scriptures, making God's law universally available.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:20-21 says: 'Wherefore, I the Lord, knowing the calamity which should come upon the inhabitants of the earth, called upon my servant Joseph Smith...That every man might speak in the name of God the Lord, even the Savior of the world.' This is the Restoration realization of Isaiah's promise: the Lord's word (torah/law) is going forth again to all nations through the restored priesthood and the restored church. D&C 88:81 teaches that members are to 'send forth the preparatory message' — participating in the work of bringing God's justice/light to all peoples.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where God's law is taught and established (D&C 110:8, 'The dedication of this house of God'). The ordinances of the temple are God's 'law' (torah) in the sense of His eternal instruction and order. Modern members who participate in temple work participate in the fulfillment of Isaiah's promise that God's judgment and justice will become a light to the nations — through the vicarious ordinances performed on behalf of all peoples.

commentary.christological_typology: The identification of God's torah with a 'light to the peoples' finds its complete fulfillment in Christ, who is 'the light of the world' (John 8:12) and who embodies all righteousness and justice (2 Corinthians 5:21). The Servant in Isaiah (chapters 49, 52-53) is both the bearer of the law and the one whose suffering fulfills the law's requirements. Christ's atonement is God's ultimate 'judgment' (mishpat) — the act that restores right order between God and humanity and that illuminates God's justice to all nations.
commentary.application: For modern members, this verse invites participation in a universal mission. The promise that God's justice will become 'a light to the peoples' is not merely about Israel's historical future but about the Church's present mission. When members share the gospel, perform acts of mercy, or live with integrity, they are participating in this ancient promise: they are bringing God's law/light to their communities and nations. The verse also teaches that God's revelation is progressive and universal: just as God sent torah through the prophets of Israel to the ancient Near East, God continues to send revelation to all peoples through the Restoration. The modern member is invited to see themselves not as recipients of an exclusive truth but as potential bearers of truth to a waiting world. This reframes mission work from a duty to an honor: you are participating in the fulfillment of Isaiah's promise to illumine all nations.

text_kjv: My righteousness is near; my salvation is gone forth, and mine arms shall judge the people; the isles shall wait upon me, and on mine arm shall they trust.

commentary.narrative: Verse 5 shifts from the promise that God's law will go forth to the promise that God Himself will go forth. The threefold declaration—'My righteousness is near, my salvation is gone forth, my arms shall judge'—establishes that God's justice is not a distant promise but an imminent reality. The 'arm' (zeroa) of the Lord becomes the central image. In Isaiah, God's 'arm' is the symbol of His power to save and to judge (see Isaiah 40:10, 52:10, 53:1). The repetition of 'my arm' in the parallel lines ('mine arms shall judge' / 'on mine arm shall they trust') emphasizes God's power as both judicial and salvific—the same arm that judges is the arm on which the nations trust. This is theologically profound: God's power to judge and God's power to save are not opposed but unified. The isles (coastlands) waiting for God's arm represents the universal scope: not merely Israel but all the distant peoples (iyyim appears repeatedly in Isaiah 40-55 to represent the Gentile world).
commentary.narrative_continued: The movement of the verse is from near-future ('righteousness is near') to already-accomplished ('salvation is gone forth') to imminent judgment ('shall judge'). This temporal layering creates a sense of inevitability: the process is already in motion. The promise addresses not merely the exiles but the watching nations: they will wait upon God, they will trust in His arm. This is the foundation of the Servant's mission: the Servant will be the instrument through which God's arm is revealed to the nations, bringing them to faith. The DSS variants do not alter the meaning here, but the consonantal text confirms the ancient stability of this verse.

word_study.meaning: near is my righteousness; karov means near in space or time, imminent; tzidki is righteousness, right order, justification
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'righteousness draws near' captures the sense that God's justice is approaching like a person drawing near. This is not merely assurance but imminence—the exiles need not wait generations but should expect God's vindication soon. In Isaiah, tzedek (righteousness) often denotes God's saving justice, not merely ethical virtue.

word_study.meaning: has gone forth my salvation; yatza means to go out, proceed (as in verse 4); yisha means salvation, deliverance, the state of being saved or safe
word_study.significance: The perfect tense 'has gone forth' (yatza) creates a paradox: from the exiles' perspective in 586 BCE, salvation has not yet come, yet Isaiah speaks of it as accomplished. This is the language of prophetic certainty: what God promises is as good as done. Yisha appears repeatedly in Isaiah 40-66 as the central promise.

word_study.meaning: my arms will judge the peoples; zeroa means arm, the strength and power of a person or God; mishpat (judgment) includes both condemnation and vindication
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'my arms will judge the peoples' clarifies that God's power (represented by His arms) will bring justice. In Isaiah, God's arm is often the instrument of both salvation and destruction—it splits the Red Sea and it sweeps down on enemies. Here, the peoples are subject to God's judgment, which means both that the oppressive powers will be judged and that the nations will recognize God's justice.

word_study.meaning: isles, coastlands, islands; often refers to distant Gentile lands, the edges of the known world
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering uses 'coastlands,' which is more precise than 'isles' — it refers to the distant coastal regions accessible by sea, representing all the Gentile nations beyond Israel. In Isaiah, iyyim appears repeatedly (41:1, 42:10, 49:1, 51:5, 59:18, 66:19) as the audience being called to attention. The waiting of the isles is not passive but expectant: they are looking to God.

word_study.meaning: they wait for, they hope in, they expect (from kawah, to wait, hope, anticipate)
word_study.significance: The verb kawah carries a sense of active waiting, not passive languishing. It implies expectation and hope. The nations are not commanded to wait but are described as already waiting—they instinctively recognize that God's salvation is the answer to their deepest needs.

word_study.meaning: they hope in, they confide in, they wait expectantly for (from yahal, to wait, hope)
word_study.significance: The parallel between 'wait' (yekawwu) and 'hope/trust' (yeyachelu) shows their near-identity: to wait for God is to trust in His arm. This is the response the Servant's mission will evoke among the nations.

cross_references.connection: Behold, the Lord GOD will come with strong hand, and his arm shall rule for him' — establishes the 'arm of the Lord' as the central symbol of God's power in the Comfort Section.

'The LORD hath made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God' — this is the fulfillment of verse 5's promise that God's arm will be revealed and nations will see His salvation.
'Who hath believed our report? and to whom is the arm of the LORD revealed?' — the Servant passage asks whether the nations will recognize God's arm revealed in the Servant's suffering.

Paul quotes Isaiah 53:1: 'But they have not all obeyed the gospel. For Esaias saith, Lord, who hath believed our report?' — connecting the Servant's arm-revelation to the gospel's reception among the Gentiles.

'The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ...And his kingdom ruleth over all' — the ultimate fulfillment of Isaiah's promise that God's arms will judge and the nations will trust in His power.

commentary.historical_context: The promise that 'the isles shall wait upon me' addressed a historical reality: by the 6th century BCE, Israel's power was gone, yet the exiles were expected to believe that the nations would look to their God. This required radical faith. In the ancient Near East, when a nation was defeated and exiled, its gods were considered defeated as well. The Babylonian creation myth explicitly framed conquest as the triumph of one god (Marduk) over others. To claim that the conquered, exiled Israel possessed a God whose arm would judge all the nations and to whom distant peoples would trust was not merely religious confidence but a direct challenge to the dominant imperial theology. Yet the historical outcome vindicated this claim: Jewish Torah, Jewish monotheism, and Jewish messianic hope shaped the entire Mediterranean world through Christianity and Islam. The 'isles' that once seemed indifferent to Israel's God eventually oriented their entire civilizations around the God of Israel.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 22:10-11 interprets Isaiah: 'And after the Gentiles do stumble nigh unto the destruction of the Gentiles, full of all manner of abominations, they shall repent...and I will show unto them my judgment, and I will save them. For the time speedily cometh that Satan shall have no more power over the hearts of the children of men.' This is the LDS reading of Isaiah's promise: the judgment on the nations leads to their repentance and salvation through the Servant's work.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:72-73 teaches: 'Wherefore, be faithful, praying always, having your lamps trimmed and burning, and oil with you...And the day cometh when all shall rise up and choose the good part.' This echoes Isaiah's promise that all nations will trust in God's arm. Additionally, D&C 1:23 states that the Lord's 'arm is over you,' promising His protective and judging power to the saints.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is where God's 'arm' is revealed sacramentally — through the ordinances and covenants, members experience God's saving and judging power. The promise that nations will 'wait upon me, and on mine arm shall they trust' is fulfilled as temple work expands to all peoples, and as the gospel is taken to every nation, kindred, tongue, and people.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is 'the arm of the Lord' (Isaiah 53:1) — the revelation of God's saving power. In the Incarnation, God's arm is made flesh and visible. The judgment mentioned in verse 5 is both the judgment Christ executes on the cross (where He judges sin) and the judgment that leads to the nations' salvation (John 12:31-32: 'Now is the judgment of this world...and I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me'). The isles waiting on God's arm is a picture of the world's anticipation of the Messiah—the waiting fulfilled in Christ.
commentary.application: For modern members, this verse teaches that God's power is nearer than we often believe. The phrase 'my righteousness is near' invites an immediacy of faith: God's justice is not a distant historical promise but a present reality. When members face injustice or suffering, they can claim this promise: God's arm of judgment and salvation is near. Second, the verse invites members to see themselves as part of the 'isles' waiting on God—whether that means waiting on God's guidance in a specific decision or waiting on the ultimate triumph of God's kingdom. Third, the verse teaches that God's judging power and saving power are the same: the God who judges oppression is the God who saves the oppressed. Modern members can trust that God's justice ultimately serves salvation, not mere condemnation. Finally, the promise that distant peoples will look to God's arm invites members to participate in fulfilling this promise: through missionary work and Christian witness, members reveal God's arm to a watching world.

text_kjv: Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look upon the earth beneath: for the heavens shall vanish away like smoke, and the earth shall wax old like a garment, and they that dwell therein shall die in like manner: but my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness shall not be abolished.

commentary.narrative: The final verse of this unit shifts from particular promise (Israel's restoration, the nations' response) to cosmic perspective. Isaiah commands the exiles to raise their eyes to the heavens and then look down to the earth—a gesture that seems to frame a universal panorama. But what the exiles see is devastating: the heavens themselves are temporary, they will 'vanish away like smoke,' and the earth will 'wax old like a garment,' worn thin and threadbare. This is radical. In ancient thought, the heavens were eternal, unchanging, the realm of the divine and the timeless. To declare that the heavens will vanish is to assert that nothing created is permanent—only God is permanent. Moreover, all who dwell on the earth will die in like manner: the transience of creation extends to all created beings. The logic is inexorable: if even the heavens fall away, why would the exiles despair over their current political catastrophe? This is a call to ultimate perspective: in a universe where even the heavens perish, the fall of Jerusalem is not the end of history but an episode within a larger pattern of divine judgment and restoration.
commentary.narrative_continued: But then the pivot: 'But my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness shall not be abolished.' Against the backdrop of universal transience, God's salvation and righteousness stand alone as eternal and unshakeable. This is eschatological theology of the highest order. The fate of the heavens and earth teaches a lesson about the true nature of reality: impermanence defines all creation, permanence defines only God. Therefore, faith grounded in God's salvation and righteousness is the only faith that will endure. The exiles are invited to stake their identity not on the permanence of earthly kingdoms or even the physical cosmos but on the permanence of God's covenant commitment. The DSS variant in verse 6 (minor consonantal variation in yiblu) does not alter meaning: both MT and 1QIsaᵃ attest to the earth's wearing out like a garment.

word_study.meaning: raise your eyes, lift up your gaze (from nesa, to lift, bear, carry); ʿeinayim means eyes but often symbolizes understanding, perception, awareness
word_study.significance: The command to 'lift up your eyes' is more than a physical gesture; it is a summons to shift perspective. This language appears throughout Isaiah (40:26, 'lift up your eyes on high'). The Covenant Rendering preserves the vividness of the physical command while suggesting the shift in spiritual perception.

word_study.meaning: heavens, sky, the upper realm where God dwells; in ancient cosmology, the eternal, unchanging sphere
word_study.significance: In ancient thought, shamayim represented permanence and divine order. To declare that shamayim will vanish is to make the most radical statement possible about the transience of creation. This is the foundation of later apocalyptic theology (2 Peter 3:12, where Peter cites this verse).

word_study.meaning: like smoke are dissolved/vanished (from melah, to dissolve, melt away); smoke (ʿashen) is the image of that which rises, disperses, and becomes invisible
word_study.significance: The comparison to smoke is vivid and tactile: once-solid matter becomes insubstantial, disperses, disappears. This image appears in Psalm 68:2, 'Let God arise, let his enemies be scattered: let them also that hate him flee before him' — enemies vanish like smoke before God. The Covenant Rendering preserves this image precisely.

word_study.meaning: like a garment will wear out, become obsolete (from balah, to wear out, grow old, become useless); beged is a garment, clothing
word_study.significance: The image of a garment wearing thin is more intimate than mere cosmic destruction. A garment that was once new and strong becomes frayed, threadbare, useless. This suggests not sudden annihilation but gradual wearing away. The earth will not explode but will age, decay, lose its vitality. This parallels Hebrews 1:11 ('they all shall wax old as doth a garment'), which cites this verse.

word_study.term_english: they that dwell therein shall die
word_study.meaning: and those who dwell in it in like manner shall die (from mut, to die, perish; yoshev means inhabitant, dweller)
word_study.significance: The logic is inexorable: just as the earth grows old and wears out, so all dwellers on it will age and die. This is a statement of universal mortality and transience. No being escapes death; no creature avoids the fate of the cosmos. This frames human life within a vast cosmic perspective.

word_study.term_english: My salvation shall be for ever
word_study.meaning: and my salvation forever will be (from yasha, to save, deliver; ʿolam means eternity, forever, the age)
word_study.significance: Against all transience, God's yeshuʿa (salvation) is established as eternal. Yeshuʿa is not merely the act of saving but the state of being saved, the condition of salvation. It is permanent, unchanging. The Covenant Rendering's 'will be forever' captures the permanence.

word_study.meaning: and my righteousness not will be broken/abolished (from chut, to break, cut off, destroy)
word_study.significance: Tzidkah (righteousness/justice) pairs with yeshuʿa to form a complementary unity: God's saving action and God's justice are both eternal. The verb chut (to break) emphasizes that God's righteousness will not be severed or interrupted. It stands forever, unchanging. This verse is cited in Matthew 24:35 and Mark 13:31, where Jesus applies it to His words: 'Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.'

cross_references.connection: 'Lift up your eyes on high, and behold who hath created these things, that bringeth out their host by number' — the same command to 'lift up your eyes' but there it is to perceive God's creative power; here to perceive creation's transience.

'They shall perish, but thou shalt endure: yea, all of them shall wax old like a garment; as a vesture shalt thou change them, and they shall be changed' — this Psalm applies Isaiah's language directly to God's permanence versus creation's transience.
Jesus says: 'Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away' — citing Isaiah 51:6 and applying it to the permanence of His teaching and covenant.

Peter describes the future dissolution of the heavens and earth: 'the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up' — an explicit parallel to Isaiah, describing the cosmic eschatology Isaiah introduced.

Modern revelation parallels Isaiah: 'And every corruptible thing...shall pass away; and all things shall become new, that my knowledge and glory may dwell upon all the earth' — the restoration of the cosmos through God's eternal righteousness.

John's vision: 'And I saw a new heaven and a new earth...And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying' — the fulfillment of Isaiah's promise that God's salvation endures when all else perishes.

commentary.historical_context: In the 6th century BCE, the exiles faced Babylonian culture and cosmology that framed the world as divided into eternal (the divine realm, the sacred) and temporary (the earthly realm). By declaring that even the heavens will vanish, Isaiah inverts this cosmology: only God is eternal; all creation, sacred and profane, is temporary. This was philosophically radical and religiously defiant. It means that Babylon's gods (Marduk, Shamash, Ishtar) who were thought to dwell in the heavens are themselves subject to transience. Only the God of Israel, the God who makes the promise of eternal salvation, transcends this cosmic decay. Moreover, the exiles' own suffering and exile—which seemed like a permanent catastrophe—is framed as an episode within a larger cosmic drama of transience and restoration. The fall of Jerusalem is not the triumph of Babylon's eternal order but a moment in the unfolding of God's eternal purpose.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 8:6 directly quotes this verse (Isaiah 51:6) as part of the nephite preservation of Isaiah. 3 Nephi 22:10 promises that mountains may depart and hills be removed, but God's kindness shall not depart. The Book of Mormon uses Isaiah's cosmic perspective to contextualize New World crises: just as the heavens will vanish but God's salvation endures, so the destruction of Nephite civilization does not negate God's covenants.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:23-24 applies Isaiah's eschatology to the Restoration: 'And then shall the Lord set his foot upon this mount, and it shall cleave in twain...And the Lord shall utter his voice...and there shall be a great hailstorm sent forth to destroy the crops of the earth. And the Lord shall utter his voice...And all things shall pass away.' This is the LDS understanding of Isaiah's cosmic eschatology. D&C 76:108-110 teaches that eternal life is dwelling in the presence of God forever—the fulfillment of the promise that God's salvation (yeshuʿa) is eternal.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple serves as a microcosm of the eternal: it is built to represent the cosmic order and to endure. The eternal covenants made in the temple (marriage sealing, priesthood ordination) are explicitly framed as 'for time and all eternity' — affirming that some things (God's covenants) are eternal, while temporary things (the mortal body, earthly kingdoms) will pass away. The temple teaches members to distinguish between the temporary and the eternal.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ embodies the promise of verse 6: His salvation is eternal ('Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever,' Hebrews 13:8). Moreover, Christ's words are explicitly identified with the permanence Isaiah promises here: 'Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away' (Matthew 24:35). Christ is the revelation of God's eternal righteousness — through His atonement, God's justice is demonstrated and made eternally efficacious. The cross is the intersection of time and eternity: in that moment, the eternal breaks into time, and what is done in time becomes eternally binding. Christ's resurrection is God's affirmation that death and decay do not have the final word; eternal life is possible through Him.
commentary.application: This verse offers profound perspective for modern members facing personal or communal crises. When circumstances feel catastrophic or permanent, Isaiah invites the reader to 'lift up your eyes' and perceive a larger reality: the things you are anxious about—political upheaval, economic uncertainty, even bodily illness and aging—are part of a larger pattern of cosmic transience. Nothing created is permanent; only God is permanent. Therefore, faith should rest not on circumstances but on God's eternal covenant. This is not escapism but realism: it teaches members to invest their deepest identity and hope not in the kingdom of this world but in the kingdom of God, which is eternal. Practically, this means that members can endure trials with greater peace when they remember that 'the heavens shall vanish away...but my salvation shall be for ever.' Second, the verse teaches members to distinguish between what deserves their ultimate loyalty (God's eternal covenant) and what is temporary (earthly success, social status, material possessions). A member facing job loss, illness, or social rejection can claim this promise: your ultimate security rests not on these temporary things but on God's eternal salvation. Finally, the verse invites members to align their own pursuit with the eternal: What choices build toward the permanent and eternal? What choices are built on temporary things that will pass away? This is the foundation of eternal perspective.

text_kjv: Hearken unto me, ye that know righteousness, the people in whose heart is my law; fear ye not the reproach of men, neither be ye afraid of their revilings.

commentary.narrative: This verse opens the third major summons in Isaiah 51 (following verses 1 and 4), now directed specifically to those who already possess righteousness and have God's law written upon their hearts. The prophet addresses a community that has internalized divine instruction—not merely external compliance, but the law residing in the heart. This anticipates Jeremiah's covenant promise (Jer. 31:33) and reflects the spiritual condition of the faithful remnant. The exhortation then pivots to the emotional challenge: do not fear human reproach or revilings. This command echoes the Servant's own resolution in Isaiah 50:7-8, where the Servant declares, 'I set my face like a flint,' unafraid of those who oppose him. The righteous in exile face mockery from their captors and perhaps from their own community who question whether restoration is possible. Isaiah calls them to courage grounded not in their own strength but in their alignment with God's law.

word_study.meaning: To know righteousness goes beyond intellectual awareness—it means to possess, practice, and embody right relationship with God. The verb yada (to know) carries relational force; these are people who have entered into and experienced divine justice.
word_study.significance: This phrase identifies the audience not by ethnic membership alone but by spiritual practice. In exile, the knowing of righteousness becomes the marker of true Israel.

word_study.meaning: Instruction, teaching, covenant word. The suffix 'my' (God's law, not human law) emphasizes divine ownership and authority.
word_study.significance: The law written in the heart (Jer. 31:33) is the deep internalization of covenant. In the wilderness and exile, this became Israel's portable, interior strength—no temple needed, only obedience written on the heart.

word_study.meaning: Shame, disgrace, scorn—the social injury of mockery or contempt. Often associated with the shame of defeat or captivity.
word_study.significance: For exiled Israel, reproach was existential: their God had not rescued them, their city lay in ruins. Enemies used their captivity as evidence of divine abandonment. Isaiah's command attacks this shame at its root.

cross_references.connection: The Servant's prior resolution not to fear revilers directly informs the command here; the righteous are called to embody the Servant's courage.
The new covenant promise that God's law will be written in the heart directly parallels 'the people in whose heart is my law.'
The psalmist's meditation on God's law dwelling in the heart reflects the same integration of instruction and identity.
Joseph Smith's revelation echoes this theme: endurance of mockery and affliction is overcome by knowing one belongs to God, not to the world's judgment.

commentary.historical_context: Exiled Israel in Babylon faced not only material deprivation but psychological warfare. Babylonian inscriptions and cuneiform records show that victorious empires deliberately humiliated conquered peoples, using mockery as a tool of subjugation. Captive peoples were often forbidden from practicing their religious rites; their gods were portrayed as defeated. For Isaiah's audience, the 'revilings' of Babylonian overlords or assimilated Jews represented existential threat to identity. The prophet's command to disregard these revilers required a radical reorientation of shame: the shame belongs not to Israel but to the powers that mock. By anchoring identity to internal covenant (law in the heart), Isaiah offers protection that external circumstances cannot touch.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Jacob 4:10 emphasizes the law of God written in the heart as the foundation of strength against external opposition. Moroni 7:33-34 echoes the call to fear God rather than men.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 98:45-48 promises protection to the faithful when they endure revilings for righteousness' sake. The pattern of internal strength versus external shame recurs throughout Restoration scripture.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The internalization of God's law is foundational to temple covenants; the endowment teaches that external opposition cannot touch the righteous who have received and committed to sacred ordinances.
