commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ embodies the righteous one who knows perfect righteousness and has God's law not merely in heart but perfectly integrated with His nature. In His passion, He endured revilings from enemies and mockers (Matt. 27:39-44, Luke 23:39) without flinching from His mission or identity. His command to His disciples—'Fear them not' (Matt. 10:26, 28)—draws directly from this Isaianic tradition. The righteous in Isaiah 51 prefigure those who follow Christ, sustained by an internal covenant rather than external validation.
commentary.application: In contemporary covenant life, members face reproach for religious conviction—whether from secular culture, family members, or institutions. Isaiah's call invokes a radical internal reorientation: your identity is not determined by others' mockery. Your law is written in your heart through baptism, confirmation, and continued obedience. The revilings of the world cannot penetrate the spiritual reality of your covenants. This verse calls us to examine whether our faith is merely external conformity or internalized law—do we know righteousness because we practice it, or do we merely know about it? The test comes in moments of reproach: does your internal covenant sustain you, or do you collapse into shame?

text_kjv: For the moth shall eat them up like a garment, and the worm shall eat them like wool: but my righteousness shall be for ever, and my salvation from generation to generation.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah now gives the reason for the command not to fear: the enemies who revile God's people are temporary and perishable, while God's righteousness is eternal. The image is visceral—the moth and worm consuming cloth, leaving nothing but holes and decay. This is not gentle decay; it is the dissolution of what seems substantial. The Hebrew word for moth (ʿāsh) and worm (sās) evoke creeping, invisible destruction. An army, an empire, a reputation can seem overwhelming until we grasp that they are subject to time and entropy. But God's righteousness (tsedāqâ) and salvation (yĕshûʿâ) stand forever, enduring across generations. The verse echoes Isaiah 50:9, where the Servant declares that his adversaries will grow old and wear out like a garment. Here that same logic is extended to comfort exiled Israel: the oppressive power that seems so absolute will crumble, but the God who sustains the righteous is everlasting. This is not abstract theology—it is political realism grounded in covenant. Empires fall. Righteousness remains.

word_study.meaning: Small creatures that consume fabric through microscopic, relentless consumption. In ancient economies where cloth was precious (dyed wool, linen garments), moths and worms represented real economic threat.
word_study.significance: The choice of these creatures is deliberately undignified—oppressive powers are reduced to the level of insects. The metaphor also suggests that destruction is quiet, inevitable, and irreversible. The Covenant Rendering captures this: enemies 'will be eaten' (passive voice), emphasizing their helplessness in the face of time.

word_study.meaning: Right relationship, justice, vindication, saving action. Not abstract morality but God's faithful action in history to uphold His covenant.
word_study.significance: God's tsidqa is not merely a quality but an active power. It 'shall be forever'—God's commitment to justice does not age, wear out, or become obsolete. This is the counterweight to the moth-eaten garment of human opposition.

word_study.meaning: Deliverance, rescue, victory. The outcome of God's righteous action—when God acts in justice, salvation results.
word_study.significance: This is not individual spiritual salvation in the later Christian sense, but corporate, historical deliverance. For exiled Israel, yeshua means the end of captivity and restoration to the land. The parallelism (righteousness || salvation) shows these are two aspects of one saving action.

word_study.term_english: for ever... from generation to generation
word_study.meaning: Without end, perpetual continuity. Dorim (generations, plural of dor) emphasizes succession and endurance across time.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering renders this 'to all generations,' capturing the sense of unbroken continuity. What God commits in righteousness He sustains across the generations—a promise with teeth for people in exile who fear their line will be cut off.

cross_references.connection: The Servant's declaration that adversaries will wear out like a garment directly parallels this verse; here Isaiah extends the promise to all the righteous.
Flesh is grass that withers, but God's word stands forever—the same contrast between human temporality and divine permanence.
Do not fret because of evildoers, for they will wither like the grass—same metaphor of enemy temporality versus righteous endurance.
The New Testament applies Isaiah's word-stands-forever theme to the gospel: all flesh fades, but God's word remains.
The revelation reiterates that God's word stands while all human opposition passes away.

commentary.historical_context: The image of moth-eaten garments would have resonated powerfully in a textile-dependent economy. Archaeological evidence from the Levant shows that garments were expensive, carefully preserved, and subject to pest damage—particularly wool (which the verse explicitly mentions), highly prized throughout the ancient Mediterranean. An exiled people watching their fine garments deteriorate in captivity would recognize the metaphor: just as the fine things of the old world crumble, so too will the oppressive system holding them captive. Ironically, Babylon was renowned for its textiles, yet even the grandest Babylonian cloth would eventually succumb to time and decay. The metaphor is thus both humble (drawn from household experience) and subversive (suggesting that even imperial power is subject to entropy).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 46:7-13 uses military metaphor rather than natural decay, but conveys the same principle: those who fight against God's righteous cause will eventually be defeated, while the righteous endure. Moroni's title of liberty embodies this conviction.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:4-7 establishes that God's work is eternal while all opposition is temporary: 'The mysteries of God shall be unfolded unto them, in those days which shall come unto them.' The righteous inherit all things when oppositions crumble.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment teaches that the plan of salvation is eternal and unalterable, while earthly opposition is ephemeral. The righteous who possess the tokens and signs are already aligned with eternal truth.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the embodiment of God's eternal righteousness and salvation. While His enemies seemed triumphant at the crucifixion—the garment-dividing soldiers, the mocking chief priests, the decaying Pharisaic establishment—Christ's resurrection vindicated eternal righteousness over temporal power. The moth-eaten metaphor applies precisely: the religious and political structures that opposed Him crumbled (Jerusalem fell within 40 years), while His saving work endures forever. His salvation extends from generation to generation (Matt. 28:20: 'I am with you always, even unto the end of the world').
commentary.application: Modern members face institutional and cultural powers that seem overwhelming: secular governments hostile to religious conviction, powerful media networks, educational systems dismissive of faith. Isaiah's promise reframes the situation: these powers, however vast, are moth-eaten garments—destined for decay. Your faith, by contrast, is connected to eternal righteousness and salvation that endures beyond all generational cycles. The practical implication: do not fear the temporal power of the world. Do not compromise conviction because current institutions seem permanent. Do not assume that what dominates today will dominate tomorrow. Instead, align yourself with what endures. This requires patience—watching for how God unfolds His purposes across generations—but it offers incomparable peace.

text_kjv: Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD; awake, as in the ancient days, in the generations of old. Art thou not it that hath cut Rahab, and wounded the dragon?

commentary.narrative: Isaiah now shifts register dramatically, moving from comfort to call and from promise to plea. The triple imperative 'Awake, awake' (with the third 'awake' connected to 'put on strength') is a call to God Himself—specifically to God's arm, the instrument of deliverance. The 'arm of the LORD' is Isaiah's recurring image for God's saving power (cf. 40:10, 53:1). The prophet urges God to act as He did in the ancient days, when His power was visibly manifest at creation and the exodus. The references to Rahab and the dragon are drawn from ancient Near Eastern mythology—Rahab was the primordial chaos monster, defeated by the divine warrior in the mythic combat that preceded creation. By invoking these names, Isaiah is doing something theologically sophisticated: he is not endorsing polytheism or pagan cosmology, but rather 'historicizing' the myth. The cosmic battle against chaos becomes identified with the concrete, historical act of the Red Sea crossing, when God defeated the waters (which represent chaos and imperial opposition) and rescued His people. This move reveals Isaiah's theological strategy: the God who controls creation is the same God who controls history. If He could cut Rahab in pieces at creation, He can cut the chains of Babylon in exile. The verb 'cut' (machatsabat, from chatsab, to hew, split) implies violent, complete destruction—no compromise, no negotiation. The same power must awaken now.

word_study.meaning: To wake up, to arouse, to rise and act. The verb is imperativus urgency—a command, not a request.
word_study.significance: The doubling and tripling of 'awake' expresses intense urgency and frustration. It is as if the prophet is shaking God awake: 'Your people are in captivity; your power seems dormant. Act!' This anthropomorphic language (as if God could sleep) is theologically bold—it expresses the exilic community's sense of God's absence.

word_study.meaning: Clothe yourself with strength, arm yourself with might. The image is of putting on armor or garments of power.
word_study.significance: God's strength (ʿôz) is not diminished; rather, the prayer asks God to clothe Himself with it visibly, to make manifest the power that is always His. This parallels the exhortation in verse 7 to the righteous to stand in their strength—here the prophet calls God to stand in His.

word_study.meaning: The primordial chaos monster of ancient Near Eastern cosmology, defeated by the divine warrior. Rahab represents cosmic opposition to God's order—not a separate god, but a force of chaos that must be subdued. In later biblical tradition (cf. Psalm 87:4, Isa. 30:7), Rahab becomes a poetic name for Egypt, linking the mythic battle to the historical exodus.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering translator notes that this is 'not polytheism but poetic appropriation'—Isaiah takes the language of cosmic mythology and applies it to history. The theological point: God's power over chaos is the same power deployed against Egypt and (by extension) against Babylon. The exiled community would hear Rahab and think 'Egypt,' then realize the prophet is saying: 'The same God who defeated Egypt can defeat Babylon.'

word_study.meaning: Pierced or wounded the sea monster. Tannin (dragon/serpent/sea creature) is another mythological chaos figure, often associated with the sea (yam). The verb mecholelet (from chalal, to pierce or wound) indicates not final destruction but wounding, weakening.
word_study.significance: The parallelism with 'cut Rahab in pieces' suggests these are two aspects of the same event—the subduing of chaos. In Isaiah's historical-mythical synthesis, this is the crossing of the Red Sea, where the waters (tannin, the dragon of the deep) are wounded and parted. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this text identically, underlining its antiquity and importance.

cross_references.connection: Another invocation of God's arm coming with might; the arm of the LORD is the recurring image for God's visible, historical power.
The question 'Who hath believed our report? and to whom is the arm of the LORD revealed?' echoes here; the arm must be revealed in power.
The Song of Moses celebrates God's arm stretched out; here Isaiah evokes the same image of the arm as instrument of deliverance.
A parallel passage where the psalmist invokes God's ancient power over the sea dragon (leviathan) as grounds for current deliverance.
In the Apocalypse, the cosmic war against the dragon (Satan) is the continuation of the ancient mythic combat; the Lamb shares in this war.

commentary.historical_context: The mythology of Rahab and the chaos dragon was widespread in the ancient Near East. Babylonian creation myth (the Enuma Elish) depicts Marduk defeating Tiamat, the primordial chaos goddess, to establish order. Canaanite texts (Ugaritic Baal cycle) depict the god Baal defeating Yam (the sea) to establish cosmic order. Isaiah, addressing an exiled community in Babylon, would have been aware of these mythological frameworks—his audience knew Babylonian creation mythology. Yet Isaiah radically reinterprets these myths: he does not deny the power of chaos or the reality of the mythological combat, but he identifies the victor not with Marduk or any Babylonian god, but with the God of Israel. More strikingly, he identifies the mythic battle with the historical exodus. This is theological genius: it says to the exiles, 'Your God is not inferior to Marduk; He is the one who controls creation and history. Babylon celebrates Marduk's victory over chaos; but we know that it was the LORD who defeated chaos at the Red Sea. Therefore, He can defeat Babylon.' The archaeological and textual evidence shows that Judean scribes during the exile would have absorbed Babylonian intellectual culture; Isaiah's reframing of Babylonian mythology as evidence for Yahweh's supremacy is a sophisticated apologetic move.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 22:15-16 invokes God's power to subdue enemies and bring about deliverance; the principle of God's arm being stretched out in power recurs throughout the Book of Mormon. Alma 36:2-3 portrays God's power 'to redeem' His people from captivity.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:16-20 recounts the cosmic war against Satan (the dragon) as an ancient and ongoing conflict; the righteous are called to align with God's power. D&C 76:26-27 identifies Satan as the one cast out in the pre-mortal conflict, echoing the Rahab/dragon imagery.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The endowment dramatizes the cosmic conflict between light and darkness; the temple teaches that God's power prevails over opposition. The use of ancient mythological language in Isaiah is paralleled in the temple's use of symbolic and mythic vocabulary to convey spiritual realities.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the embodiment of God's arm and the one who defeats the dragon. In Revelation 12:7-9, Michael and his angels war against the dragon (Satan) and cast him out—a war in which Christ is the ultimate protagonist. Christ's resurrection is the definitive moment when God's arm is 'awoken' and extended to defeat death, the final chaos. The Gospels depict Christ calming the sea (Mark 4:39)—a direct echo of God subduing the waters/dragon. The casting out of demons, the resurrection of the dead, the final judgment—all are acts of the divine arm extended through Christ. When Isaiah calls on God's arm to awaken, he prophesies Christ's coming as the full manifestation of God's power over all opposition.
commentary.application: In seasons when the righteous feel oppressed or when God's power seems hidden, this verse calls us to remember: God's arm has not weakened; it has simply seemed to slumber. Prayer, particularly in corporate worship and covenant contexts (the temple, fast and testimony meetings), functions as the call to awaken—not because God does not know our plight, but because we must align ourselves with His power through faith and petition. Modern members may feel that secular powers, institutional hostility, or personal oppression represents an overwhelming chaos. This verse teaches a radically different perspective: the same God who ordered creation and defeated the greatest empires can order your circumstances and deliver you. But the delivery may require waiting, watching, and calling upon Him with the urgency and faith of the exiled remnant. The application is not passive (waiting for God to act) but active (crying out to align ourselves with His power, knowing that He will act in His time).

text_kjv: Art thou not it which hath dried the sea, the waters of the great deep; that hath made the depths of the sea a way for the ransomed to pass over?

commentary.narrative: This verse provides the historical concretization of the mythological language in verse 9. The prophet answers his own question: Yes, you are the one who dried the sea at the exodus. The 'great deep' (tehôm rabbâ) refers to the primordial waters of chaos, which in the exodus narrative becomes the Red Sea. By drying the sea (a direct reference to Exodus 14), Isaiah collapses the mythic time of creation into the historical time of liberation. This is not merely poetic flourish; it is theological strategy. For exiles in Babylon facing another empire, Isaiah is saying: the God who defeated chaos in creation and Egypt in history is unchanged. He can and will defeat Babylon. The phrase 'the depths of the sea a way for the ransomed' is crucial. The Hebrew word for ransomed (ge'ulîm, from the root go'ēl, kinsman-redeemer) carries covenantal weight. The ransomed are those bought back, redeemed by kinship and legal obligation. God does not merely save them; He ransoms them as a kinsman redeems a relative from slavery. The depths of the sea, which would normally be impassable and deadly, become a way (derekh)—a road for passage. This recalls the crossing of the Red Sea in Exodus 14:21-22, where the waters are divided and Israel passes through on dry ground. The miracle is not merely the drying of water, but the transformation of an obstacle into a pathway. For the exiled Judeans, this is profound hope: the waters that separate them from return (the literal geography of the journey from Babylon to Judah) will be made into a pathway. More broadly, the obstacles to redemption—whether political, military, or geographic—are not insurmountable to the God whose arm dried the sea.

word_study.meaning: To make desolate, to dry up, to make a wasteland. The verb charab (to be desolate, dry) emphasizes the complete removal of the water's obstacle.
word_study.significance: The verb choice—not merely 'parted' or 'divided' but 'dried'—emphasizes the completeness and permanence of God's action. It is not a temporary miracle but a transformation of nature itself.

word_study.meaning: The primordial waters, the abyss, cosmic chaos. Tehom is the Hebrew word for the chaotic waters of creation (Gen. 1:2). Rabbâ (great) intensifies the magnitude.
word_study.significance: By using tehom (the creation word for chaos), Isaiah identifies the Red Sea with the primordial chaos. The exodus becomes a recapitulation of creation—God ordering chaos. This mythic-historical fusion is the key to Isaiah's theology of hope.

word_study.meaning: The redeemed, those bought back. From the root go'ēl (kinsman-redeemer), the term carries the legal and covenantal sense of redemption through kinship obligation. In Israelite law, a kinsman could redeem a family member sold into slavery.
word_study.significance: This is not abstract spiritual salvation but familial, covenantal redemption. God acts as kinsman, bound by relation and law to redeem His people. The Covenant Rendering's choice of 'ransomed' (rather than merely 'redeemed') captures this transactional aspect—someone pays a price to free the captive.

word_study.term_english: a way for the ransomed to pass over
word_study.meaning: A path, road, or way for crossing. The verb ʿābar (to pass, cross, go over) emphasizes the active movement of the redeemed.
word_study.significance: The depths (maʿamaqê yam) that normally swallow ships become a derekh—a navigable, purposeful way. This transforms the obstacle into the very means of liberation. For exiles, this promised they would not merely be freed but given a way to return.

cross_references.connection: The historical miracle of the sea dividing and Israel crossing on dry ground; this verse is the direct fulfillment Isaiah invokes.
The Song of Moses celebrates God's right hand and power in the exodus; Isaiah echoes this same tradition of God's strength.
Another passage where Isaiah recalls the same miracle: 'Thus saith the LORD, which maketh a way in the sea,' directly parallel to 51:10.
A later recitation of the exodus miracle in prayer: 'The sea thou didst divide before them, so that they went through the midst of the sea on the dry land.'
Paul identifies the exodus as a type of baptism; the passing through the sea becomes the pattern for Christian redemption.

commentary.historical_context: The Dead Sea Scrolls (1QIsaᵃ) preserve this verse identically to the Masoretic Text, indicating no variant reading—the text's antiquity and stability are assured. Archaeologically, while the precise location and nature of the Red Sea crossing remain debated, Egyptian inscriptions and Levantine geography confirm that the Egyptians deployed their chariotry in pursuit of escaped slaves, and that the Reed Sea/Red Sea region was navigable and dangerous. The miracle of drying the sea would have been understood not as scientific impossibility but as unprecedented divine intervention—the natural becomes the supernatural. For exiles in Babylon, the memory of the exodus would have been kept alive through oral tradition, prayer, and the Torah. Reciting these narratives in captivity was an act of resistance and hope: our God did this once; He will do it again. The Babylonian exile itself (586-539 BCE) lasted about 48 years; Cyrus's edict permitting return (539 BCE) fulfilled Isaiah's prophecy in a manner that seemed like a second exodus. Some scholars note that the journey from Babylon to Judah would have required crossing rivers and potentially the Euphrates—again, the imagery of 'crossing waters' would be literally relevant to the exiles' anticipated return.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 4:2 invokes the same principle: 'Let us be faithful in keeping the commandments of the Lord; for behold he is mightier than all the earth. Why then should we murmur against the Lord? Let us yield to him, for he is able to do all things according to his will.' The exodus pattern is recapitulated in Lehi's family crossing the wilderness to reach the promised land.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:68-71 promises a gathering of the elect and their return to Zion, using language reminiscent of the exodus and the promised pathway. The principle of God making a way through obstacles recurs in Doctrine and Covenants.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The ritual crossing of waters in baptism (often depicted as entering the waters and coming forth) echoes the Red Sea crossing pattern. The temple endowment teaches that God makes a way for the righteous through obstacles and trials; the veil represents the final passage into the divine presence.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate kinsman-redeemer (go'ēl) who ransoms His people through His sacrifice. The waters through which the righteous pass foreshadow baptism in Christ's name. In 1 Corinthians 10:1-4, Paul identifies the exodus crossing with baptism into Christ and eating the spiritual meat and drinking the spiritual drink (Christ). The sea that drowns the enemies of Israel becomes, in the New Testament, the waters of baptism into which the Christian is baptized to die to sin and rise to new life. Christ's resurrection is the ultimate 'drying of the sea'—the defeat of death's obstacle and the opening of a pathway for the ransomed to pass into eternal life.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse speaks to the reality of obstacles that seem impassable: addiction, grief, family breakdown, institutional hostility, vocational dead-ends. Isaiah's theology teaches that these obstacles are not the final reality; they are the 'sea' that God transforms into a pathway. The ransom has already been paid through Christ; you have been bought back at a price. The way is being made, even if you cannot yet see it. The application requires faith and patience. The exiles had to trust Isaiah's word and maintain covenant practice (circumcision, dietary laws, prayer) in a foreign land for decades before the pathway to return actually opened. Modern members similarly must maintain covenants and faith in times when the obstacle seems only to be deepening. But the promise is sure: God's arm has already dried the sea; the way for the ransomed is being prepared. Your part is to position yourself as one of the ransomed—redeemed through Christ, aligned with His covenant—and trust that the obstacles will become the pathway.

text_kjv: Therefore the redeemed of the LORD shall return, and come with singing unto Zion; and everlasting joy shall be upon their head: they shall obtain gladness and joy; and sorrow and mourning shall flee away.

commentary.narrative: This verse is the logical and emotional culmination of verses 9-10. Because the LORD has dried the sea and made a pathway, therefore the ransomed shall return. The particle 'therefore' (no'am in Hebrew causality) marks the inevitable outcome: the victory of God's arm necessitates the liberation of His people. The verse now shifts from the mythic-historical past (verses 9-10) to the promised future. The redeemed do not merely escape; they return with singing. This is not grim survival but joyful homecoming. The Hebrew pelut means 'those who escaped' or 'the escaped,' but here more specifically 'the redeemed,' those bought back. They return (yashubuv, will turn back) to Zion—not merely to Judah geographically, but to Zion as the covenant center, the dwelling place of God's presence. 'With singing' (birenah) indicates joy so complete that it demands vocal expression. In Hebrew thought, singing is the proper response to deliverance; it is the language of the redeemed (cf. the Song of Moses in Exodus 15, the Song of Deborah in Judges 5). The verse is nearly identical to Isaiah 35:10, forming an intentional echo across the prophecy. This repetition signals that the promise is not casual—it is woven into the very structure of the prophecy. Everlasting joy (simchat ʿôlâm) shall crown their heads (ʿal roʾšâm)—joy becomes their diadems, their marks of status. They shall 'attain' or 'overtake' (yaśśîgû, from nasag, to reach, overtake, obtain) gladness and joy. The verbs suggest that joy is something pursued and finally caught—after the long night of exile, the fugitive reaches and grasps the happiness that has eluded them. Finally, sorrow and sighing flee (nasû yagon venaḥah). The verb nasû (to flee, take flight) uses the same root as the earlier reference to 'redeemed' escaping/fleeing Egypt. Now it is reversed: not the people fleeing, but sorrow and mourning fleeing from the redeemed. The exile's grief will not linger; it will not haunt the return. This is comprehensive healing.

word_study.meaning: Those ransomed by the LORD, those bought back from captivity. Padah (to ransom) is related to but distinct from ga'al (to redeem as kinsman); it emphasizes the transactional aspect of redemption through payment.
word_study.significance: The possession form ('redeemed of the LORD') indicates that these people belong to God by virtue of His ransom payment. In the covenant, God has purchased them; they are His acquired possession.

word_study.meaning: To turn back, to return, to come again. The verb carries the sense of completing a cycle—what was lost or taken is recovered.
word_study.significance: This is not escape or flight but return—restoration to the original place and status. For exiles, it means not merely freedom but homecoming.

word_study.meaning: With shout, cry of joy, singing. Renah denotes the sound of exultation and celebration.
word_study.significance: The sonic quality—the audible expression of joy—is crucial. The redeemed do not return silently; they make known their deliverance. This public, vocal celebration is the appropriate response to God's mighty acts.

word_study.term_english: everlasting joy shall be upon their head
word_study.term_original: שִׂמְחַת עוֹלָם עַל־רֹאשָׁם (simchat ʿôlâm ʿal roʾšâm)
word_study.meaning: Everlasting, permanent joy shall be their crown, their distinguishing feature. The joy is ʿôlâm (eternal, perpetual), not momentary.
word_study.significance: Joy becomes a permanent condition, not a transient emotion. It marks their status before God and the world. The image of joy as something worn 'on the head' (as crowns are) elevates joy to a sign of triumph and honor.

word_study.meaning: To reach, overtake, attain gladness and joy. Sason (gladness, exultation) and simcha (joy, celebration) are paired for emphasis. The verb nasag suggests pursuit and capture.
word_study.significance: The exiles pursue joy as one pursues a fleeing enemy or a desired prize. After exile, they finally overtake and grasp the happiness that is rightfully theirs. This active pursuit and attainment underscores the reality and solidity of the joy—it is not imaginary but achieved.

word_study.term_english: sorrow and mourning shall flee away
word_study.meaning: Shall flee, take flight—sorrow and sighing. Yagon is deep sorrow, grief; anacha is sighing, lamentation.
word_study.significance: The reversal is complete: where the redeemed formerly fled (natsu, from the same root) from oppression, now sorrow and sighing flee from them. The grammatical reversal mirrors the spiritual reversal—what was victim becomes victor.

cross_references.connection: This verse is nearly identical to 35:10, forming an intentional echo that signals the prophecy's internal coherence and the certainty of the promise.
The Song of Moses celebrates deliverance with singing, the pattern Isaiah invokes for the return from Babylon.
A post-exilic psalm celebrating the return: 'When the LORD turned again the captivity of Zion, we were like them that dream. Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing.'
Peter applies the promise to the Christian's eternal inheritance: an inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you.

The apocalyptic vision of God's tabernacle with men: 'And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain.'

commentary.historical_context: The 1QIsaᵃ (Dead Sea Scrolls) preserves this verse identically to the Masoretic Text, confirming its stable transmission. Historically, Cyrus's edict (539 BCE) did permit the return of exiles; the book of Ezra records the actual return and rebuilding of the temple. Archaeological evidence from Judean sites shows a resettlement in the late 6th century BCE. However, the return was not the triumphant homecoming that apocalyptic prophecy might suggest—the exiles faced opposition, economic hardship, and the rebuilt temple was modest compared to Solomon's. This gap between Isaiah's triumphant vision and the sober historical reality has generated scholarly debate. Some scholars see this as unfulfilled prophecy; others argue that Isaiah's vision was spiritually fulfilled even if the historical return was modest; still others see the prophecy as pointing beyond the first return to an eschatological, messianic restoration. The Church of Jesus Christ would understand this verse as having multiple fulfillments: the literal return from Babylon, the spiritual return of individual believers through Christ, and the ultimate gathering of Zion in the latter days.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 8:11 quotes this verse directly, applying it to the latter-day gathering of Israel. The Book of Mormon understands Isaiah's return of the redeemed as pointing to the restoration and gathering under the Latter-day Restoration.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:24-25 promises that 'those who are in the resurrection of the righteous shall inherit the kingdom and are filled with everlasting joy.' D&C 113 applies this verse to the gathering of Israel in the latter days.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple symbolism of return and restoration is central to Latter-day Saint theology. Members return to the temple for eternal covenants; the endowment dramatizes the return to God's presence, which is the ultimate version of this return to Zion. The phrase 'everlasting joy' echoes temple language of eternal exaltation.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the one who purchases the redeemed with His blood (1 Pet. 1:18-19); He is the ransomed redeemer. The return to Zion in this verse foreshadows the believer's return to God through Christ. Revelation 14:1-5 depicts the 144,000 standing with the Lamb on Mount Zion, singing a new song—the prophetic vision of the redeemed singing before God. Christ Himself was the first to return from exile (from death), and His resurrection opened the pathway for all the redeemed to return to the presence of God.
commentary.application: For covenant members navigating loss, grief, or spiritual exile, this verse is a charter of hope. It promises that return is not merely possible but inevitable for those who maintain covenant. The return will not be grim survival but joyful restoration. More, the joy will not be temporary—it shall be everlasting, permanent, a defining feature of your renewed life. The application invites us to ask: Where am I in exile? Where have I been taken captive by fear, addiction, false teaching, or circumstance? Who is my redeemer? The answer: Christ, who has paid the ransom (His blood), opened the pathway, and promises the return. The path back requires action (repentance, covenant renewal, faith), but the destination is sure. When we experience moments of joy in recovery, in returned faith, in reconciliation—these are foretastes of the everlasting joy promised to the redeemed. The application also includes corporate dimension: as members, we participate in the gathering of Israel, the literal and spiritual return of God's people to covenant and Zion. This may be through missionary work, family history work, or the building of temples—all modes of facilitating the return of the redeemed to their covenant God.

text_kjv: I, even I, am he that comforteth you: who art thou, that thou shouldest be afraid of a man that shall die, and of the son of man which shall be made as grass;

commentary.narrative: After the rousing call to God to awaken (verses 9-10) and the promised return of the redeemed with singing (verse 11), the prophet now returns to the comfort of direct address. God Himself speaks, breaking into the prophecy with the emphatic double declaration 'I, I am He' (anokhi anokhi hu). This is the divine self-identification formula, asserting God's unique, absolute being and authority. The doubling (anokhi anokhi) is extraordinary emphasis, as if God is saying, 'Listen carefully: I am the one, and there is no other.' This echoes Deuteronomy 32:39, where Moses declares God's absoluteness. God's role is 'to comfort you' (menachem). The verb nacham (to comfort, to console, to repent, to change one's mind) carries the sense of changing a tragic situation—not mere sympathy but active consolation that transforms circumstance. In the context of exiled Israel, God is the one who transforms their captivity into restoration. Then God poses a rhetorically devastating question: Who are you to fear mortals? The question assumes the answer: you are the redeemed of the eternal God. Therefore, your fear of mortals is disproportionate, irrational, unworthy. The phrase 'a man that shall die' (enosh yamutvt) emphasizes human mortality and frailty. Enosh (from a root meaning 'frail, weak') is chosen deliberately to stress humanity's weakness. Similarly, 'son of man' (ben adam) is made 'as grass' (kasir, from chatsir). The image recalls Isaiah 40:6-8, where all flesh is grass and withers. God's rebuke cuts to the heart: you are afraid of something temporary. The man dies. The grass withers. Your fear is misplaced. You should fear God, who endures forever. This is not callous dismissal of human suffering or oppression; rather, it is ultimate perspective. The oppressor seems powerful today, but he is subject to time and death. God is eternal. Therefore, align your fear (reverence, ultimate concern) with the eternal, not the temporal. The verse thus completes Isaiah's logic: God's arm is not sleeping (verse 9); He dried the sea (verse 10); He will return the redeemed (verse 11); therefore (verse 12), do not fear mortals. You belong to the eternal God.

word_study.meaning: The emphatic doubled first person ('I, I myself') with the demonstrative 'he/it,' affirming identity and existence with absolute force. This is a divine self-identification formula.
word_study.significance: The doubling is not poetic redundancy but theological assertion of divine supremacy and exclusivity. God alone is the comforter; no other power—no Babylonian god, no earthly king, no false hope—can fulfill this role. The Covenant Rendering notes the 'expanded meaning' connecting this to Deuteronomy 32:39, where Moses asserts God's unique power to wound and heal.

word_study.meaning: One who comforts, consoles, changes the situation from tragedy to solace. The verb nacham (to comfort, console, repent, relent) is active—it transforms circumstance.
word_study.significance: God's comfort is not passive sympathy but active intervention. In exile, this means God changes Israel's condition from captivity to freedom. For individuals, it means transformation of sorrow into consolation. The participle form (menachem) emphasizes God's ongoing, habitual role as comforter.

word_study.meaning: A mortal man who dies, finite human being subject to death. Enosh (from a root meaning weak, frail, mortal) specifically denotes human fragility.
word_study.significance: The deliberate choice of enosh (rather than ish, man, or geber, mighty man) emphasizes weakness and mortality. God is asking: Why fear that which is inherently weak and temporary? The Covenant Rendering translator's note highlights that enosh 'emphasizes human frailty.'

word_study.term_english: son of man which shall be made as grass
word_study.meaning: A human being (son of Adam, descendant of humanity) who is appointed/given the nature of grass. Chatsir (grass) withers and dies; yinathen (will be given/appointed) indicates that frailty is the inevitable condition.
word_study.significance: The parallelism with Isaiah 40:6-8 is clear: 'All flesh is as grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth, but the word of our God shall stand for ever.' God is asking the exiles to see their oppressors sub specie aeternitatis—under the aspect of eternity. From that perspective, the oppressor is grass, and their threat is transient.

cross_references.connection: Moses' assertion of God's uniqueness: 'See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god with me.' Isaiah echoes this formula of exclusive divine power.
The earlier passage that establishes the metaphor of grass withering; verse 12 applies this image to the oppressor, reinforcing the theme of human transience versus God's eternity.
The Servant's prior resolution to fear God rather than revilers; verse 12 extends this same call to the community.
A parallel exhortation: 'Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help. His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish.'

Peter applies the grass metaphor: 'For all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass. The grass withereth, and the flower thereof falleth away, but the word of the Lord endureth for ever.'

commentary.historical_context: The 1QIsaᵃ (Dead Sea Scrolls) preserves this verse identically to the Masoretic Text, confirming textual stability. The Covenant Rendering translator notes the 'doubled anokhi (I, I)' as 'intensely emphatic,' underlining that scribal traditions across centuries recognized the theological weight of this doubling. Historically, for exiled Judeans in Babylon, the human authorities they feared were real and powerful: Babylonian kings with vast military resources, their local oppressors, and the assimilationist pressures to abandon faith. The verb yinathen (will be given/made) in the phrase 'will be made as grass' uses a form that suggests destiny or appointment—it is written into the nature of things that mortals shall wither. This would have been countercultural rhetoric in Babylon, where the king (Nabonidus, later Cyrus) claimed immortal glory and cosmic significance. Isaiah's message undermines this propaganda: your king is grass; your kingdom will wither; the God of Israel alone endures.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 9:7-9 emphasizes that death (the temporal power) has been overcome through Christ; the righteous need not fear death or those who can kill the body. The principle of not fearing mortals is woven throughout the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 3:7-8 reprises this principle: 'And thus with the sword and by the blood of them that are the Lord's chosen, he marked a way for the righteous to go forth, and by the power of the mighty arm of the Lord shall Satan be removed, and the last shall be first.' The emphasis is on God's power, not mortal power.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that the powers of darkness and mortal opposition are ultimately subject to God's priesthood authority. The ritual progression from the lone and dreary world to the presence of God enacts the spiritual reality that Isaiah teaches: do not fear mortals; fear God and alignment with Him.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the ultimate manifestation of God saying, 'I, I am He' (John 8:24, 8:58, 18:6). Christ embodies the comfort of God—He is called the Wonderful Counselor (Isaiah 9:6), and His presence comforts the grieving and fearful throughout the Gospels. In Gethsemane and on the cross, Christ faced ultimate human opposition and death itself, yet He did not fear—He feared God and fulfilling His mission. His resurrection vindicated His refusal to fear mortal opposition; the grave that made Him 'as grass' was overcome. In His ascension, Christ demonstrated that mortals—even those with power to crucify—are ultimately subject to God's eternal power. Believers are invited to adopt Christ's fearlessness grounded in alignment with the eternal God.
commentary.application: In our current age, members face social pressure to conform to secular values, institutional criticism of the Church, family members hostile to faith, and media mockery of religious conviction. This verse cuts through the anxiety and fear that such opposition generates. Ask yourself: Whom do I fear? And why? If I fear a person, a government, an institution, or public opinion, I am ultimately fearing grass—something temporary, subject to death, destined to wither. God says, 'I am your comforter; I am eternal; I will transform your situation.' The application is not to be arrogant or dismissive of real opposition, but to achieve ultimate perspective: the mortal powers that oppose the righteous are not ultimate; God is ultimate. This reframes our response to opposition. We do not fear retaliation, loss of status, mockery, or even martyrdom—not because these are not painful, but because they are temporary. We fear God, which means we align our hearts and actions with His eternal purposes. This is the comfort Isaiah offers: whatever your present opposition, whatever mortal powers array against you, you belong to the eternal God who has power over all things and has promised to comfort and restore His people. This shifts the emotional register from anxiety to peace, from defensiveness to faith.

text_kjv: These two things are come unto thee; who shall be sorry for thee? desolation, and destruction, and the famine, and the sword: by whom shall I comfort thee?

commentary.narrative: Isaiah pivots abruptly from the sweeping promise of verse 12 ('I, even I, am he that comforteth you') to confront the devastating reality of Jerusalem's affliction. The 'two things' that have befallen the city are not merely abstract theological concepts but concrete, layered calamities: devastation and destruction (the physical ravaging of the land and cities), famine and sword (the consequent human suffering and warfare). This enumeration is not exhaustive but representative—it names the categories of judgment that characterize exile. The prophet's rhetorical question 'who shall be sorry for thee?' does not expect an answer from human voices. No foreign ally, no earthly power, no sympathetic nation steps forward in Jerusalem's darkest hour. The isolation is absolute.
commentary.narrative_continued: The final question—'by whom shall I comfort thee?'—is the pivot point of the entire passage. It appears to confirm hopelessness: no one can comfort you. But this rhetorical question functions as a hinge. In the previous verse, God declared 'I, even I, am he that comforteth you.' Now the prophet asks, in effect: 'Do you understand your helplessness? Do you see that human consolation is worthless?' The purpose is not to deepen despair but to strip away false hope so that God's comfort alone becomes visible. This is the pedagogical move of the entire chapter: the reader must first acknowledge total dependence before experiencing redemption.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The Dead Sea Scrolls confirm the text without significant variation here, though the minor orthographic differences (שְׁתַּיִם vs שתים) do not affect meaning. The Covenant Rendering's emphasis on the structure—'two pairs' rather than a flat list—clarifies Isaiah's rhetorical architecture: devastation/destruction (political), famine/sword (personal). The prophet is both journalist of suffering and herald of the reversal to come.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members often face a season where human support proves insufficient—loss of faith, family rupture, spiritual emptiness. Isaiah's question 'who can comfort thee?' cuts through false remedies (therapy, medication, community sympathy—though not invalid, these are not sufficient). The verse is a call to radical dependence on God. The prophet asks us to see our affliction clearly, name it, and recognize its magnitude, precisely so that we stop expecting human solutions and open ourselves to divine comfort that operates at a different level: not removal of suffering but transformation of its meaning.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 21:19 quotes this verse in its discussion of Israel's latter-day restoration. Nephi applies the 'two things' to the restoration context, showing how the principle of testing followed by deliverance applies to all covenant peoples.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 101:2 and 103:7 echo this structure of judgment followed by promise: the Saints would experience tribulation but would ultimately be comforted and vindicated by the Lord.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The pattern of suffering followed by God's comfort reflects the temple drama: the initiate moves from confusion and darkness (the 'famine' and 'sword' of ignorance) to the light of divine presence. The reversal promised in verse 22 parallels the removal of shame and the bestowal of clothing and identity in temple ordinances.

cross_references.connection: God's declaration 'I, even I, am he that comforteth you' sets the rhetorical stage for verse 19's challenge: if no one else can comfort, only God remains.
Lists sword, famine, and plague as the three covenantal curses for violation of the law, paralleling Isaiah's enumeration of devastation.
Jerusalem's isolation and the absence of comforters ('all her friends have dealt treacherously with her') echoes Isaiah's rhetorical question about who will grieve or console.
Jeremiah similarly catalogs Jerusalem's incurable wounds and asks who will plead her cause, establishing a pattern of exile despair that Isaiah reverses with redemption.
The Book of Mormon quotes this verse directly, applying it to latter-day Israel's afflictions and God's promise of restoration.

word_study.meaning: The feminine plural 'two things' with the verb 'come upon' or 'befall' (qar'ah). The use of the feminine is syntactically required by the plural construct, but it also personalizes the calamities as active agents approaching the city.
word_study.significance: This is not passive suffering but an onslaught. The verb qar'ah (קרא) means literally 'to happen to' or 'to befall,' with a sense of inevitability. In covenant contexts, calamities that 'befall' a people are sent by God as judgment for covenant violation.

word_study.meaning: Devastation, ruin, waste; the laying bare of land and cities. In prophetic literature, it denotes the material destruction wrought by siege and conquest.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering captures shod as 'devastation' (external calamity), contrasting it with the internal human response that follows.

word_study.meaning: Breaking, fracture, collapse; the breaking of things, structures, peoples. It emphasizes the shattering or disintegration of what was whole.
word_study.significance: Paired with shod, shever emphasizes not just ruin but active breaking—the collapse of institutions, walls, and social order.

word_study.meaning: Hunger, deprivation, want; one of the three great curses of covenant violation (plague, sword, famine).
word_study.significance: Famine moves the lament from structural damage to bodily suffering. It is both a result of siege and a direct judgment.

word_study.meaning: Blade, weapon; used metonymically for violence, warfare, bloodshed, and death.
word_study.significance: The 'sword' is the instrument of conquest and the symbol of human agency in destruction. Together with famine, it represents the two modes of siege warfare.

word_study.meaning: To comfort, console, soothe; also to relent or change one's mind (when God is the subject). The root carries the sense of emotional empathy and active relief.
word_study.significance: The verb nacham echoes verse 12's promise: 'I am he that comforteth you.' The question 'who can comfort you?' is unanswerable by human means, leaving only God's comfort as valid.

commentary.christological_typology: The cup of wrath that Jerusalem drinks (verse 22, immediately following) prefigures Christ's own drinking of that cup in Gethsemane. Just as Jerusalem's 'two things' represent the totality of judgment, so Christ absorbs the complete cup of divine justice. The comfort that only God can provide is ultimately the comfort of substitutionary atonement—Christ taking upon Himself what no human can bear.
commentary.historical_context: By the time of the Babylonian siege and exile (586 BCE), Jerusalem had experienced waves of deprivation: Assyrian invasions in 701 BCE, Egyptian interference, and ultimately Babylonian blockade. Siege warfare in the ancient Near East relied on attrition: cutting supply lines to force famine, then assault. Archaeological evidence from siege ramps (notably at Lachish, documented in Assyrian reliefs) and skeletal remains show signs of malnutrition and trauma consistent with siege conditions. The 'sword' was wielded by Babylonian soldiers; the 'famine' was the systematic starvation engineered by siege. The absence of international sympathy reflected the ancient political reality: small kingdoms rarely received aid from distant powers once defeat seemed inevitable. Survival was a city's own responsibility.

text_kjv: Thy sons have fainted, they lie at the head of all the streets, as a wild bull in a net: they are full of the fury of the LORD, the rebuke of thy God.

commentary.narrative: The prophet moves from abstract calamity to the concrete spectacle of human collapse. 'Thy sons have fainted' is not poetic metaphor but literal testimony: during siege, bodies of the starving and slain litter the streets of Jerusalem. They 'lie at the head of all the streets'—at the main intersections where traffic converges—suggesting both the indiscriminate nature of death (it reaches everywhere) and the public, humiliating visibility of the corpses. This is not death on a battlefield where honor accrues; it is death from starvation and collapse in public view, a complete erasure of dignity.
commentary.narrative_continued: The image of the 'wild bull in a net' (or antelope, as the Covenant Rendering more accurately renders the Hebrew to, referring to the swift antelope of the Levantine wilderness) is among Isaiah's most visceral. The to is trapped, struggling, increasingly weakened, unable to escape. The comparison identifies Jerusalem's 'sons' with wild creatures—no longer soldiers or citizens but animals thrashing in a snare. The image captures both the momentum of panic and the futility of resistance. Unlike a hunter's trophy, these are creatures caught not for display but for destruction.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The final clause—'they are full of the fury of the LORD, the rebuke of thy God'—is theologically crucial. This is not random suffering or historical misfortune. The corpses are 'full of' God's wrath (chêmâ) and rebuke (ga'arah), as if these divine emotions are poured into them like drink filling a cup. This echoes the cup metaphor that will dominate verse 22. The young men are not victims of Babylonian cruelty alone; they are vessels of God's own judgment. This connects personal tragedy to covenantal framework: judgment has a divine author.
commentary.application: Verse 20 confronts the modern reader with the reality that covenant judgment is not theoretical or distant—it manifests in visible, material ways. For individuals who have experienced spiritual collapse—loss of faith, moral failure, or deep disillusionment—the image of fainting and being trapped is uncomfortably accurate. The verse teaches that such a state, while it appears final, is not final if one understands it as part of God's covenant process. The judgment is real, but it precedes restoration. The application is not to minimize suffering but to recognize that God's rebuke, while it appears destructive, is not random punishment but the refining fire of covenant faithfulness. The question for the modern reader: Am I willing to acknowledge complete helplessness before I reach for restoration?

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon uses similar imagery in Mosiah 12:2, where King Noah's people are warned of being scattered as a hunted beast, capturing the same sense of helplessness and divine judgment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 63:32-34 speaks of those filled with God's wrath, echoing the idea that judgment is not merely external but becomes internal—one is 'full of' it. This language describes the state of those who reject covenant.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The exhaustion and collapse of Jerusalem's sons contrasts with the spiritual vitality promised in the temple. The cup of wrath (verse 22) that fills them will be replaced with the cup of salvation in the ordinance of communion, restoring what was emptied out.

cross_references.connection: Lamentations similarly describes children and nursing infants fainting in the streets of Jerusalem, uniting physical devastation with the poet's emotional response.
Jeremiah prophesies that those who reject the word will perish by famine and sword, with the dead left unburied—a fate that involves public exposure similar to Isaiah's image.
Lists being scattered before enemies as a curse for covenant violation, paralleling the helplessness of the trapped antelope in Isaiah's metaphor.
Asks God to remember the bloodshed of His servants and the groaning of prisoners, expressing similar lament over visible suffering in the covenant community.
The Lord describes judgments that include war, famine, and plague—connecting Joseph Smith's experience with these classic covenant curses and their purpose in spiritual refinement.

word_study.meaning: To swoon, faint, collapse from exhaustion or shock. The Niphal form suggests a passive state of being overwhelmed.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes involuntary collapse rather than chosen rest. It evokes the final stages of starvation and despair.

word_study.meaning: To lie at the head (chief point) of every street; to occupy the most visible, central locations. Rosh (head) and chutz (street/outside) emphasize public exposure.
word_study.significance: This detail underscores the visibility of the tragedy and the ubiquity of death—not hidden in alleys but displayed at the busiest intersections.

word_study.meaning: Antelope, gazelle, or wild ox; a swift, untamed creature of the wilderness. The Covenant Rendering correctly identifies this as antelope (to), not 'wild bull' as the KJV suggests.
word_study.significance: The to was known for its speed and strength. In a net, even the strongest creature becomes helpless. The image inverts the power dynamic: what seemed free and powerful is suddenly entrapped.

word_study.meaning: The heat of wrath, divine anger. Chemah (fury/heat) is literally the burning of God's anger, often depicted as consuming fire or overflowing cup.
word_study.significance: This is not merely human violence but the active expression of God's covenant wrath. The young men are filled with it as a cup is filled with wine.

word_study.meaning: Sharp reproval, stern rebuke; a verbal expression of anger that carries the force of judgment. Ga'arah can also mean 'to drive away' or 'to scatter.'
word_study.significance: The pairing of fury and rebuke shows both the internal (wrath) and external (condemnation) aspects of divine judgment. The young men embody both.

commentary.christological_typology: The young men of Jerusalem, trapped and helpless as a wild creature in a net, prefigure Christ in Gethsemane—encompassed by forces He could not escape through human means, filled with the cup of divine wrath that had to be borne by the Lamb. Just as Jerusalem's sons are described as 'full of the fury of the LORD,' so Christ becomes the vessel of divine judgment. Yet the reversal is also key: their filling with wrath leads to death; Christ's assumption of wrath leads to resurrection and redemption for others.
commentary.historical_context: Babylonian siege practices, documented in cuneiform sources and corroborated by archaeological evidence, systematized starvation as a siege weapon. Lachish's destruction layer (c. 586 BCE) contains skeletal remains showing severe malnutrition and traumatic injury. Dead bodies in besieged cities were often left unburied due to the siege conditions themselves—burial required venturing outside the walls or using precious space within them. The shameful exposure of the dead was particularly offensive in ancient Near Eastern honor cultures, where proper burial was essential for the soul's peace and the family's dignity. Isaiah's image of corpses at street intersections reflects the documented horror of siege conditions in the Levant during the Iron Age collapse and Babylonian conquest. The 'net' metaphor also has ancient parallels in Assyrian and Babylonian hunting reliefs, where captured animals are depicted in precisely the kind of trapped, struggling posture Isaiah evokes.

text_kjv: Therefore hear now this, thou afflicted, and drunken, but not with wine:

commentary.narrative: The word 'Therefore' (lakhein) marks the prophetic turn. After cataloging devastation in verse 19 and the literal collapse of verse 20, Isaiah commands attention: 'hear now this.' The imperative is addressed to Jerusalem personified as a feminine subject ('thou afflicted')—the city is the primary audience, though the message extends to the exiled community. The metaphor of drunkenness without wine is the key to understanding the entire passage: Jerusalem staggers, reels, and loses control not from intoxication by fermented drink but from the cup of divine wrath. This is a crucial theological move: the people's apparent moral laxity or voluntary excess is not the cause of their state. Instead, they are overwhelmed by forces beyond their control—specifically, God's judgment.
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase 'drunk, but not with wine' recalls Isaiah 29:9, where the people are 'drunk, but not with wine; they stagger, but not with strong drink.' In that earlier passage, the blindness comes from spiritual insensitivity to prophecy. Here, the drunkenness is literal and metaphorical: the people are literally starving and collapsing (verse 20), and they are spiritually overwhelmed by God's judgment. The paradox is that they appear guilty of excess while actually being victims of divine discipline. This distinction is essential: Isaiah is not excusing Jerusalem's sin but reframing the exile. Yes, there was covenant violation. But the visible suffering is the consequence of God's hand, not merely the natural result of the people's folly.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The vocative 'thou afflicted' (aniyyah) establishes a relationship between the prophet and his audience: I see you. I name your condition. You are afflicted. In Hebrew thought, naming the condition is the first step toward transformation. The prophet is not offering false comfort ('everything is fine') but truthful diagnosis ('you are drunk from God's cup') as the prerequisite for the healing promised in verse 22.
commentary.application: Modern believers often experience seasons of spiritual disorientation that feel like drunkenness: confusion, loss of agency, inability to think clearly. This verse teaches that such a state—when it comes as a consequence of covenant violation or when God permits testing—is not a sign of weakness or personal failure that can be fixed by personal effort alone. Instead, it is a condition that only God can address. The application is to stop trying to sober oneself through one's own strength and to instead 'hear' what God is saying (verse 22: the removal of the cup). This requires radical surrender—acknowledging that one is drunk and cannot fix it, and listening for God's Word rather than one's own inner voice.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon applies the cup metaphor in 1 Nephi 8 (Lehi's vision) and 3 Nephi 11 (Christ's covenant meal), establishing that the cup of wrath is transformed into the cup of salvation through the Atonement.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 27:2-3 and 88:141 discuss the sacramental cup as the symbol of the new covenant, explicitly connecting the cup of wrath (what Christ drank) to the cup of blessing (what saints drink).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The drunkenness without wine parallels the bewilderment of the uninitiated in temple narrative—they are 'drunk' on confusion and lack of understanding. The solution, like Jerusalem's, is to hear and understand the Lord's word, which opens the path to restoration.

cross_references.connection: Uses nearly identical language ('drunk, but not with wine; they stagger, but not with strong drink'), but in that context describes spiritual blindness to prophecy rather than covenant judgment.
Describes the cup in God's hand as full of wine mixed with spice—a metaphor for divine judgment that parallels Isaiah's cup of wrath.
Jeremiah is commanded to make nations drink from a cup of wine (wrath) until they stagger, developing the same metaphor of judgment as intoxication.
In Gethsemane, Christ prays 'let this cup pass from me,' referring to the cup of God's wrath that He will drink in place of humanity.
Alma speaks of Christ taking upon Himself the pains and afflictions of all people, bearing what the cup represents.

word_study.meaning: Therefore, for this reason; a connective particle that links consequence to premise. It signals that what follows is a logical or revelatory conclusion.
word_study.significance: This 'therefore' does not follow naturally from verse 20. The reader expects continued lament, but instead the prophet pivots to address and command, showing that understanding judgment's true source (God, not chance) opens the door to revelation.

word_study.meaning: Afflicted, oppressed, poor; in feminine form to address Jerusalem as the city-woman. The root ayin-noon-aleph conveys lowliness, humiliation, and suffering.
word_study.significance: To name oneself 'afflicted' is to acknowledge one's true condition before God. This is not self-pity but spiritual honesty.

word_study.meaning: Drunk, intoxicated; in the stative sense, describing a condition of being overwhelmed and disoriented.
word_study.significance: The metaphor of drunkenness appears throughout Isaiah (19:14, 29:9, 63:6) to describe divine judgment. It captures both the internal experience (loss of control) and the external appearance (staggering, incoherent).

word_study.meaning: Wine, fermented grape drink; used metonymically for intoxication, celebration, but also for divine wrath (the cup of wrath is filled with wine/poison).
word_study.significance: The negation 'but not with wine' clarifies that the drunkenness is not from voluntary excess or moral failure but from involuntary overwhelm—drinking the cup of God's wrath.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah's description of Jerusalem as drunk without wine is a direct typological parallel to Christ's suffering in Gethsemane, where He drinks the cup of God's wrath on behalf of humanity. Just as Jerusalem cannot escape her condition through human remedy or virtue, Christ cannot evade the cup. But where Jerusalem's drunkenness leads to death, Christ's drinking of the cup leads to resurrection and redemption. The verse is also a type of the last supper, where the cup is offered as the sign of the new covenant—the reversal of the cup of wrath into the cup of salvation.
commentary.historical_context: The metaphor of the cup of wrath is deeply embedded in ancient Near Eastern ritual and literature. Drinking cups were vessels of covenant and communion; in judgment contexts, they became symbols of enforced participation in divine condemnation. Mesopotamian texts describe defeated enemies being forced to drink bitter draughts or poison as part of their punishment. The use of wine in ancient Israelite sacrifice and covenant meal (particularly evident in later Jewish practice) made the reversal of the cup from blessing to curse a powerful theological statement. By the time of the Babylonian exile, Jerusalem's population would have been acutely aware of both the scarcity of wine (siege deprivation) and its symbolic power (covenant blessing vs. curse). Isaiah's paradox—drunk without wine—reflects the surreal experience of siege: one staggers and loses rational control not from abundance but from extreme deprivation and trauma.

text_kjv: Thus saith thy Lord the LORD, and thy God that pleadeth the cause of his people, Behold, I have taken out of thine hand the cup of trembling, even the dregs of the cup of my fury; thou shalt no more drink it again:

commentary.narrative: This is the great turning point of Isaiah 51, and arguably of the entire Suffering Servant section (chapters 40-55). After verses of relentless judgment, devastation, and divine wrath, the Lord Himself speaks. The opening—'Thus saith thy Lord the LORD'—is emphatic in the Hebrew, piling up divine titles (adonayikh YHWH, ve'elohayikh) to establish unquestionable authority. The phrase 'that pleadeth the cause of his people' is crucial: God is not distant or indifferent. He is an advocate, actively contending for His people's vindication. The word 'behold' (hinneh) alerts the reader: something crucial is about to be revealed.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verb 'I have taken' (laqaachti, perfect tense) is revelatory. The action is already complete in God's determination, though its earthly manifestation lies in the future. God has already seized the cup from Jerusalem's hand. The cup of 'trembling' (tareel) is the cup that causes staggering—the very drunkenness described in verse 21. Even more specifically, Isaiah identifies it as 'the dregs of the cup of my fury'—not just a taste of wrath but its deepest, most concentrated form. The 'dregs' are what settles at the bottom, the most bitter and potent part. Jerusalem has drunk to the very bottom of God's judgment.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The final promise—'thou shalt no more drink it again'—operates at multiple levels. Literally, it means the exile will end; God will not perpetuate judgment forever. But theologically, it means that this species of judgment (covenant judgment through exile and dispossession) will not be repeated in the same way. The cup is removed permanently. This is not a temporary reprieve but a fundamental reorientation of Jerusalem's relationship to God. The chapter's great pedagogical arc becomes clear: one must understand the fullness of judgment (verses 19-21) to appreciate the reality of restoration (verse 22).
commentary.application: This verse addresses the moment when God's Word cuts through human despair and establishes a new reality. For covenant members in spiritual crisis—whether from personal sin, covenant violation, or testing—verse 22 represents the turning point where external circumstances have not yet changed, but God's determination has. The application is to hear this verse as a literal promise: your cup will be removed. This requires faith before circumstance changes. It requires trusting God's forensic action ('I have taken') even before one experiences the consequences ('thou shalt no more drink'). Modern believers can rehearse this faith: When you pray for deliverance from addiction, spiritual blindness, or judgment, you are asking God to take the cup from your hand as He took it from Jerusalem's. The promise is real, already established in God's mind, and awaiting only your acceptance and obedience.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 3:11 and 2 Nephi 9:21-22 describe how Christ takes upon Himself the cup of God's wrath, breaking the power of death and enabling salvation. Isaiah's promise to Jerusalem becomes universally applicable through the Atonement.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:141 describes the sacramental cup as 'the new and everlasting covenant,' explicitly connecting the cup of wrath (what Christ drank) to the cup of blessing (what saints drink). The promise in verse 22 is realized fully in latter-day temple practice.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The removal of the cup from Jerusalem parallels the ritual progression in temple ordinances: the initiate moves from a state of 'condemnation' or 'nakedness' to a state of covenant blessing and clothing. The cup of trembling is removed; the water and wine of the covenant meal are offered instead. This is the spiritual journey enacted in temple endowment.

cross_references.connection: The earlier declaration 'I, even I, am he that comforteth you' finds its fullest expression here: comfort means the removal of the cup itself.
Jeremiah is commanded to make nations drink from the cup of God's wrath, but Isaiah 51:22 promises that Jerusalem specifically will drink no more—a reversal of the judgment pattern.
Describes God's hand holding a cup 'full of mixture'—the same metaphor of divine judgment as a cup that only the guilty must drink.
Christ prays in Gethsemane, 'Let this cup pass from me,' accepting what Isaiah's Jerusalem must drink, but with the promise (Isaiah 53) that through His suffering comes redemption.
The Lord promises that if the saints keep His covenant, they shall drink wine (the sacramental cup) with Christ—the reversal of the cup of wrath into communion.

word_study.term_english: Thus saith thy Lord the LORD
word_study.meaning: This is the classical prophetic messenger formula, introducing a direct word from God. The triple title (Lord, LORD, your God) emphasizes authority and relationship.
word_study.significance: The accumulation of titles signals the gravity and certainty of what follows. This is not Isaiah's opinion but God's oath.

word_study.meaning: To contend, argue, or plead a case in a legal or covenant context. Rib is the language of covenant litigation—God is not withdrawing but actively defending His people.
word_study.significance: This reverses the dynamic of judgment. Rather than a distant judge condemning, God is an advocate arguing for His people's restoration. It echoes the role established in verse 12.

word_study.meaning: Perfect tense of laqach (to take, seize, grasp). The completed action emphasizes that in God's determination, the cup is already removed, even if earthly experience has not yet caught up.
word_study.significance: The use of the perfect tense (Hebrew prophetic perfect) means God speaks of future restoration as if it is already accomplished—emphasizing its certainty.

word_study.meaning: The cup that causes reeling or staggering. Tarela derives from tara'al (to reel, totter). It is the cup of judgment that overwhelms the drinker.
word_study.significance: This is the same cup mentioned in verse 21 ('drunken, but not with wine'). The metaphor is now fully articulated.

word_study.meaning: The sediment, grounds, or dregs of a drink; the most potent, concentrated part. It literally means 'the cup-bottom.'
word_study.significance: Jerusalem has not tasted judgment peripherally but has drunk to the deepest, bitterest dregs. The completeness of judgment emphasizes the totality of restoration.

word_study.meaning: My wrath, burning anger. Chemah is the heat of divine anger, fully poured out.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that the Dead Sea Scrolls confirm this reading without significant variant. The 'fury' is God's own emotion, not a depersonalized force.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 51:22 reaches its fullest meaning only in light of Isaiah 53, where the Suffering Servant takes upon Himself the very cup of wrath that Jerusalem drinks. Verse 22 promises Jerusalem deliverance; Isaiah 53 reveals how that deliverance is purchased—through vicarious suffering. Jesus Christ drinks the cup that verse 22 removes from Jerusalem's hand. In Matthew 26:39-42, Christ explicitly quotes this framework, accepting the cup in Gethsemane because it is the only way to deliver others from drinking it. The typology is this: just as God's advocacy for Jerusalem (verse 22, 'pleadeth the cause of his people') results in removal of the cup, so Christ's advocacy for all humanity results in the cup of wrath being transferred to Him rather than to us.
commentary.historical_context: The cup of wrath was not merely metaphorical in the ancient Near East. In ritual contexts, sacred cups contained wine mixed with spices and herbs; in judgment, they might contain poison or bitter draughts. The practice of forced consumption as punishment is documented in Assyrian and Egyptian sources. The promise that Jerusalem 'shall no more drink it again' reflects the ancient covenant concept of 'perpetual' arrangements—once a judgment is executed completely, its restoration is secured. The exiles in Babylon (c. 597-538 BCE) would have understood this as a solemn promise that their children would return and rebuilding would occur. The historical fulfillment came with Cyrus's edict (539 BCE) and the return under Zerubbabel and Joshua (c. 538 BCE), validating the prophetic claim. However, Isaiah's promise operates at a level deeper than political restoration: it is about the restoration of covenant relationship itself.

text_kjv: But I will put it into the hand of them that afflict thee; which have said to thy soul, Bow down, that we may go over: and thou hast laid thy body as the ground, and as the street, to them that went over.

commentary.narrative: The final verse of this passage completes the reversal. If verse 22 removes the cup from Jerusalem's hand, verse 23 specifies the cup's new destination: it goes to 'them that afflict thee'—to the oppressors themselves. This is the principle of measure-for-measure judgment: those who forced Jerusalem to drink the cup of wrath now drink it. The verse then reveals the specific humiliation inflicted upon Jerusalem: 'Bow down, that we may go over.' The oppressors forced the city to lie face-down like a roadway, so they could literally walk over the bodies of the vanquished. This is not mere metaphor. Ancient Near Eastern victory reliefs (from Assyria and Egypt) explicitly depict conquered peoples lying prostrate while victors walk over them—a practiced humiliation designed to demonstrate absolute dominion.
commentary.narrative_continued: Jerusalem's passive acceptance—'thou hast laid thy body as the ground, and as the street'—is both historical acknowledgment and theological insight. The people literally did lie prone before the Babylonian conquerors. But the profound significance is that they did so under God's covenant discipline. The verb 'laid' (sim) can mean 'caused to be' or 'appointed,' suggesting that Jerusalem's abasement was appointed by God as judgment, not merely inflicted by human malice. This is crucial: the humiliation was real, but its source and purpose are divine. Now that purpose is fulfilled. The cup is removed from Jerusalem, and those same oppressors will drink from it instead.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The structural completion is elegant. Verse 19 catalogs what befell Jerusalem (desolation, destruction, famine, sword). Verse 20 shows the human toll (sons fainting). Verse 21 identifies the cause (drunk from God's cup). Verse 22 announces the removal (I have taken the cup). Verse 23 specifies the destination (put into the hand of them that afflict thee). The cycle is complete: judgment is assigned, executed, and transferred. Jerusalem, having drunk to the dregs, is freed. Her oppressors, having perpetrated the violence, now face their own reckoning. The promise is not only negative (no more suffering) but also positive (vindication through the reversal of roles).
commentary.application: Verse 23 teaches that God's justice is not merely restorative (removing Jerusalem's cup) but also retributive (placing it in the oppressors' hands). For modern believers, this carries both comfort and warning. Comfort: those who suffer unjust oppression can be assured that God sees it, tracks it, and will render justice. Evil-doers do not escape; they drink the cup they forced upon others. Warning: those who persist in afflicting others—through abuse of power, exploitation, or deliberate cruelty—face the same reversal. This is not vengeance for the believer to undertake but God's own prerogative. The application is twofold: (1) Stop trying to avenge yourself; trust that God will transfer the cup to those who deserve it. (2) Examine yourself: am I afflicting anyone?
