The 'arm of the LORD revealed' through the Servant's suffering is the same arm revealed in the cross: God's power working through apparent weakness and death. The paradox of Isaiah 53:1—that God's might is hidden in the Servant's rejection—points to the scandal of the cross as the center of Christian faith.
commentary.application: Modern disciples encounter the same disbelief that Isaiah 53:1 laments. The gospel message about redemption through Christ's suffering and death remains 'foolishness' to those who have not believed (1 Corinthians 1:18). We are called not simply to believe the report ourselves, but to testify of it in a world that often rejects the message. The question 'who has believed our report?' also invites self-examination: Have we truly believed what we profess to teach? Do we recognize God's power at work in the 'weak things' of the gospel, or do we expect divine power only in visible triumph?

text_kjv: For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 2 begins the portrait of the Servant with a striking paradox: growth and vitality from unpromising origins, yet an appearance so unremarkable that it repels desire. The Covenant Rendering's 'he grew up before him like a young plant' uses past tense, shifting into narrative—this is not prophecy about the future, but testimony about what has already occurred. The metaphor of a yoneq (tender shoot, a suckling plant) and a shoresh (root) growing from erets tsiyyah (dry ground) evokes an image of something fragile, unexpected, thriving despite hostile conditions.

The second half of the verse pivots from origin to appearance: 'He had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him.' The triple negation (no form, no majesty, no beauty) is emphatic. In a culture where physical beauty was often read as a sign of divine favor (as in David's selection as king: 1 Samuel 16:12), the Servant's lack of striking appearance becomes a sign of rejection and insignificance. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this verse with plene spelling (fuller vowel markings) but identical meaning, confirming the ancient consensus that the Servant emerges from humble origins and possesses no outward glory. Theologically, this verse inverts the expectation of a messianic king: no crowning splendor, no visible majesty. The Servant will be utterly unremarkable to human eyes.

word_study.meaning: A young plant, sucker, shoot, or sprout—literally 'a suckling' (from yanaq, to suckle). The term can refer to a young twig or sapling, something newly sprouted and still tender. It connotes fragility, vulnerability, and newness.
word_study.significance: The Servant grows like a yoneq—not as a mature, established tree, but as something vulnerable and dependent. This humility of origin prefigures the Servant's condition: one who grows in dependence on God (the Hebrew 'before him' suggests growth in God's presence and care), not in independent glory.

word_study.meaning: A root (shoresh) from dry ground (erets tsiyyah, wasteland or parched earth). The root is invisible, hidden in earth, drawing moisture and nourishment from an inhospitable place. Tsiyyah emphasizes barrenness and scarcity.
word_study.significance: The root metaphor echoes Isaiah 11:1 ('a shoot will come up from the stump of Jesse') and suggests hidden growth beneath the surface. The Servant's glory is not external and visible, but rooted deep in the soil of humility and hardship. The dry ground recalls the wilderness, exile, and desolation—contexts in which God's power becomes most visible.

word_study.meaning: Toar: appearance, form, shape. Hadar: majesty, splendor, glory, honor. Mar'eh: appearance, look, what is seen. Together these terms denote the external, visible qualities that command attention and admiration in human societies.
word_study.significance: The absence of toar, hadar, and mar'eh signals that the Servant will not attract followers through charisma, power, or aesthetic appeal. In a world that judges by external qualities, the Servant appears as nothing. This prepares for the radical inversion: true redemptive power works through apparent weakness and unattractiveness.

cross_references.connection: Both passages use the imagery of a shoot/branch arising from humble origins; Isaiah 11:1 refers to 'a shoot from the stump of Jesse,' echoing the root metaphor of Isaiah 53:2.
David is selected as king because of his handsome appearance, contrasting with the Servant's complete lack of outward beauty or majesty.
Paul warns against judging Christ 'according to the flesh' (external appearance), directly addressing the problem Isaiah 53:2 poses: the Servant's unremarkable outward form.
Jesus is described as the carpenter's son from a humble village, with no reputation or striking appearance—fulfilling the portrait of the Servant in Isaiah 53:2.
Peter calls Christ a 'living stone, rejected by humans but in God's sight chosen and precious'—embodying the paradox of Isaiah 53:2: outwardly rejected yet spiritually valued.

commentary.historical_context: The metaphor of growth from dry ground carried particular power in the post-exilic context. Exiled Israel experienced exile as a kind of death, a cutting down of the royal line and national independence (similar to Isaiah 6:13's image of a stump remaining after the forest is felled). The promise of a shoot growing from a stump or root in barren ground became a symbol of restoration after catastrophe. The imagery also reflects ancient Near Eastern realities: Palestine's semi-arid climate meant that water scarcity was a perpetual concern. A plant thriving in dry ground would appear impossibly fragile yet full of stubborn life. The DSS evidence shows that this text was preserved with careful attention to every letter, indicating its theological significance was recognized in pre-Christian Judaism.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 14:2 preserves Isaiah 53:2 unchanged in the Book of Mormon rendering. The text is attributed to Abinadi, who recites it to King Noah's priests. The LDS tradition has consistently interpreted this verse as referring to Jesus Christ's humble birth and obscure origins in Nazareth—a village so insignificant that Nathanael asked, 'Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?' (John 1:46).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:34 speaks of how God's work will be accomplished through 'weak things' that become mighty—directly illustrating the principle of Isaiah 53:2, where the Servant's apparent weakness and lack of external beauty become the vehicle of redemption.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The theme of hidden growth and depth mirrors temple theology: external ordinances and symbols conceal profound spiritual realities. The Servant, like temple worship itself, works through forms that external observers may judge as plain or unattractive but that contain infinite spiritual power.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 53:2 is explicitly applied to Jesus in Christian interpretation, particularly his birth in Bethlehem (the least of Judah's clans) and his obscure upbringing in Nazareth. Matthew 2:23 interprets Jesus's move to Nazareth as fulfillment of prophecy, though no Old Testament text explicitly says 'he shall be called a Nazarene'—suggesting Matthew may have understood Isaiah 53:2's humility motif as encompassing Jesus's unremarkable earthly origins. The Servant's lack of external majesty contrasts sharply with popular messianic expectation of a conquering king. In Jesus's crucifixion, the apparent weakness and ugliness of death become the paradoxical revelation of God's power.
commentary.application: We live in a culture saturated with images of power, beauty, and celebrity. Isaiah 53:2 challenges us to recognize that divine redemption does not work through such external measures. Our own spiritual growth may feel invisible, occurring in the 'dry ground' of ordinary circumstances, without the recognition or admiration of others. The verse calls us to value depth over appearance, character over charisma, and faithful perseverance over external success. When we are tempted to judge people or causes by their external attractiveness or visibility, Isaiah 53:2 reminds us that God's most redemptive work often occurs in the hidden, overlooked places.

text_kjv: He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 3 intensifies the portrait of the Servant from physical unattractiveness to active social rejection. The opening line is emphatic: 'He was despised and rejected by men'—the Hebrew chadal ishim conveys not merely dislike but a cessation of regard, as if the Servant has ceased to matter as a human being. The phrase 'a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief' does not mean the Servant is weak or broken by suffering; rather, he is intimate with suffering, living constantly in its presence. The Covenant Rendering's rendering of yadu'a choli as 'acquainted with grief/illness' captures the sense that the Servant knows suffering experientially, not as an observer but as a participant who has internalized it.

The second half of the verse shifts to the collective response of rejection: 'As one from whom men hide their faces he was despised, and we esteemed him not.' The phrase 'hide their faces' suggests the visceral human impulse to look away from suffering, illness, or shame. To hide one's face from someone is to refuse recognition and fellowship. The final verb, chashavnuhu, is an accounting term meaning 'we esteemed,' 'we reckoned,' or 'we counted'—suggesting that the Servant was literally not counted among those of value. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this verse with only orthographic variations (fuller vowel marks), confirming the pre-Christian text read the same way. This verse is the pivot point between the Servant's condition and the community's culpability in causing and perpetuating that rejection.

word_study.meaning: Nivzeh: despised, regarded with contempt or loathing. Chadal: ceased, ceased to be, forsaken, abandoned. Ishim: men, people. The phrase conveys both active contempt and passive abandonment—the Servant is both actively despised and has ceased to be regarded as a person of consequence.
word_study.significance: The combination of active rejection (despised) and passive abandonment (ceased to be counted among men) captures the total social death of the Servant. This is not merely unpopularity but a kind of social excommunication.

word_study.term_english: man of sorrows / acquainted with grief
word_study.term_original: אִישׁ מַכְאֹבוֹת וִידוּעַ חֹלִי (ish makh'ovot vidua choli)
word_study.meaning: Ish makh'ovot: literally 'man of pains/sorrows.' The plural makh'ovot suggests multiple, repeated, accumulated sorrows. Yadu'a choli: literally 'known to illness' or 'acquainted with sickness'—yadu'a carries the sense of intimate knowledge (as in 'to know' someone in the biblical sense of relationship). Choli can mean illness, suffering, or weakness.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes yadu'a choli as 'acquainted with grief/illness'—the Servant does not merely endure suffering but knows it intimately. This is not passive victimhood but an active, internalized relationship with suffering. The Servant becomes a living embodiment of humanity's pain.

word_study.meaning: Master: hiding, concealment. Panim: face, person, presence. The phrase literally means 'like one who hides his face'—a gesture of refusal, shame, or disgust. To hide one's face from someone is to refuse recognition and fellowship.
word_study.significance: The metaphor captures human revulsion and avoidance. Just as we look away from suffering we cannot bear or from something we despise, so people turned away from the Servant. This gesture of hiding faces is both a sign of the Servant's degradation and an indictment of the community's moral failure to witness and acknowledge his suffering.

word_study.meaning: From the root חׁשׁב (chashav): to think, reckon, account, esteem, value. Chashavnuhu means 'we reckoned him' or 'we esteemed him'—in negative context, 'we did not count him as having worth.' It is an accounting metaphor: the Servant was literally not counted among the valuable.
word_study.significance: The term's association with accounting and valuation emphasizes that the Servant's rejection was total and systematic—not a passing dislike but a fundamental refusal to grant him worth or place in the community.

cross_references.connection: The Psalmist cries, 'I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised of the people'—a passage traditionally interpreted as messianic and echoed in Isaiah 53:3's language of despising and rejection.

The speaker laments, 'Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by? behold, and see if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow'—paralleling the Servant's acquaintance with grief and the world's refusal to acknowledge it.
After Jesus's arrest, the Sanhedrin strikes him and spits in his face—literally fulfilling the gesture of hiding one's face in contempt described in Isaiah 53:3.
The Prologue states that the Word 'came unto his own, and his own received him not'—capturing the theme of recognition refused and the Servant rejected by those who should have known him.
Jesus 'suffered outside the gate' of Jerusalem—a concrete historical instance of the Servant being cast out and despised, separated from the community.

commentary.historical_context: The language of Isaiah 53:3 reflects the social and ritual dynamics of ancient Israel and the Near East. To be 'despised' (nivzeh) could carry legal and ritual dimensions—in Levitical law, individuals with leprosy or certain conditions were excluded from the community and required to hide their faces. The phrase 'acquainted with grief/illness' recalls this legal and religious separation: one struck by God's judgment was regarded as ritually defiled and socially dead. The gesture of 'hiding one's face' from the Servant reflects the visceral human response to suffering, death, and shame. In exilic and post-exilic contexts, the Servant's rejection may have resonated with Israel's own experience of exile and diaspora—a people despised and rejected among the nations. The DSS evidence shows this verse was scrupulously copied, indicating its centrality to Jewish theological reflection on suffering and redemption.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 14:3 quotes Isaiah 53:3 verbatim in the Book of Mormon. The text is part of Abinadi's testimony before King Noah's court, where Abinadi himself faces rejection and will eventually be martyred—embodying in his own life the pattern of the rejected Servant. This creates a typological parallel: Abinadi is rejected for testifying of the Servant who is rejected.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 122:8-9 contains language echoing Isaiah 53:3: 'And if thou be cast into the pit, or into the hands of murderers, and the sentence of death passed upon thee... know thou, my son, that all these things shall give thee experience'—the Lord consoles Joseph Smith with the assurance that even rejection and suffering can be redemptive, echoing the Servant's model.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Servant's rejection and social death parallel aspects of temple covenants where initiates symbolically die to the world and are born into a new community. The contrast between the Servant's rejection by the outer world and his ultimate vindication by God mirrors the temple narrative of death and resurrection.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 53:3 is explicitly understood in Christian tradition as describing Jesus's rejection by Jewish and Gentile authorities. The 'man of sorrows' becomes an epithet for Christ throughout Christian theology and art, particularly in meditation on the Passion. The phrase 'acquainted with grief' is understood to mean that Christ experienced human suffering not merely externally but internally—he knew grief, sorrow, and anguish in the depths of his being. The hiding of faces anticipates the mockery and spitting Jesus endured. Most profoundly, the verse captures the scandal of the cross: not a glorious messianic triumph but a rejected, despised death.
commentary.application: Isaiah 53:3 speaks to anyone who has experienced rejection, mockery, or social isolation. It assures us that the Servant—and Christ—was not spared such suffering but embraced it. For modern disciples, this verse challenges us to examine our own complicity in the culture of rejection: Do we hide our faces from those who suffer? Do we withhold recognition from those society despises? The verse also speaks to those in the wilderness of rejection: your suffering is not meaningless, nor are you abandoned by God. The Servant's acquaintance with grief becomes the foundation of his redemptive work. Finally, the verse invites us to recognize Christ in the rejected and despised of our own time, as Matthew 25:31-46 makes explicit—'inasmuch as ye did it to the least of these...'

text_kjv: Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 4 is the theological hinge of the Suffering Servant passage. It begins with akhen (surely, verily), an emphatic particle that introduces a solemn truth that has just been realized or confessed. This is the moment of recognition: the speakers now understand what they previously misunderstood. The Servant 'has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows'—using language drawn from the vocabulary of burden-bearing and vicarious substitution. The Covenant Rendering's 'he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows' emphasizes continuous, completed action: the work is done.

But the verse contains a crucial confession of misinterpretation: 'Yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted.' This second half reveals that the speakers initially misread the Servant's suffering. They assumed it was punishment—divine wrath directed at the Servant himself. The word nagu'a (stricken) was used in Levitical law to describe someone with leprosy or ritual defilement (Leviticus 13:45). Mukkeh elohim (smitten by God) is language of divine judgment—appearing elsewhere in Scripture to describe those struck down for their own sin. The speakers confess: we thought he was being punished for his own transgressions. We were wrong. We now understand: he bore OUR griefs, carried OUR sorrows—his suffering is not punishment for his sins but substitution for ours. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this verse identically to the Masoretic Text, confirming this revolutionary understanding of vicarious atonement was present in pre-Christian Judaism.

word_study.meaning: Nasa: to bear, carry, lift, endure, sustain. Can mean to bear a burden, to carry guilt, to wear a name, or to endure punishment. Saval: to bear, carry, transport a load. Both terms are used for physical burden-bearing and for bearing the weight of sin or guilt.
word_study.significance: These verbs transform the Servant's suffering into active work on behalf of others. He does not passively endure; he actively bears and carries—performing a redemptive labor. The parallel structure (nasa...saval) and the double object (our griefs...our sorrows) emphasize both the completeness and the substitutionary nature of the act.

word_study.meaning: Stricken, touched, afflicted by disease. In Levitical usage, particularly in Leviticus 13, nagu'a describes someone with an infectious disease (leprosy), marking them as ritually unclean and requiring separation from the community. The term carries connotations of divine disfavor or punishment.
word_study.significance: The speakers initially interpreted the Servant's suffering as though he were a leper or one struck by God's wrath for his own sins. This misunderstanding reflects how suffering was commonly interpreted in ancient Israel: as a sign of God's judgment upon sin. The confession 'yet we esteemed him stricken' reveals the tragic misreading that observers made—and that the Servant bore without correcting.

word_study.term_english: smitten of God / smitten by God
word_study.meaning: Mukkeh: smitten, struck, wounded. Elohim: God, the divine. The phrase literally means 'struck by God' and carries the theological sense of being under divine judgment or punishment. It is used elsewhere to describe those whom God has struck down.
word_study.significance: This phrase captures the tragic theology that the observers held: they read the Servant's suffering as evidence of divine wrath against him. Their confession 'yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten of God' amounts to admitting: we were profoundly mistaken about what God was doing. We attributed his suffering to his own guilt, when in fact it was bearing our guilt.

word_study.meaning: Afflicted, oppressed, subjected to suffering or humiliation. Related to the verb anah, to afflict, oppress, or humiliate. The term can refer to suffering in general or to systematic oppression.
word_study.significance: The triple characterization—nagu'a, mukkeh elohim, me'unna—creates a cumulative picture of wretchedness. The confessors now see through this misreading: the Servant's visible wretchedness was not evidence of his guilt but of his vicarious bearing of guilt.

cross_references.connection: Describes someone with leprosy as 'having leprosy' (nagu'a), providing context for the Servant's being viewed as ritually defiled in Isaiah 53:4.
Matthew explicitly quotes Isaiah 53:4, interpreting Jesus's healing ministry as fulfilling 'he took our infirmities and bare our sicknesses'—reapplying the verse to Christ's redemptive healing work.
Applies Isaiah 53:4's language of bearing griefs to Christ: 'Who his own self bare our sins in his body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness.'
Describes Christ as the propitiation for sins, embodying the vicarious atonement principle that Isaiah 53:4 announces—God's wrath against sin is borne by Christ, not by the guilty.
Christ 'was once offered to bear the sins of many'—using bear language identical to Isaiah 53:4's nasa and saval to describe Christ's redemptive substitution.

commentary.historical_context: Isaiah 53:4's confession of misunderstanding reflects a broader ancient Near Eastern and Israelite theology of suffering. The principle of retributive justice—that suffering indicates sin and blessing indicates righteousness—was deeply embedded in wisdom literature and popular theology (as reflected in the Book of Job's friends' arguments). When someone was visibly sick, diseased, or afflicted, observers naturally concluded they had incurred divine wrath. Isaiah 53:4's revolutionary claim is that this interpretive lens has been radically inverted: the one who appears most afflicted by God is in fact bearing the affliction that rightly belongs to others. The DSS evidence confirms that this challenging theology was already ancient and revered in Jewish tradition. The reference to leprosy and ritual defilement anticipates Matthew's healing narrative: Jesus, by touching lepers and healing the sick, takes upon himself the condition of those deemed unclean—embodying in action what Isaiah 53:4 describes theologically.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 14:4 preserves Isaiah 53:4 exactly as it appears in the KJV tradition. In Alma 7:11-12, Alma expands on this principle: Christ 'shall take upon him the pains and the sicknesses of his people... that his bowels may be filled with mercy, according to the flesh, that he may know according to the flesh how to succor his people according to their infirmities.' Alma interprets the Servant's burden-bearing in explicitly soteriological terms: Christ must experience human suffering to effectively redeem and succor his people.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 19:15-19 contains Christ's description of bearing the sins of the world: 'Therefore I command you to repent... that you may not suffer the consequences of your sins... which suffering caused myself, even God, the greatest of all, to tremble because of pain, and to bleed at every pore, and to suffer both body and spirit.' This is Isaiah 53:4 recast in first-person voice—Christ himself explaining the vicarious nature of his bearing of human sin and suffering.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The concept of one bearing the sins of many is central to temple symbolism. The Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur) liturgy describes the high priest bearing the sins of Israel (Leviticus 16). Christ's atonement fulfills and supersedes the Levitical system: he is the ultimate High Priest who bears the sins of the world once and for all.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 53:4 is explicitly messianic in Christian theology. Matthew's quotation in Matthew 8:16-17 directly applies the verse to Jesus's healing miracles, understanding his power over sickness as an expression of his redemptive work. The deeper typological meaning involves Christ as the ultimate bearer of human suffering—both physical (sickness, pain) and spiritual (sin, guilt). Just as the Servant bears griefs and sorrows that are not his own, Christ bears the sins of the world. The misreading that observers made—interpreting the Servant's suffering as divine punishment upon him—parallels how many observers of Jesus's crucifixion initially understood it as evidence of his guilt ('If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross'). The verse's confession represents a post-resurrection recognition: what looked like judgment was actually redemption.
commentary.application: Verse 4 invites us to reexamine our interpretations of suffering—both our own and others'. Our culture, like the ancient observers, tends to interpret visible suffering as a sign of failure or guilt. Isaiah 53:4 subverts this: suffering can be redemptive, even vicarious, bearing the weight of others' burdens. For individuals in crisis or chronic suffering, the verse offers a reframing: your suffering is not necessarily evidence that you are being punished for sin. It may be part of participating in Christ's redemptive work—bearing sorrows on behalf of others. For disciples more broadly, the verse calls us to recognize Christ in our own bearing of others' burdens: when we comfort the grieving, care for the sick, or stand with the suffering, we are performing the work the Servant performs—bearing others' griefs and sorrows in the name of redemption.

text_kjv: But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 5 is arguably the most densely theological verse in the entire Hebrew Bible on the doctrine of vicarious atonement. It deepens the confession of verse 4 with explicit language of substitution: 'But he was pierced for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities.' The Covenant Rendering's rendering of mecholal as 'pierced' captures a more visceral sense than 'wounded'—this is penetrating violence, a piercing through. The preposition min (from, because of, on account of) makes the causality unmistakable: the Servant was pierced BECAUSE OF our transgressions, not his own. His crushed condition (medukkah) is explicitly attributed to our iniquities (avonotenu).

The second half of the verse shifts from substitution to remedy: 'Upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and by his wounds we are healed.' The word musar (chastisement, discipline, correction) ordinarily refers to corrective punishment—the kind that produces repentance and transformation. Shalom (peace, wholeness, completeness) here means not merely the absence of conflict but the restoration of right relationship with God. The final clause, uvacharurato nirpa-lanu ('by his wounds/stripes we are healed'), represents the fullest theological summary of redemption in the Hebrew Bible. The plural 'wounds' (chaburot, from chavar, to wound or break) suggests multiple, sustained injuries. The verb nirpa-lanu (we are healed) uses the passive form: healing is not our achievement but something effected upon us. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve verse 5 identically to the Masoretic Text, indicating that this revolutionary doctrine of vicarious atonement and substitutionary healing was not a late Christian insertion but integral to the original prophecy.

word_study.meaning: Pierced, wounded, perforated. From the root chalal, which can mean to pierce, perforate, wound, or (secondarily) to profane or desecrate. The Covenant Rendering notes that mecholal is chosen over 'wounded' because the parallel with medukkah ('crushed') points to specific physical violence. A mecholal wound is one that goes through, penetrating to the interior.
word_study.significance: The term's visceral specificity—piercing rather than general wounding—prefigures the piercing of the crucifixion (John 19:34) and creates a stark image of violence endured. This is not metaphorical pain but concrete, bodily suffering.

word_study.meaning: Pesha: transgression, rebellion, breach of covenant. Avon: iniquity, guilt, sin, crooked behavior, the consequence of sin. Pesha emphasizes willful violation of known law; avon emphasizes the twisted condition that sin produces. Together, they cover the full range of human sin: deliberate rebellion and its twisted consequences.
word_study.significance: The dual terminology ensures that no category of human sin is excluded from what the Servant bears: not merely unintentional mistakes but deliberate transgressions, and not merely the acts but the inner corruption (avon) that sin produces.

word_study.meaning: Crushed, broken, pressed upon. From the root dakah, to crush or break. The condition of medukkah suggests something that has been subjected to overwhelming pressure, smashed rather than cut. It conveys utter devastation and loss of form.
word_study.significance: Combined with mecholal (pierced), medukkah creates a complete picture of violence: from without (piercing) and from within (crushing). The parallelism of 'pierced for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities' assigns specific categories of human sin to specific aspects of the Servant's suffering, suggesting a detailed correspondence between sin and redemptive suffering.

word_study.meaning: Chastisement, discipline, correction, punishment that educates. From the root yasar, to instruct, correct, or discipline. Musar is corrective punishment—the kind that aims at transformation and restoration, not mere retribution.
word_study.significance: The use of musar rather than a term for retributive justice suggests that the Servant's suffering serves a redemptive purpose: it corrects the world's sin and produces shalom (wholeness). This transforms punishment into cure.

word_study.meaning: Peace, completeness, wholeness, well-being, right relationship. In this context, shalom is not merely the absence of war but the restoration of harmony between God and humanity. Shelomenu ('our peace') is what the Servant's suffering secures for us.
word_study.significance: The theme of 'chastisement of our peace' inverts the usual logic: our peace (wholeness, right relationship) is purchased through the Servant's chastisement. His suffering is curative, producing in us the condition of shalom.

word_study.meaning: Wound, stripe, mark from beating. From chavar, to wound, beat, or break. The plural chaburot (wounds/stripes) suggests repeated beating or multiple wounds.
word_study.significance: The image of stripes recalls the physical punishment of scourging in both Jewish and Roman contexts. The theology embedded in 'by his wounds we are healed' is that physical suffering inflicted on the Servant becomes the mechanism of spiritual healing for others. The repetition of 'wounds' (plural) emphasizes that this is not a single blow but sustained, systematic violence endured.

cross_references.connection: The guilt offering (asham) system requires that the sinner bring an offering to 'make atonement for him' through a substitute; Isaiah 53:5 reimagines this on a cosmic scale with the Servant as the ultimate asham.
The Passover lamb, slain and its blood applied to doorposts, prefigures the Servant as a lamb offered for the redemption of the people. Isaiah 53:5's piercing echoes the Passover lamb's death.
Matthew quotes Isaiah 53:4 in the context of Jesus's healing ministry, establishing that the Servant's bearing of griefs and sorrows is demonstrated in Christ's power over sickness.

Peter directly quotes Isaiah 53:5, applying it to Christ: 'Who his own self bare our sins in his body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.'

Paul describes Christ's death as the ultimate expression of love and justification: 'God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us'—embodying the substitutionary principle of Isaiah 53:5.

Christ describes his own atoning suffering in Isaiah 53:5 terms: 'I command you to repent... that you may not suffer... which suffering caused myself, even God, the greatest of all, to tremble because of pain, and to bleed at every pore, and to suffer both body and spirit.'

commentary.historical_context: Isaiah 53:5's doctrine of vicarious atonement represents a profound theological development in Israelite religion. The Levitical sacrificial system (Leviticus 1-7) prescribed that animals be offered to make atonement (kaphar) for sin. The Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur, Leviticus 16) involved the high priest placing the sins of Israel on a scapegoat, which was sent into the wilderness. Isaiah 53:5 transfigures these practices: a human Servant—not animals, not a temporary ritual—becomes the permanent, cosmic bearer of human sin. The language of piercing and crushing echoes both the scapegoat ritual and ancient Near Eastern practices of human sacrifice (which Israel prohibited). The verse's originality lies in its claim that one human being's suffering can bear the weight of an entire people's sin—a principle that would be radically reinterpreted in early Christianity. The DSS evidence confirms that this text, preserved with extraordinary care, was central to Jewish theological reflection in the Second Temple period.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 14:5 preserves Isaiah 53:5 exactly. Alma 7:13 expands the meaning: 'And he will take upon him the death of the captive; and his name shall be the Son of God... that he may loose the bands of death which bindeth his people.' The Book of Mormon emphasizes that the Servant's piercing and crushing effect the loosing of death's bonds—the resurrection becomes integral to the atonement.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 19:16-18 contains Christ's explicit description of his atonement in Isaiah 53:5 language: 'Therefore I command you to repent, and keep the commandments which you have received... Wherefore, I command you again to repent, lest I humble you with my almighty power; and that you confess your sins, lest you suffer these punishments of which I have spoken, of which in the smallest, yea, even in the least degree you have tasted at the time I withdrew my Spirit.' The revelation makes plain that Christ's atonement is effective for those who repent and accept its terms.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The entire Levitical temple system—particularly the guilt offering (asham), the sin offering (chatat), and the Day of Atonement—finds its fulfillment in Isaiah 53:5. Christ becomes both the High Priest and the eternal offering. The piercing of the Servant anticipates the veil of the temple torn in two (Matthew 27:51), symbolizing access to the Holy of Holies granted through his sacrifice.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 53:5 is the most explicitly messianic verse in the Hebrew Bible outside of the royal psalms. Christian theology universally interprets the pierced and crushed Servant as Jesus Christ on the cross. The verse's language of 'for our transgressions' and 'for our iniquities' establishes the substitutionary atonement doctrine at Christianity's heart. Jesus himself, in Luke 22:37, quotes Isaiah 53:12 ('he was numbered with the transgressors') as a prediction of his imminent crucifixion. 1 Peter 2:24 applies Isaiah 53:5 directly to Christ's redemptive work. The theology is clear: Christ's piercing (crucifixion) and crushing (his spiritual and emotional anguish) effect the healing of humanity from sin through vicarious substitution.
commentary.application: Isaiah 53:5 stands at the center of Christian faith and Mormon covenant theology. For individuals bearing guilt or shame, the verse offers radical news: the chastisement that properly belongs to you has been borne by another. Your peace (shalom—wholeness, right relationship with God) has been purchased through the Servant's wounds. This is not cheap grace but grace bought at infinite cost. The doctrine invites a response: recognition, gratitude, and repentance that accepts the substitution. For disciples, the verse also establishes a pattern: as the Servant bore what others should bear, so we are invited to participate in bearing others' griefs, sharing their burdens, and becoming instruments of healing. The piercing wounds that heal also become the measure of authentic love: willingness to be wounded for the sake of another's wholeness.

text_kjv: All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 6 is structured as an inclusive bracket: kullanu (all of us) opens the verse, and kullanu appears again near the close ('the iniquity of us all'), creating a theological frame that extends the Servant's vicarious bearing to the entire human community. The verse opens with the pastoral metaphor: 'All we like sheep have gone astray.' Sheep imagery in biblical literature typically suggests not stupidity but vulnerability to being lost—sheep naturally wander from the path, vulnerable to predators, dependent on a shepherd. The confession 'we have turned, each one, to his own way' (paninu, ish ledarko) shifts from collective wandering to individual self-will. Each person has pursued his own course, his own desires, without regard for the collective good or the shepherd's guidance. This captures the essence of human sin: not merely external transgression but the inward condition of rebellious self-interest.

The final clause delivers the ultimate reversal: 'and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.' The Covenant Rendering's hipgia (laid on, caused to fall upon) creates a stark contrast: we turned, each to our own way, but the LORD (with emphasis, suggesting divine initiative and power) placed upon the one Servant the accumulation of all our iniquities. The logic is extraordinary: our scattered rebellion, our multiple individual turnings away, are consolidated into a single burden borne by a single figure. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this verse identically, confirming that this doctrine of universal guilt borne by one was integral to the original prophecy. The verb hipgia is significant: elsewhere in Isaiah (it appears in verse 12, though the DSS note doesn't specify), the same root paga is used for interceding (standing in the breach)—suggesting that the Servant both bears the burden and intercedes for those whose burden he bears.
commentary.application: Isaiah 53:6 speaks to the condition of spiritual lostness that every human being experiences apart from God. We have gone astray; we have turned, each to our own way. The verse does not minimize this condition with gentle language—it is serious, universal, deserving of judgment. Yet the verse simultaneously announces that the LORD has acted: he has laid our iniquity upon the Servant. For those burdened by guilt, shame, or a sense of being lost, the verse offers radical substitution: you do not bear the weight of your iniquity because another has borne it. The verse invites confession ('we have gone astray'), acceptance ('the LORD has laid on him'), and transformation. For disciples, the verse establishes a pattern of following the Shepherd: as the Servant bears the iniquity of the flock, we are called to bear one another's burdens and to go after the lost sheep in our midst. The universal scope of the verse ('us all,' 'every one') also means no one is beyond redemption—the Servant's sacrifice encompasses all humanity.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 14:6 preserves Isaiah 53:6 identically to the KJV. The fuller context of Mosiah 15 interprets this verse: 'Now I say unto you, who shall declare his generation? Behold, I say unto you, that when his soul has been made an offering for sin he shall see his seed' (Mosiah 15:10). The Book of Mormon interpretation emphasizes that the Servant's bearing of iniquity results in spiritual offspring—those redeemed become his seed.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:6 states that the Son 'is in the bosom of the Father, and he is in your midst; and ye are in him, and he is in you; thus he is in your midst and ye in him.' This covenant language suggests that through the Servant's bearing of iniquity (Isaiah 53:6), a union is effected between the Servant and the redeemed community. We are gathered into him as the scattered sheep are gathered to the shepherd.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The scapegoat ritual (Leviticus 16:20-22) provides the Old Testament type for Isaiah 53:6: the high priest places Israel's sins upon the scapegoat, which is sent into the wilderness, bearing the iniquity of the people away. Isaiah 53:6 reimagines this ritual on a cosmic, eternal scale: the Servant (the ultimate scapegoat) bears not merely a year's sins but the iniquity of all humanity, all time. The temple's holy place becomes unnecessary when the Servant's sacrifice accomplishes what the veil and the inner sanctuary symbolized.

cross_references.connection: The foundational shepherd/sheep passage: 'The LORD is my shepherd, I shall not want... though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil.' Isaiah 53:6's sheep imagery presupposes this relationship and confesses its breach—we have wandered despite having a shepherd.

Jeremiah indicts Israel: 'My people hath been lost sheep: their shepherds have caused them to go astray.' Isaiah 53:6 echoes this lament but adds that the true Shepherd will gather the scattered flock through the Servant's redemptive work.

Jesus teaches the parable of the Lost Sheep, in which a shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to find the one lost sheep—illustrating the principle that Isaiah 53:6 announces: the shepherd acts to recover those who have gone astray.

Jesus declares, 'I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.' This directly applies Isaiah 53:6's shepherd imagery to Christ, with the explicit soteriological claim that the shepherd's role involves giving his life.

Peter quotes Isaiah 53:5, then continues: 'For ye were as sheep going astray; but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls'—applying Isaiah 53:6's pastoral metaphor and its resolution through Christ.
Paul writes, 'All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God'—echoing Isaiah 53:6's universal confession that all, like sheep, have gone astray.

word_study.meaning: Kullanu: all of us (emphatic). Tson: sheep, flock. Ta'inu: we have gone astray, wandered, erred. The root ta'ah means to wander, go astray, be lost. Sheep are characterized throughout Scripture as creatures that wander and require shepherding (Psalm 23).
word_study.significance: The pastoral metaphor captures human sin not as deliberate rebellion against a known master but as aimless wandering. The confessors speak of themselves as vulnerable creatures who have lost the path. This inverts the potential defiance of 'we have turned to our own way'—the sheep are not proudly asserting independence but admitting lostness. The shepherd/sheep relationship becomes the underlying structure for understanding sin and redemption.

word_study.term_english: turned / each to his own way
word_study.meaning: Paninu: we have turned (panah means to turn, face, direct). Ish: man, person. Derech: way, path, course of life. Ledarko: to his own way (the preposition le combines with the pronominal suffix to indicate 'to his own'). Together, the phrase suggests each individual turning to pursue his own path.
word_study.significance: The shift from collective wandering (we like sheep have gone astray) to individual turning (each to his own way) captures both dimensions of human sin: the corporate condition of being lost and the individual willfulness of choosing one's own path over God's. The use of derech (way) recalls the imagery of the Two Ways that appears throughout Wisdom literature—the way of life and the way of death. Each person here has chosen 'his own way' rather than the path God has marked out.

word_study.term_english: laid on / caused to fall upon
word_study.meaning: Caused to fall upon, laid upon, struck against. From the root paga, which can mean to meet, encounter, strike against, or (in other contexts) to intercede, plead with. The hiphil form (hipgia) makes this a causative action: the LORD caused [the iniquity] to meet/fall upon [the Servant].
word_study.significance: The verb hipgia emphasizes divine action: it is not the Servant's choice or the speakers' action, but the LORD who actively places the burden upon him. The root paga's association with intercession (paga can mean 'to intercede,' as in Genesis 18:29) creates a theological resonance: the one upon whom the iniquity is laid is also the one who intercedes. The Servant bears the burden and pleads for those whose burden he bears.

word_study.meaning: Avon: iniquity, guilt, the twisted consequence of sin (see verse 5). Kullanu: all of us (emphatic, with plural pronoun). The phrase 'iniquity of us all' creates a collective singularity—the aggregate of all individual iniquities is treated as a single entity placed upon the Servant.
word_study.significance: The repetition of kullanu (all of us) at the opening and closing of verse 6 creates an inclusio, framing the whole confessional statement with the theme of universality. Every human being, collectively, has gone astray and turned to his own way. That complete, universal iniquity has been consolidated and placed upon the Servant. No category of human sin is excluded; no individual is exempted from the collective guilt.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 53:6 is universally understood in Christian theology as describing Christ's redemptive work. Christ becomes the Shepherd who seeks and saves the lost sheep (Matthew 18:10-14, John 10:11). More profoundly, Christ becomes the Servant who bears the collective iniquity of all humanity. The verse's claim that the LORD has laid upon the Servant the iniquity of us all is understood to describe Christ's substitutionary atonement on the cross. The scattered sheep—humanity in its rebellion and lostness—are gathered through the Servant's sacrifice. The image is both juridical (legal substitution: the Servant bears the penalty for others' sin) and pastoral (the Shepherd gathers the lost flock). This combination—justice and mercy, law and love—defines Christian soteriology.
commentary.historical_context: The pastoral metaphor of wandering sheep was deeply embedded in Israelite culture and theology. Sheep were the primary livestock; shepherding was a fundamental occupation and metaphor for leadership. David, the paradigmatic king, was a shepherd (1 Samuel 16:11). The prophets repeatedly used shepherd imagery to indict Israel's leaders for leading the people astray (Jeremiah 23:1-4, Ezekiel 34). In this context, Isaiah 53:6 makes a revolutionary claim: instead of blaming the leaders (the shepherds), the people (the sheep) confess collective guilt. We have gone astray. Each has turned to his own way. Yet instead of facing the consequences, the Servant bears them. The verse reflects the exilic experience: Israel's loss of land, Temple, and independence could be interpreted as punishment for collective sin. But Isaiah 53:6 transforms that catastrophe into redemption: the exile and suffering is the Servant's bearing of the people's iniquity, not merely punishment. The DSS evidence confirms that this text was treated with extraordinary reverence and care—Column XLIV of 1QIsaᵃ is among the most carefully copied columns in Qumran.

text_kjv: He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah 53:7 presents the Servant's voluntary silence in the face of oppression and affliction. The double affirmation—'he opened not his mouth'—frames the verse and emphasizes this silence as a deliberate choice, not a condition imposed upon him. The prophetic text moves beyond the mere fact of suffering to highlight the manner of suffering: the Servant endures without protest, without self-defense, without demanding vindication. This silence distinguishes the Servant from typical human response to injustice.

The similes of the lamb led to slaughter and the sheep before its shearers are not random pastoral imagery but densely laden with sacrificial meaning. In ancient Israel, the lamb (seh) immediately evokes the Passover lamb of Exodus 12—the lamb whose blood marked the doorposts and delivered Israel from death. The sheep (rachel) before its shearers suggests not merely silence but submission, a creature utterly without recourse or resistance. The Covenant Rendering captures this dynamic: 'like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent.' Both animals are creatures of sacrifice, yet both are silent—not protesting their fate but accepting it. For the Israelite reader, this would conjure the daily tamid offering (the perpetual sacrifice) where lambs were brought without fanfare or resistance.

The theological weight lies in what the Servant does not do. He does not open his mouth to curse his oppressors, to plead his innocence, to summon divine intervention. His silence is not weakness but an extraordinary act of self-restraint and trust. Later Christian interpretation would see in this silence the restraint of Jesus before the Sanhedrin and Pilate (Matthew 26:63; Mark 14:61; Luke 23:9)—a restraint that required power, not its absence. The Ethiopian eunuch, reading this passage in Acts 8:32-35, would have grasped immediately that such silence could only belong to the Messiah.

word_study.meaning: To press upon, oppress, treat harshly. The niphal passive form suggests the Servant is subjected to oppression by external force, yet this passivity is paired with the active 'he opened not his mouth'—indicating that even under pressure, the silence is chosen.
word_study.significance: The verb carries the sense of relentless pressure from authority figures or enemies. In contexts of legal proceedings or judgment, nagash often describes the unjust treatment of the powerless by the powerful.

word_study.meaning: To afflict, humble, bring low. The niphal form indicates suffering imposed from outside, yet again the Servant does not respond in kind. The root can mean both 'to oppress' and 'to answer'—a wordplay suggesting the Servant is oppressed yet chooses not to answer back.
word_study.significance: The parallel verbs 'oppressed' and 'afflicted' form a hendiadys (two terms expressing one idea), emphasizing the totality of the Servant's suffering. Yet the silence that follows negates any expectation of retaliation or self-defense.

word_study.meaning: A young sheep or lamb, particularly one suitable for sacrifice. The term appears in Exodus 12:3 (Passover lamb) and throughout Leviticus in sacrificial contexts. The lamb is innocent, helpless, and brought voluntarily to the altar.
word_study.significance: The choice of seh over other Hebrew words for sheep (like ayil, a ram, or taleh, a young kid) deliberately invokes sacrificial language. The Servant is not merely compared to any animal but to an animal designated for holy purpose.

word_study.meaning: Those who shear or cut wool from sheep. The verb can also mean 'to cut off' or 'to divide.' The shearers are agents who reduce the sheep to utility, removing what is valuable without regard for the sheep's will.
word_study.significance: The image of shearers suggests those who strip away dignity or possessions from the Servant without remorse. The sheep does not resist its shearing—it stands mute before those who profit from its exploitation.

word_study.meaning: Silent, mute, unable or unwilling to speak. The form is feminine, agreeing with 'sheep' (rachel, also feminine). The root carries the sense of being bound to silence, struck mute.
word_study.significance: Unlike ordinary silence, ne'elmah suggests a condition in which speech itself becomes impossible or forbidden. Yet when applied to the Servant, this silence represents the height of dignity—not a loss of voice but a refusal to voice complaint.

cross_references.connection: The Passover lamb is brought to the household and kept until the fourteenth day, then sacrificed—evoking the voluntary nature of the lamb's selection and the redemptive purpose of its death.
The asham (guilt offering) is a specific Levitical sacrifice; the connection to verse 10 is anticipated here, establishing the sacrificial framework of the Servant Song.
Peter describes Christ's silence before accusation: 'Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously.'
The Ethiopian eunuch reads Isaiah 53:7-8 aloud, and Philip uses this passage to teach him about Christ, confirming early Christian understanding of the Servant as Messiah.

The Lord describes His suffering: 'Which suffering caused myself, even God the greatest of all, to tremble because of pain, and to bleed at every pore'—echoing the Servant's voluntary submission to suffering.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern royal and legal contexts, silence before a superior or court was often enforced—the accused or subordinate was expected to remain silent while judgment was pronounced. However, the Servant's silence is voluntary, which would have been extraordinary. The imagery of the lamb and sheep being led to slaughter reflects the daily practice of the Jerusalem Temple, where thousands of animals were sacrificed annually. An Israelite reader would recognize in these similes not foreign or exotic imagery but the landscape of their own religious practice. The shearers' treatment of the sheep without the sheep's consent reflects ancient attitudes toward property and animals as wholly subject to human will. What makes the Servant Song radical is that this silent, obedient victim is not merely animal—the language suggests a conscious, willing submission. The legal language ('oppressed,' 'judgment,' 'transgression') suggests the Servant's suffering occurs within a framework of false accusation and unjust proceedings, similar to how prophets in Israel faced opposition and legal harassment for speaking God's word.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 14:7 quotes Isaiah 53:7 almost identically: 'He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he opened not his mouth.' This verbatim inclusion in the Book of Mormon confirms that Latter-day Saints received the same Servant Song passage and understood it as messianic prophecy.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:107 describes the resurrected Christ's glory; the Servant Song is the background for understanding how one who suffered in such silence comes to exaltation and power. D&C 45:4-5 describes the Son's role as mediator and suffering servant.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Servant's silence and sacrificial submission parallel the covenant language of the temple: the willingness to sacrifice self-will to God's will. The lamb imagery connects to the Passover and the daily sacrifices that sanctified the temple service. In LDS theology, Christ is both the Lamb and the High Priest—He both offers and is offered.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 53:7 is among the clearest Old Testament predictions of Christ's Passion. The Servant's silence before oppression parallels Christ's silence before the Sanhedrin and Pilate. The lamb simile connects directly to John 1:29 ('Behold the Lamb of God') and establishes Christ as the fulfillment of all sacrificial lambs in the Old Testament economy. The voluntary nature of the silence suggests not victimhood but agency—the Servant chooses silence as part of His redemptive purpose. In Christian typology, Christ is both the lamb (victim) and the shepherd (leader); Isaiah 53:7 emphasizes the lamb aspect. The refusal to defend Himself or call down divine intervention (as He could have done, per Matthew 26:53) demonstrates the restraint and purposefulness of His suffering.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 53:7 challenges us to examine how we respond to unjust treatment, false accusation, or suffering we did not cause. The Servant's silence is not passive acceptance of wrong but active restraint chosen for a higher purpose. In contexts where we are tempted to defend ourselves, retaliate, or demand vindication, the Servant's example invites us to consider whether our silence might serve a redemptive purpose beyond our immediate circumstance. This does not mean never speaking truth or never standing against injustice—but it calls us to distinguish between defending our reputation and serving Christ's larger purposes. When we endure suffering with dignity and without bitterness, we participate in the Servant's witnessing power. The imagery of the lamb and sheep also invites reflection on our role not only as those who suffer but as those who, like the Servant, may need to give ourselves over to the will of God, holding back the natural desire to protect our own interests when the kingdom's work requires it.

text_kjv: He was taken from prison and from judgment: and who shall declare his generation? for he was cut off out of the land of the living: for the transgression of my people was he stricken.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah 53:8 marks a tonal shift in the Servant Song: the focus moves from the manner of suffering (silence) to the fact and meaning of suffering. The opening phrase—'He was taken from prison and from judgment'—has haunted interpreters for centuries. The Covenant Rendering reads: 'By oppression and judgment he was taken away; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of my people?' This rendering clarifies that the Servant is not taken out of prison to safety but is taken away through an unjust legal proceeding ('oppression and judgment'). He is removed, taken away to death through judicial process.

The rhetorical question 'who shall declare his generation?'—or as The Covenant Rendering renders it, 'who considered?'—is one of the most theologically loaded questions in the Hebrew Bible. The word 'generation' (doro) can mean the Servant's offspring, his era, his type or nature, or his fate. To 'declare' or 'consider' such a thing would require understanding the Servant's true significance. The question implies that at the moment of His death, no one—neither His contemporaries nor the powers that removed Him—grasped what was actually occurring. The Servant died uncomprehended, His true meaning hidden from those who witnessed it.

The verse then provides the theological interpretive key: 'he was cut off out of the land of the living: for the transgression of my people was he stricken.' The phrase 'cut off out of the land of the living' (nigzar me'erets chayyim) is the Hebrew Bible's primary language for death—a sudden, unjust severing from life itself. The Dead Sea Scrolls manuscript 1QIsaᵃ preserves this reading identically, confirming its antiquity. The final clause introduces the vicarious nature of the Servant's suffering: God now speaks in first person—'my people'—declaring that the Servant's death is not for His own transgression but for the transgression of God's covenant people. This is substitutionary suffering: the innocent One bears the consequence of the guilty many.

word_study.meaning: To take, seize, remove. The passive form (niphal) suggests the Servant is seized and carried away, not departing voluntarily. In legal contexts, the term can mean to arrest or apprehend.
word_study.significance: The verb establishes the Servant as the object of someone else's action—taken by force through unjust legal proceedings. Unlike verse 7's voluntary silence, verse 8 emphasizes what is done to the Servant.

word_study.meaning: Confinement, prison, restraint. The root can mean 'to restrain' or 'to shut up.' Some scholars argue otzer here means 'oppression' rather than literal imprisonment.
word_study.significance: Whether literal or metaphorical, otzer indicates the Servant's powerlessness and deprivation. Combined with 'judgment,' it suggests both illegal confinement and unjust legal proceedings.

word_study.meaning: Legal judgment, justice, due process. The term encompasses both the ideal (proper justice) and the reality (whatever judgment is rendered). When corrupted, mishpat becomes injustice.
word_study.significance: The pairing of 'oppression and judgment' suggests a false or perverted legal proceeding in which the powerless Servant is condemned by the instruments of human justice.

word_study.meaning: A generation, an age, a people, or (in some contexts) offspring or descendants. The term's semantic range is unusually broad and has generated centuries of interpretive debate.
word_study.significance: The ambiguity is likely intentional. The Servant's 'generation'—whether His offspring, His contemporaries, or His true nature—remains uncomprehended. No one 'considered' what was truly happening at His death.

word_study.meaning: To cut off, sever, divide. The niphal passive suggests an action imposed upon the Servant from outside. In biblical usage, nigzar typically indicates death, particularly sudden or violent death.
word_study.significance: The verb is definitive: the Servant is severed from the land of the living—cut off from ongoing life and community. This is death as termination, as separation from all that constitutes life in Israel's understanding.

word_study.meaning: The land of the living; the realm of life as opposed to the grave or Sheol. This phrase emphasizes that death is an exile from life itself, a removal to a different realm altogether.
word_study.significance: The poetic phrase suggests more than biological death—it implies a removal from the covenant community, from the land of Israel, from participation in God's people and God's work. To be 'cut off from the land of the living' is to be utterly severed.

word_study.meaning: Rebellion, transgression, sin against authority. The term carries the sense of deliberate disobedience or covenant-breaking, not merely error or inadvertence.
word_study.significance: The Servant is stricken for the pesha (rebellious transgression) of God's people—the deliberate covenant-breaking that constitutes rebellion against God. The weight of the term emphasizes that what the Servant bears is not mere mistake but willful sin.

cross_references.connection: The psalmist describes being 'cut off from the land of the living' (v. 5), a parallel phrase suggesting that premature or unjust death meant total severance from the community and God's work—the fate Isaiah predicts for the Servant.

The Israelite who does not afflict his soul on Yom Kippur 'shall be cut off from among his people'—a phrase using the same root (gazar) as Isaiah 53:8, suggesting the Servant's death as a judicial cutting off.
Jesus is brought before the Sanhedrin for trial, a legal proceeding that leads to His removal to crucifixion—the fulfillment of being 'taken from prison and judgment.'

Paul writes of Christ being 'made to be sin for us, who knew no sin'—explicating the principle of substitutionary suffering that Isaiah 53:8 announces: the innocent bearing the penalty for the guilty.
The vision describes the Savior's suffering in Gethsemane for all mankind, evoking Isaiah 53:8's principle that the Servant bears the transgression of 'my people'—all who accept His sacrifice.
King Benjamin's vision quotes Isaiah 53:8 identically (KJV), confirming that the Book of Mormon preserved this verse as messianic prophecy and that Nephite prophets understood the Servant as Christ.

commentary.historical_context: Ancient Near Eastern royal inscriptions often record the removal of enemies or rebels from the land through execution or exile—a way of erasing them from the community and history. However, the Servant Song inverts this pattern: the one removed is innocent, and His removal serves a redemptive purpose. The Dead Sea Scrolls manuscripts confirm the text's antiquity, showing that even by 125 BCE, Jewish readers grappled with the seeming contradiction that an innocent person would be 'cut off' for others' sins. The legal language ('prison,' 'judgment') suggests a deliberate miscarriage of justice—the Servant is condemned through corrupt legal process, not divine wrath. Jewish readers in the Second Temple period would have recognized this as a pattern familiar from their own history: prophets and righteous individuals persecuted and executed by the authorities. The phrase 'generation,' ambiguous in Hebrew, may have been intentionally multivalent, allowing both Jewish and later Christian interpreters to see different applications of the verse without requiring the original author to have explicitly predicted one or the other.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 14:8 quotes this verse: 'And he was taken from prison and from judgment: and who shall declare his generation? for he was cut off out of the land of the living: for the transgression of my people was he stricken.' King Benjamin presents the Servant Song to Nephite people, establishing that the pre-mortal Christ revealed to Nephite prophets the terms of His coming sacrifice. The Book of Mormon's inclusion of the full Servant Song confirms that the Restoration affirms Isaiah 53 as central messianic prophecy.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 133:50 describes Christ's suffering: 'Yea, verily I say unto you, that all those who say they would do the Lord's will, but have not done it, nor have they come into the covenant of the Lord, are not the elect.' The Servant's vicarious suffering for the covenant people anticipates the LDS understanding of Christ's atonement working for all who enter covenant with Him. D&C 45:4-5 describes the Son's role as Advocate before the Father—extending beyond the vicarious suffering of Isaiah 53:8 to ongoing intercessory work.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The judicial nature of the Servant's removal—'taken from prison and judgment'—parallels the temple law of sacrifice whereby the animal victim is brought to the altar through judicial or priestly authority. In the temple endowment, the covenant pattern involves willing submission to judgment and ordeal as the pathway to exaltation. The Servant's vicarious suffering for 'my people' prefigures the principle of temple proxy work, in which the living act on behalf of the dead.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 53:8 is foundational to Christian understanding of substitutionary atonement—the doctrine that Christ died not for His own sins (He had none) but for the sins of others. The phrase 'for the transgression of my people was he stricken' is cited or alluded to throughout the New Testament as the interpretive lens for Christ's death. The legal language ('prison and judgment') connects to the trial narratives in the Gospels, where Christ is condemned through judicial process. The phrase 'cut off from the land of the living' connects to language of resurrection in the New Testament: Christ is severed from life through death, yet this severance is not final but becomes the doorway to new life. The 'generation' that fails to understand the Servant at His death parallels the disciples' confusion about Jesus's purpose until the Resurrection and Pentecost. In Jewish messianic tradition, some interpreters understood verse 8 as referring to Israel's suffering in exile; Christian interpretation applied it to Christ as the Servant who bears Israel's punishment to effect Israel's redemption.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 53:8 invites us to grasp the reality of Christ's substitutionary suffering. The verse states unambiguously that the Servant is stricken 'for the transgression of my people'—not for His own failures but for ours. This is not a matter of sympathy or example but of actual substitution: the burden that should have fallen on us fell instead on Him. The phrase 'who shall declare his generation?'—meaning 'who understood what was happening?'—challenges us to examine whether we have truly 'considered' what the Atonement means. For many of us, like the original witnesses to Christ's death, the deepest meaning of His suffering may remain hidden until we experience it transformatively in our own lives through repentance and covenant. The verse also calls us to awareness of how readily human justice systems can become instruments of injustice, and how in God's economy, the innocent often bear consequences meant for the guilty—inviting us to both gratitude for Christ's bearing our consequences and care for victims of injustice in our own time.

text_kjv: And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death; because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah 53:9 deepens the paradox of the Servant's innocence and humiliation. The verse opens with the statement that the Servant's grave is made with the wicked and with a rich man—placing Him simultaneously in the company of transgressors and in burial befitting wealth. The Covenant Rendering clarifies: 'They made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death, although he had done no violence, and there was no deceit in his mouth.' The language suggests that at death, the Servant was treated as a criminal, grouped with the wicked; yet the grave prepared for Him belonged to a rich man—a paradox that Christian tradition resolved through the account of Joseph of Arimathea, a wealthy member of the Sanhedrin, who buried Jesus in his own new tomb (Matthew 27:57-60; John 19:38-42).

The double-negative assertion of innocence—'he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth'—is extraordinary in its absoluteness. The Servant did not perpetrate violence (chamas) nor did He employ deception or treachery (mirmah). Both terms carry moral weight: chamas suggests not merely physical violence but injustice and oppression; mirmah suggests not mere dishonesty but the betrayal of trust. The Covenant Rendering preserves this parallelism: nothing violent in action, nothing deceitful in speech. This total innocence stands in stark contrast to the transgression of 'my people' for which the Servant is stricken (v. 8). He bears the consequences of what He did not do.

The Dead Sea Scrolls variant in this verse (bemotav, 'in his deaths' vs. the apparent plural in MT) suggests an unusual or violent death—not a natural passing but something extraordinary. The wording 'in his death(s)' may be an intensive plural, emphasizing the violence or strangeness of the dying itself. The combination of execution-style burial (with the wicked) and rich-man's burial creates an image of radical reversal: the Servant, innocent and guiltless, receives a burial that mingles shame and honor, rejection and care, exactly as the Gospel narratives describe—condemned and crucified as a criminal, yet laid in a tomb befitting a nobleman.

word_study.meaning: Grave, burial place, sepulcher. The term refers to the physical location of burial and, by extension, the shame or honor associated with one's final resting place.
word_study.significance: In ancient Israel, the location and manner of burial carried profound meaning: burial with one's ancestors signified covenant continuity; denial of burial was the ultimate shame. The Servant is buried with the wicked (dishonor) and with a rich man (honor)—a paradox resolved only through the Gospel accounts.

word_study.meaning: Wicked, evil, guilty of transgression. The plural form indicates multiple transgressors. In prophetic literature, the resha'im are often the enemies of God's people or those who pervert justice.
word_study.significance: To be buried with the wicked is to be classified with transgressors—the ultimate shame for an innocent person. The Servant's humiliation includes being associated with evil, though He is entirely free from evil.

word_study.meaning: Rich, wealthy. The term indicates material abundance and, in the context of ancient Israel, often implicitly judgment (wealth could be earned justly or through oppression).
word_study.significance: The rich man's association with the wicked in prophetic literature often carried negative connotation—the wealthy who oppress the poor. Yet here, the rich man's wealth is used for redemptive purpose: to provide the Servant a proper burial. Christian interpretation identifies this rich man as Joseph of Arimathea, whose wealth serves the Servant's dignity in death.

word_study.meaning: Violence, oppression, wrongdoing. The term encompasses not merely physical force but injustice, the violation of covenant, the exploitation of power for selfish gain.
word_study.significance: The assertion that the Servant did no chamas is a claim to absolute integrity—He never violated the rights or persons of others, never used power unjustly. This makes His suffering for others' transgression even more striking.

word_study.meaning: Deceit, treachery, falsehood. The term specifically suggests deception that violates trust or covenant, not merely mistaken speech.
word_study.significance: The claim that no deceit was in the Servant's mouth is a claim to absolute truthfulness and trustworthiness in speech. Combined with the claim to no violence in action, it establishes total innocence in both deed and word—the Servant never violated justice through either violence or deception.

word_study.meaning: Mouth, speech, language. The term emphasizes the instrument of communication and covenant.
word_study.significance: The Servant's mouth, which in verse 7 opened not in protest, is here certified as free from all deceit—whatever the Servant spoke was truthful and trustworthy. The focus on speech at both ends of the Servant's ministry (silence in suffering, truthfulness in all utterance) emphasizes the integrity of His communication.

cross_references.connection: Joseph of Arimathea, a rich man and member of the Sanhedrin, takes Jesus's body and places it in his own new tomb—the historical fulfillment of Isaiah 53:9.
Peter quotes Isaiah 53:9 exactly: 'Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth'—establishing that the Servant Song was understood in early Christian teaching as describing Christ.

John's Gospel provides an expanded account of the burial, describing Joseph of Arimathea as a 'disciple of Jesus' (not mentioned in other Gospels), emphasizing the honor rendered to Jesus despite the disgrace of crucifixion.

King Benjamin prophesies that the Son of God 'shall go forth, suffering pains and afflictions and temptations of every kind; and this that the word might be fulfilled which saith he will take upon him the pains and the sicknesses of his people'—echoing the absolute innocence of the Servant who suffers without cause of His own.
The epistle declares that the High Priest (Christ) was 'in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin'—affirming the Servant's absolute innocence that Isaiah 53:9 asserts.
The vision describes those who are exalted as receiving 'all things' and being in the presence of the Father and Son—the vindication of the innocent Servant after His burial and humiliation.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern burial practices, the location and manner of burial were crucial to one's honor and identity. Criminals were often cast into common graves or left unburied as the ultimate disgrace; the wealthy were buried in rock-hewn tombs, often family sepulchers. For the Servant to be buried simultaneously with the wicked (suggesting execution and mass burial or communal dishonor) and with a rich man (suggesting individual honor and careful preparation) would have seemed paradoxical to ancient readers. The Gospels' accounts of Jesus's crucifixion between two criminals and His burial in Joseph's tomb make perfect sense in this context: the Servant receives the shame of execution and the honor of careful burial. The Dead Sea Scrolls variants suggest that even by 125 BCE, Jewish scribes were intensely engaged with this verse, recognizing its prediction of an unusual death and unusual burial. The assertion of absolute innocence ('no violence, no deceit') would have resonated with Jewish readers familiar with the tradition of righteous suffering (represented by figures like the Maccabean martyrs, who were celebrated for dying without guilt) and anticipated messianic hope that the Messiah would be wrongly condemned.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 14:9 quotes Isaiah 53:9 with slight variation in punctuation and emphasis, but the substance is identical. King Benjamin's presentation of this verse to Nephite people confirms that the Restoration recognizes Isaiah 53:9 as messianic prophecy fulfilled in Christ's burial.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:24-29 describes the Savior's victory following His humiliation and death: 'And now, after the many testimonies which have been given of him, this is the testimony, last of all, which we give of him: That he lives!' The humiliation of the grave (Isaiah 53:9) is followed by the vindication of resurrection. D&C 19:16-17 describes Christ's suffering: He 'descended below all things' before ascending. The grave with the wicked and the rich man is that 'below all things.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The paradox of the Servant being buried with both the wicked and the rich mirrors the temple principle of vicarious work: the innocent endure the consequences intended for the guilty, yet receive honor in the process. The Servant's burial in a tomb belonging to one who becomes His disciple (as John's Gospel suggests) anticipates the temple principle of the living acting on behalf of the dead.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 53:9 is crucial to Christian interpretation of the Passion. The verse establishes that the one who suffers is not suffering for His own transgression but for others', and that this suffering paradoxically results in both shame (burial with the wicked, as a criminal) and honor (burial in a rich man's tomb, with care and respect). The Gospel accounts of Jesus's death—crucified between criminals, buried by a member of the very court that condemned Him—fulfill this dual paradox.
