His willingness to drink the cup of judgment (Matthew 26:39) — the complete opposite of the leaders' presumptuous drinking — is His redemptive work. Where they pursued shekar (intoxicants), He approached His passion with perfect clarity. Where they believed in perpetual abundance divorced from consequence, He accepted the consequence of human sin. The Eucharist/Sacrament becomes the counterpoint to Isaiah 56:12 — the wine Christ offers is not a symbol of careless indulgence but of redemptive sacrifice.
commentary.application: For modern readers, Isaiah 56:12 warns against the theology of presumption that seduces the comfortable and powerful. It asks: Do you assume tomorrow will be as today because you have insulated yourself from consequences? Do you drink (metaphorically or literally) to escape moral awareness? Do you surround yourself with others who affirm your choices without calling you to account? The verse also warns against a subtler presumption: that progress is inevitable, that technology or wealth guarantees security, that consequences don't apply to the privileged. For leaders in particular, it is a wake-up call: the health of your organization (family, ward, business, nation) depends not on yesterday's momentum but on your present faithfulness to principle. Complacency is the enemy of stewardship. Finally, for all of us, it calls us to genuine sobriety — not mere abstinence from alcohol, but spiritual clarity, moral alertness, and humility before God's sovereignty. Tomorrow is not guaranteed to be like today. Justice will come. The only security is covenant faithfulness.

text_kjv: The righteous perisheth, and no man layeth it to heart: and merciful men are taken away, none considering that the righteous is taken away from the evil to come.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah opens this chapter with a paradoxical lament that reframes death as mercy. The righteous are perishing—being swept away from the land of the living—yet the people around them barely notice or mourn. This is not carelessness; it is a divine providence so subtle that it goes unrecognized. The term "merciful men" (anshei chesed in Hebrew) refers specifically to those bound by covenant loyalty, the faithful remnant who have remained true to YHWH in an age of widespread apostasy. Their removal from the scene is not punishment but protection: they are being taken away *from* the evil to come, spared from witnessing the full measure of Judah's judgment.

word_study.meaning: The just one; one who stands in right relationship with God and covenant community. The article suggests a specific category or archetypal figure, not merely individuals.
word_study.significance: The righteous are identified not by personal merit alone but by their faithfulness to the covenant. In Isaiah's context, they are the anawim—the poor, humble remnant who have not bowed to idolatry.

word_study.term_english: merciful men / men of steadfast love
word_study.meaning: Men of hesed (steadfast love, covenant loyalty, enduring mercy). Chesed denotes the binding loyalty of covenant relationship, the faithful devotion that persists regardless of circumstance.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes that these are 'covenant-loyal ones'—not sentimentalists, but those whose entire identity is bound up in faithfulness to YHWH's covenant. Their removal is a mercy precisely because they are spared the coming calamity.

word_study.meaning: To be gathered, collected, swept away. The verb can mean death (being gathered to one's fathers) or removal from a place. Here it carries both senses simultaneously.
word_study.significance: The verb choice is tender but unambiguous. Death for the righteous is not pictured as violent destruction but as a gentle gathering, a removal from the scene of judgment to come.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'from the face of the evil' or 'from the presence of the calamity.' Ra'ah can mean evil, disaster, calamity, or misfortune.
word_study.significance: This clause provides the theological interpretation of what seems like premature death: the righteous are not being punished but rescued, removed from the stage before the full weight of judgment falls on the nation.

cross_references.connection: The opening movement of Isaiah 57 introduces the theme of the righteous perishing unnoticed, which frames the entire chapter's contrast between the humble faithful and the idolatrous majority.
When King Josiah is told he will die in peace and be gathered to his grave before the evil comes upon Jerusalem, this echoes Isaiah's promise that the righteous are taken away from coming judgment.
The righteous are remembered with blessing when they perish—contrasting with Isaiah's lament that no one takes the righteous' death to heart, suggesting spiritual blindness in the community.
Nephi's vision of the righteous being gathered (those who love YHWH) parallels Isaiah's comfort that the covenant-loyal are removed to safety, separated from those who embrace idolatry.
The Lord promises that the righteous shall be gathered in mine own place, echoing Isaiah's promise that death for the faithful is a removal to safety and peace.

commentary.historical_context: Isaiah 57 is set in the context of Judah's spiritual deterioration in the late 8th century BCE. While the prophet has been calling for return to YHWH, the majority of the nation—especially the urban elite and certain religious leaders—have embraced syncretistic worship, incorporating elements of Canaanite fertility religion and other pagan practices. The "righteous" in this context are the faithful minority: those who have rejected idolatry despite intense social pressure. The removal of such individuals through natural death may have seemed to contemporaries like a sign of divine disfavor (a common assumption in the ancient Near East: death = punishment from the gods). Isaiah reinterprets this tragedy as the opposite—a mercy, a rescue. Ancient funeral practices in Israel involved communal lamentation and remembrance; the lament here is that even this basic recognition is withheld, suggesting either the righteous die in isolation or the community is too spiritually blind to recognize their loss.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 12:37, Alma describes how the righteous are 'taken away from the evil to come,' echoing Isaiah's promise of protection through removal. Similarly, the Book of Mormon consistently teaches that the faithful remnant will be separated—gathered—from those who embrace wickedness, suggesting continuity between Isaiah's promise and restored covenant theology.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:34-45 describes the gathering of the elect in the last days, with particular emphasis on the separation of the righteous from the wicked before judgment falls. This is Isaiah's 'taken away from the evil to come' restated in latter-day terms. The gathering is not merely physical relocation but spiritual rescue.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where the righteous (anshei chesed, covenant-loyal ones) gather to renew their steadfast love for YHWH. Isaiah's opening promise that such ones are 'taken away' unto peace can be understood as an anticipation of the covenant's ultimate fulfillment—that those who faithfully keep their temple covenants will be gathered to the Lord's house at last.

commentary.christological_typology: The righteous one who perishes unnoticed prefigures Christ himself. Jesus, the ultimate Tsaddiq (the Righteous One), would be taken away to his death while few understood the merciful purpose of that removal—that he was being taken away *for* the evil of the world, bearing it so that others might be spared eternal judgment. The gathering of the anshei chesed anticipates the gathering of the faithful in Christ.
commentary.application: This verse calls modern covenant members to recognize a paradoxical truth: the death of faithful saints is not a sign of divine failure but of divine mercy. When a devout member dies young, or when faithful individuals are removed from a community, we should not interpret their passing as punishment or abandonment. Instead, we are invited to trust that YHWH sees what we cannot—that those who have kept covenant faithfulness are being protected, gathered unto a place of rest. For us personally, this suggests that our faithful bearing of covenant obligations, even when unnoticed or undervalued by the world, is being witnessed and honored by the Father. Our service matters, our steadfast love (chesed) is counted, and we will be gathered.

text_kjv: He shall enter into peace: they shall rest in their beds, each one walking in his uprightness.

commentary.narrative: This verse completes Isaiah's eulogy for the righteous, presenting death not as an ending but as an entrance into peace (shalom). The language is among the gentlest in the Old Testament: the righteous do not fall to judgment, do not suffer defeat, but rather *enter* into peace—a transition, a passage, almost a homecoming. The image of resting "on their beds" evokes both the sleep of death and the ultimate rest promised to the faithful. The final clause—"each one walking in his uprightness"—clarifies that this rest belongs to those who have lived faithfully. The plural "they shall rest" indicates that this promise encompasses all the covenant-loyal who die, not merely one individual. Death for the righteous is thus reframed from curse to blessing, from punishment to reward.

word_study.meaning: Wholeness, completeness, well-being, absence of conflict. Shalom is not merely the absence of war but the presence of right relationship, flourishing, and integrity.
word_study.significance: That the righteous 'enter into peace' suggests a transition from the fractured, conflicted state of the world (torn by idolatry and injustice) into a state of complete wholeness and restoration. This is the ultimate fulfillment of covenant relationship—not just forgiveness, but restoration to the Father's presence.

word_study.meaning: They rest upon their beds. Nuach means to rest, settle, be at ease. Mishkab denotes a bed (for sleep or death). The imagery evokes both restful sleep and the finality of death.
word_study.significance: The bed is a place of vulnerability and restoration—where the body repairs itself in sleep. For the righteous, death is presented as rest, not as waking torment. This gentle imagery contrasts sharply with the fate of the idolatrous, which will be characterized by agitation and burning.

word_study.meaning: Straightness, directness, uprightness. Derived from a root meaning 'straight' or 'level.' It denotes walking directly in the way of covenant, without deviation or duplicity.
word_study.significance: The righteous one who has walked straight—not turned aside to idolatry, not compromised the covenant—enters into peace. Uprightness is the condition and the character that qualifies one for this rest.

word_study.meaning: The participle 'walking' combined with 'uprightness' suggests an ongoing condition of faithful walk, not a single act.
word_study.significance: The righteous are not those who walked uprightly once, but those whose entire lives have been characterized by faithful, straight walking in covenant. This habitually righteous life earns the right to rest.

cross_references.connection: Abraham is promised that he will go to his fathers 'in peace'—a death in old age after a fulfilled life, echoing Isaiah's promise that the righteous enter into peace.
The shepherd psalm promises that the righteous will be led to rest in green pastures and fear no evil—a similar reframing of death and vulnerability as occasions for divine care and peace.

The New Testament explicitly connects Isaiah's theme of entering into rest with the Sabbath and the promise that the righteous will 'enter into His rest,' using identical terminology from the Septuagint.
Alma teaches that the spirits of the righteous are received into a state of happiness and rest, precisely echoing Isaiah's promise that the righteous enter into peace and rest on their beds.
The Lord promises 'peace in this world, and eternal life in the world to come,' mirroring Isaiah's promise that the righteous enter into shalom.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, death was generally feared as a descent into Sheol, a gray and diminished existence. The concept of entering into *peace* at death was countercultural—a profound statement of hope in YHWH's faithfulness. Israelite burial practices involved laying the dead to rest in tombs or graves, often in family burial sites; the image of resting on beds thus had literal resonance. The phrase "entering into peace" also carries political overtones: peace (shalom) in the ancient Near East was the result of a covenant arrangement, often between a greater and lesser power. Here, Isaiah suggests that the righteous have a covenant arrangement with YHWH that guarantees them peace even in death—a status and a security that transcends earthly calamity.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 2:41 teaches that those who yield to the enticings of the Holy Spirit and obey God will find rest in this life and eternal life in the world to come—a direct echo of Isaiah's promise. The Book of Mormon consistently teaches that covenant faithfulness leads to rest and peace, reinforcing Isaiah's vision.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 84:24 speaks of those who are sanctified through obedience receiving 'all that [the Father] hath,' which is presented as a state of peace and rest. The promise of entering into peace parallels the temple covenant promise of exaltation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The bed imagery may allude to the altar or to the sanctuary as a place of rest. In temple theology, the faithful are promised that they will rest from their labors and enter into the Lord's rest—a direct fulfillment of Isaiah's promise. The temple is the place where the righteous are sealed unto peace.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate Righteous One who enters into peace through death—not as an end, but as a transition to exaltation. His resurrection is the guarantee that all who walk uprightly in Him will likewise enter into peace. The promise of rest prefigures the resurrection and the ultimate rest that comes through the Atonement.
commentary.application: For modern members, this verse offers profound comfort in the face of death—both our own and that of loved ones. The death of a faithful saint need not be met with despair but with the assurance that they have 'entered into peace,' that their labor in the vineyard is now complete and they rest from their labors. For those grieving, this verse invites us to trust that the righteous are in a state of wholeness and restoration. For ourselves, it calls us to walk uprightly now—to live with integrity and covenant faithfulness—so that when our time comes, we too will enter into peace with confidence.

text_kjv: But draw near hither, ye sons of the sorceress, the seed of the adulterer and the whore.

commentary.narrative: The tone shifts violently. After the tender eulogy for the righteous in verses 1-2, Isaiah now issues a courtroom summons against the idolaters of Judah. The word "but" (Hebrew vav, often untranslated) marks the dramatic pivot: from consolation to accusation. The address—"draw near hither"—mimics the language of legal proceedings; the accused are called to stand before the judge. The epithets that follow are blistering: "sons of the sorceress, seed of the adulterer and the whore." These are not merely insults but genealogical accusations suggesting that idolatry and sexual immorality run through the bloodline of Judah's leadership. The term "sorceress" (onenah in Hebrew) may refer to practitioners of divination and magic, but more broadly characterizes those who deceive through false promises and false gods. The accusation of adultery points to the core sin of idolatry in prophetic rhetoric: covenant infidelity, the unfaithfulness of a bride who betrays her husband.

word_study.meaning: Draw near, approach, come close. In legal contexts, it summons the accused to present themselves before judgment. In worship contexts, it can mean to offer oneself in service.
word_study.significance: The imperative form is a command, not a request. This is the language of divine authority, summoning the accused to stand trial. The irony is that those who 'draw near' to false gods are now being summoned to draw near to judgment.

word_study.meaning: A female practitioner of divination, enchantment, or sorcery. Related to 'onen,' which can mean to mutter spells or practice augury. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this word with plene spelling (with waw), emphasizing its clarity.
word_study.significance: In Israel's law code (Exodus 22:18, Leviticus 19:26), sorcery is strictly forbidden. The accusation that the idolaters are 'sons of the sorceress' suggests they inherit spiritual deception—they have been taught to rely on false spiritual power rather than on YHWH.

word_study.meaning: One who commits adultery, one who breaks the marriage covenant. In prophetic rhetoric, this term is used metaphorically for Israel's unfaithfulness to YHWH in the covenant.
word_study.significance: The metaphor is consistent throughout Isaiah and the prophetic corpus: Israel is the bride of YHWH; idolatry is adultery. The 'seed of the adulterer' are those born of this covenantal infidelity, inheritors of apostasy.

word_study.meaning: One who commits sexual immorality (znut), often used metaphorically for idolatry. The verb means to stray, to deviate from the covenant path.
word_study.significance: The imagery of prostitution and sexual immorality is tightly bound to idolatry in Isaiah and throughout the prophets. Canaanite fertility religion involved ritual prostitution and sexual acts as part of worship; the language reflects the actual practice that has infected Judah.

cross_references.connection: Jeremiah uses identical metaphors of Israel as an unfaithful bride and harlot, emphasizing that idolatry is covenant infidelity. The language of genealogical corruption ('seed of') is also present.
Hosea's marriage metaphor depicts Israel as an unfaithful wife who 'goes after lovers' (idols), using nearly identical language to Isaiah's accusation of adultery and harlotry.
Earlier in Isaiah, Jerusalem is depicted as a harlot, and her leaders are accused of infidelity. Isaiah 57:3 continues this consistent theme of Judah's apostasy as sexual betrayal.
Alma condemns those who have 'cast off the commandments of God and denied the Holy Ghost,' using similar language of spiritual adultery and betrayal of covenant.
The Lord describes those who rebel against His commandments as breaking covenant and thereby aligning themselves with darkness, mirroring Isaiah's accusation of spiritual infidelity.

commentary.historical_context: In the late 8th century BCE, Judah was experiencing significant religious syncretism. Archaeological and textual evidence suggests that Asherah worship (a Canaanite goddess) had been incorporated into the Jerusalem temple itself; fertility cults, divination practices, and sexual ritual were permeating Judean society. The accusation of 'sons of the sorceress' likely refers to the widespread practice of consulting mediums and diviners (condemned in Deuteronomy 18:10-12), possibly including practitioners trained in Mesopotamian astrology during the reign of Manasseh. The accusation of adultery and harlotry reflects both the metaphorical language of covenant breach and the literal practice of cultic prostitution associated with fertility worship. Isaiah's courtroom language ('draw near') echoes the rib pattern common in prophetic rhetoric, where YHWH brings a lawsuit against His unfaithful people.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 5:49-52 contains a similar courtroom summons, where Alma calls the people to answer for their spiritual condition. The call to 'draw near' and face judgment for covenant infidelity is paralleled in Nephite prophecy and preaching.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:20-21 describes the Lord's indictment of the Church members for 'taking the name of the Lord in vain' and breaking covenant, using language of accusation and summons similar to Isaiah's courtroom drama.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The contrast between the righteous (who enter the temple in peace and covenant) and the idolaters (summoned to judgment) reinforces the temple as the place of true covenant and the alternative worship systems as spiritual adultery against the marriage covenant with YHWH.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus will be the ultimate judge who calls the unfaithful to account. His imagery of judgment often invokes courtroom language ('draw near'), and His condemnation of those who follow false spirits parallels Isaiah's accusation here. The Atonement makes clear that covenant infidelity (spiritual adultery) is the core sin that separates us from God, but only Christ's sacrifice can restore the broken marriage relationship.
commentary.application: This verse calls us to examine our own spiritual fidelity. Are we 'sons and daughters of the sorceress'—inheriting from a culture of spiritual deception, consulting sources other than revelation, relying on false prophets and counterfeit spirituality? Are we committing 'adultery' against our covenant with YHWH by placing other loyalties (wealth, power, worldly approval) before our marriage covenant with Him? The summons to 'draw near' is ultimately an invitation to stand before the Lord in honesty about our spiritual condition and to choose true covenant faithfulness over inherited apostasy.

text_kjv: Against whom do ye sport yourselves? against whom make ye a wide mouth, and draw out the tongue? are ye not children of transgression, a seed of falsehood,

commentary.narrative: The accusation intensifies with vivid imagery of mockery and contempt. The idolaters are not merely unfaithful; they are actively *mocking* something or someone—likely the prophets of YHWH or YHWH Himself. The gestures described—opening the mouth wide and sticking out the tongue—are the universal language of taunting and derision, found in both ancient and modern contexts as signs of extreme disrespect. The progression from genealogy (verse 3: "sons of the sorceress") to behavior (verse 4: "mocking, jeering") builds Isaiah's case. The rhetorical questions—"Against whom do ye sport yourselves?"—invite the accused to name their target. The answer, left implicit but clear from context, is that they mock YHWH and His representatives. The final accusation—"children of transgression, seed of falsehood"—echoes verse 3's genealogical language but shifts from inherited corruption to active rebellion. "Transgression" (pesha in Hebrew) denotes willful rebellion, not mere error; "falsehood" suggests that the entire religious system they have embraced is built on lies.

word_study.meaning: To delight in, to take pleasure in, to sport or jest. In this context, it carries the sense of mocking, ridiculing, or making light of something. The root suggests a delighting that is contemptuous.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes not merely disagreement but active delight in mockery—a spiritual pleasure taken in scorning the truth. This suggests a hardened heart, not merely an honest intellectual doubt.

word_study.meaning: To widen or expand the mouth. Pe means mouth or opening. The image is of an exaggerated, gaping expression of contempt.
word_study.significance: The physical gesture reinforces the verbal mockery—the entire body becomes an instrument of derision. In ancient contexts, such gestures were considered deeply insulting, equivalent to modern obscene gestures.

word_study.meaning: To extend, prolong, or stick out the tongue. Arach means to make long or extend; lashon means tongue. The physical act of protruding the tongue is a universal gesture of mockery and contempt.
word_study.significance: The tongue is the instrument of speech and prophecy. By sticking out their tongues at the prophets or at YHWH, the idolaters are literally silencing truth and asserting their own false speech in its place.

word_study.meaning: Transgression, rebellion, willful violation of covenant. Pesha specifically denotes deliberate disobedience, not inadvertent error.
word_study.significance: The accusation is not that Judah has made a mistake but that they have willfully rebelled. Their mockery is not innocent humor but defiant scorn of the covenant itself.

word_study.meaning: Falsehood, lie, deceit, unreliability. Shaqer refers to speech or reality that does not correspond to truth; it is the opposite of 'truth' (emet).
word_study.significance: To be 'seed of falsehood' is to be rooted in a system built on lies—false gods, false priests, false promises. The idolatrous system is fundamentally unreal, a delusion.

cross_references.connection: The psalmist describes enemies who 'gnashed upon me with their teeth,' using similar language of physical mockery and contemptuous gesture directed against the righteous.
Those who pass by Jerusalem after her fall 'hiss and shake their head,' using similar gestures of contempt and mockery, suggesting this was a conventional sign of scorn in the ancient Near East.
Those who mock Jesus on the cross 'wagged their heads' and opened their mouths to jeer at Him, using gestures nearly identical to those Isaiah describes here.

Nephi prophesies of false teachers who 'preach up unto themselves their own power and their own glory,' mocking true doctrine in favor of comfortable lies—precisely the 'seed of falsehood' Isaiah describes.
The Lord describes those who sign themselves over to the devil as those who 'despise the words of life,' engaging in deliberate transgression against covenant truth.

commentary.historical_context: The mockery described here was likely directed at prophetic figures or at the prophetic message itself. In the ancient Near East, prophets (nevi'im) were viewed as conduits of divine truth; to mock the prophet was to mock the god who sent him. The gestures of contempt—gaping mouth, protruding tongue—are documented in Egyptian tomb paintings and reliefs as signs of mockery and derision. In the context of late 8th-century Judah, the 'children of transgression' who mocked the prophets would have included court officials confident in their alliance with Assyria, religious leaders invested in syncretistic practices, and urban elites comfortable with idolatry. The accusation of being 'seed of falsehood' places this mockery in a theological framework: these are not merely politically astute men but spiritually deluded ones, whose entire worldview is built on delusion.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 19:7-9, Nephi describes how 'the wicked' will mock and 'despise the words of righteousness,' using language that echoes Isaiah's depiction of active, gleeful contempt for truth. The Book of Mormon repeatedly warns against this posture of willful mockery.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 84:53-57 warns that 'many shall say unto you: Master, we know that thou art a true teacher; by your words we shall be judged; we receive the abundance of your mercies; but those who do not believe shall say: This is not of God.' The mocking of those who reject YHWH's word is a sign of the 'seed of falsehood' being sown.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The mocking of YHWH's truth is the antithesis of the reverent, truthful covenants made in the temple. Those who mock are inverting the temple's central purpose—the honest interchange between God and man.

commentary.christological_typology: The mockery described here anticipates the mockery of Christ. Jesus, the Truth incarnate, would be mocked by those rooted in falsehood. The gestures of contempt—the gaping mouths, the jeering—would be directed at Him on the cross. His crucifixion is the ultimate revelation of how the 'seed of falsehood' responds to the seed of truth.
commentary.application: We must examine whether we have fallen into the posture of mockery toward truth. Do we jest at the words of living prophets? Do we scoff at priesthood authority or at sacred ordinances? Do we make light of covenant obligations? This verse warns that such mockery is not innocent humor but active rebellion, a sign that we are aligning ourselves with the 'seed of falsehood' rather than with truth. Conversely, it calls us to reverence toward sacred things and to a serious, non-mocking posture toward the Lord's word. The mocking gesture of the open mouth and extended tongue becomes, in this context, a symbol of spiritual deafness and blindness—we must ensure that our mouths are instruments of truth, not tools of scorn.

text_kjv: Enflaming yourselves with idols under every green tree, slaying the children in the valleys under the clifts of the rocks?

commentary.narrative: Isaiah now catalogs the specific practices of Judah's apostasy, bringing the courtroom indictment from abstract mockery to concrete, horrifying deed. Two grave sins are laid bare: idolatrous worship in sacred groves ("under every green tree") and child sacrifice ("slaying the children in the valleys"). The term "enflaming yourselves with idols" (Hebrew nechamim ba'elim) carries multiple layers of meaning—burning with lust (a reference to fertility cult practices), burning with fervent devotion to false gods, and possibly burning children in fire as offerings. The green trees were sacred spaces in Canaanite religion where worshippers engaged in fertility rites, divination, and various forms of ritual that the law of Moses strictly forbade. But the mention of child sacrifice elevates the accusation from ritual impropriety to moral atrocity. The valleys "under the clefts of the rocks" almost certainly refer to the Valley of Hinnom (Gehenna), which had become a site of Molech worship—a practice explicitly condemned in Levitical law (Leviticus 18:21, 20:2-5). Isaiah is not exaggerating; historical and archaeological evidence confirms that child sacrifice was indeed practiced in Judah during certain periods, particularly under kings like Manasseh.

word_study.meaning: Those who burn, are inflamed, or are in a state of fervent desire. Related to 'necham' (comfort, console) but used here in the sense of burning with passion or lust. The Covenant Rendering captures this as 'burn with lust.'
word_study.significance: The burning imagery suggests both the fires of desire (the sensual practices of fertility religion) and the fires of Molech (into which children were thrown). The word carries a single emotional and physical state—the heated fervor of the idolaters.

word_study.meaning: Among the elim (oaks, terebinths, or possibly 'gods'—elim can mean either trees or deities). The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this reading identically. The double meaning may be intentional: the sacred oaks were believed to be dwelling places of the divine.
word_study.significance: The ambiguity of elim (trees/gods) captures the syncretism precisely: the Canaanite worship system identified sacred trees as divine manifestations. Isaiah's language refuses to separate the physical practice from the theological delusion.

word_study.meaning: A verdant, flourishing, green tree. Ra'anan suggests vitality, moisture, life. The phrase 'every green tree' appears frequently in prophetic denunciations of Canaanite practice.
word_study.significance: The green trees symbolized fertility, life, and the renewal of crops and flocks—the central concern of agricultural societies. Worship under these trees was seen as a way to ensure fertility; it was thoroughly practical religious syncretism, not merely doctrinal error.

word_study.meaning: Those who slaughter, butcher, or sacrifice children. Shachat means to kill, slay, or sacrifice (used in temple sacrificial contexts but here applied to human sacrifice). Yeladim means children, youth.
word_study.significance: The word shachat, normally used for legitimate animal sacrifice, is here used for the illegitimate killing of children. The juxtaposition highlights the perversion: what is lawful for animals is being committed against children.

word_study.meaning: In the valleys, wadis, or stream beds. Nachal refers to a flowing stream or the valley containing it. The specific valley is almost certainly the Valley of the Son of Hinnom (Ge Hinnom in Hebrew), which became the site of Molech worship.
word_study.significance: The valley was chosen for child sacrifice because it was hidden from public view, removed from the city proper—a physical manifestation of the hidden horror of apostasy. Hinnom later becomes the Hebrew word for hell (Gehenna), suggesting that the place of child sacrifice became symbolically associated with perdition.

word_study.meaning: Clefts, crevices, or branches (se'if can mean both crevice and branch) of the rocks (selah). The term evokes dark, hidden places within rocky terrain.
word_study.significance: The imagery of hidden places reinforces the secretive, shameful nature of the practice. Child sacrifice was not carried out in daylight or in public; it was hidden in the rocky crevices and valleys, suggesting the practitioners knew it violated both law and conscience.

cross_references.connection: The law explicitly forbids passing children through fire to Molech, showing that Isaiah's accusation reflects a direct violation of Mosaic law that was apparently being practiced in Judah.

When King Josiah reforms Judah's religion, he defiles Topheth in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom to prevent child sacrifice to Molech, confirming that such practices were indeed occurring in Judah during Isaiah's era.
Jeremiah condemns the same practice of burning children in the Valley of Hinnom, using nearly identical language to Isaiah and also linking it to Baal worship.
Nephi quotes Isaiah's denunciations of Judah's sins, including the turning to false gods and corrupt practices, applying Isaiah's pattern to the Nephite records as well.
The Lord warns of spiritual death and perdition for those who reject the covenant and embrace false worship—using language that echoes the ultimate consequence of the path Isaiah describes.

commentary.historical_context: Archaeological evidence from sites like Carthage (where Phoenician/Canaanite practice was prominent) and textual references in classical authors (Plutarch, Diodorus Siculus) confirm that child sacrifice was indeed part of Molech worship in the Levantine world. In Judah specifically, the practice appears to have been most prevalent during the reign of Manasseh (687-642 BCE), when Assyrian religious influence and cultural pressure led to widespread syncretism. The Valley of Hinnom (Gehenna) was the primary site of such sacrifice in Jerusalem; archaeological work has uncovered evidence of infant burial and cremation in the area. Fertility cult practices under sacred trees were ubiquitous in Canaanite religion and persistently infiltrated Israelite worship. The worship under 'every green tree' reflects actual practice: archaeology has found evidence of sacred tree imagery in Palestinian temple sites. Isaiah's language, while certainly rhetorical and designed to shock, reflects actual practices that were occurring in 8th-century Judah, making the accusation devastatingly real rather than merely metaphorical.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 37:21-32, Alma teaches that wickedness leads to the shedding of innocent blood and the abandonment of truth, using language that echoes Isaiah's denunciation of child sacrifice as the ultimate expression of covenant abandonment. Moroni 9:7-10 describes similar horrors in the Nephite wars, suggesting that the pattern Isaiah identifies transcends time and place.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:103-109 describes the 'sons of perdition' as those who crucify Christ anew and thereby reject mercy—a spiritual parallel to Isaiah's accusation that those who sacrifice children have committed the ultimate violation of covenant. The pattern of escalating wickedness leading to the shedding of innocent blood appears throughout the Doctrine and Covenants.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple was the place of legitimate sacrifice—animals offered in atonement for sin. The perversion of sacrifice into child sacrifice in the valleys represents the inversion of the temple's sacred purpose. The temple teaches covenant; these practices teach the abandonment of covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: Child sacrifice in the Valley of Hinnom represents the ultimate perversion of the archetypal sacrifice—that of God's own Son. Christ, the only-begotten, is offered for the sins of the world; the sacrifice of children to Molech is the dark inversion of this redemptive sacrifice. Where Christ's sacrifice redeems life, Molech's sacrifice destroys it. Isaiah's denunciation of child sacrifice thus prefigures Christ's radical valuation of children (Matthew 19:14) and His protection of the innocent.
commentary.application: While modern readers are not literally sacrificing children to Molech, the principle underlying Isaiah's accusation remains vital: we must examine whether we have subordinated the lives and well-being of children—and innocents generally—to false gods and worldly desires. Do we sacrifice our children's spiritual well-being to the gods of entertainment, social media, secular achievement, or materialism? Do we allow them to be 'slaughtered' in the moral wilderness of our culture while we offer fervent devotion to false values? Isaiah's horror over child sacrifice should awaken us to the subtle ways we might be sacrificing the next generation on the altars of false gods. The call is to fierce protection of the innocent and to the redirection of our fervent devotion toward YHWH and His covenants.

text_kjv: Among the smooth stones of the stream is thy portion; they, they are thy lot: even to them hast thou poured a drink offering, thou hast offered a meat offering. Should I receive comfort in these?

commentary.narrative: Isaiah reaches the climax of his accusation with a bitter wordplay that captures the entire tragedy of Judah's apostasy in a single image. The "smooth stones of the valley" (chalqei nachal) refers to the polished river stones used in pagan worship—stones that were rubbed smooth by water and repurposed as altars or idols. But the Hebrew term chalqei (smooth stones) sounds remarkably similar to cheleq (portion, inheritance, allotted share). This is the core scandal: Israel was promised an inheritance (cheleq) from YHWH—the land of Canaan, the covenant blessings, the presence of God. Instead, they have claimed as their inheritance smooth stones in a valley. The repetition "they, they are thy lot" (the pronoun 'they' is emphatic in Hebrew) underscores the absurdity: *these* are what you have chosen. To add insult to injury, they have poured out drink offerings and brought grain offerings to these stones—the very sacrifices meant for YHWH in the temple are now being offered to worthless rocks. The rhetorical question at the end—"Should I receive comfort in these?"—is searing. YHWH asks: Should I find consolation or acceptance in these perversions? The answer is implicitly no. The accusation crescendos: not only have they abandoned true worship, but they have redefined their inheritance, their very identity and future, around that abandonment.

word_study.meaning: Chalqei (smooth stones, polished pieces); nachal (stream, valley). Cheleq (portion, inheritance, allotted share). The Covenant Rendering highlights the wordplay explicitly: smooth stones that form one's 'portion.'
word_study.significance: This is Isaiah's master stroke—a pun that encapsulates theological tragedy. Israel rejected the cheleq (inheritance/portion) YHWH offered them and accepted instead chalqei (smooth rocks). The words are similar enough in sound that the connection would be immediately audible to a Hebrew speaker. The Covenant Rendering captures this by translating both as 'portion': 'Among the smooth stones of the valley is your portion; they, they are your lot!' (translator notes emphasize the wordplay on 'chelqei' and 'cheleq').

word_study.meaning: Your lot, your destiny, your allotted portion. Goral refers to that which is distributed by lot or by divine allocation—one's destined share. In the Pentateuch, it often refers to the tribal portions of the Promised Land.
word_study.significance: By using goral alongside cheleq, Isaiah reinforces the idea of covenant inheritance. The 'lot' of Israel should be the land YHWH gave them; instead, they have made river stones their lot—a tragic reversal.

word_study.meaning: You have poured out a drink offering (libation). Shafach means to pour, spill, or shed (often used of shedding blood). Nesech is a libation—wine or liquid poured out as an offering in worship.
word_study.significance: The drink offering was a legitimate part of temple sacrifice (Numbers 28:7-10), poured out before YHWH at the altar. That the people now pour these out to 'smooth stones' is a wholesale perversion of proper worship.

word_study.meaning: A grain offering, meal offering, or gift offering. Minchah could be uncooked grain, flour, baked goods, or a general term for a gift or tribute to a superior (YHWH or a king).
word_study.significance: The minchah was an essential part of daily temple worship, offered twice daily. That it is being offered to river stones represents the complete inversion of the sacrificial system.

word_study.meaning: Shall I be comforted, shall I find rest or satisfaction, shall I relent (change my mind, show mercy). Nacham can mean to comfort, console, or to regret/repent (change one's mind). Here, the Lord is asking if He should be satisfied or comforted by these offerings to false gods.
word_study.significance: The rhetorical question is YHWH's response: Should I accept these offerings? Should I relent in my judgment? The implied answer is an emphatic no. YHWH will not be comforted by false worship; judgment must come.

cross_references.connection: Joshua allots the inheritance (cheleq) of the tribes; YHWH's covenant promise was land as inheritance. Isaiah's bitter reversal—that Israel has chosen stones instead of inheritance—pointedly subverts this promise.
Moses describes Israel as 'the portion [cheleq] of YHWH'—chosen, set apart, treasured. By redefining their portion as river stones, Judah has rejected their own identity as YHWH's cheleq.
The law prescribes drink offerings and grain offerings in the tabernacle service; Isaiah's accusation is that these offerings are being redirected to false altars, a direct violation of Mosaic law.
Nephi warns that the wicked choose 'spiritual death' by rejecting the inheritance YHWH offers—a parallel to Isaiah's depiction of choosing stones over covenant inheritance.

The Lord describes those who reject the covenant and receive a lesser law, thereby losing the greater inheritance—precisely mirroring Isaiah's accusation that Israel has traded their true inheritance for worthless substitutes.

commentary.historical_context: The worship practices Isaiah describes involved the use of sacred stones as altars or idols. In Canaanite religion, smooth stones (often collected from riverbeds and polished) were used as masseboth (standing stones) or fetishes representing divine presence. Pouring out libations and leaving offerings at stone altars was a standard Canaanite practice adopted by certain Israelite groups. The Valley of Hinnom (implied by verse 5) actually had such stone altars, some of which have been excavated. The wordplay on chalqei/cheleq would have been immediately evident to an 8th-century Judean audience—a devastating critique rendered through language itself. The contrast between YHWH's covenant allocation of the Promised Land (the true cheleq) and the fraudulent 'inheritance' of river stones captures the spiritual bankruptcy Isaiah perceives. Ancient Near Eastern cultures generally believed that offering sacrifices to idols was transactional—that proper offerings would secure divine favor. Isaiah's rhetorical question ('Should I receive comfort in these?') undercuts this entire premise: YHWH does not accept such offerings, nor will they earn His favor.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 12:27, Abinadi teaches that if the people keep the law of Moses but lose their faith in Christ, they 'cannot save themselves'—they cling to 'smooth stones' (the letter of the law) while rejecting the inheritance (the Spirit and redemption) that the law was meant to foreshadow. The Book of Mormon repeatedly warns against settling for false or diminished inheritances.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:32-33 describes those who 'honor me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me' and whose 'minds are darkened'—they offer empty sacrifices. The language of Isaiah 57:6 is echoed in the Doctrine and Covenants' critique of hollow religiosity.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple was the place where drink offerings and grain offerings were properly given to YHWH. Those who redirected these offerings to false altars and worthless stones were inverting the temple covenant. The true inheritance promised in the temple—exaltation, the presence of God—is traded away for spiritual trinkets.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the true inheritance, the true portion, the true altar to which all offerings should be directed. The stones placed at river beds represent the natural man's futile attempt to anchor spiritual meaning in the physical and material. Christ, the living stone (1 Peter 2:4), becomes the cornerstone on which the true inheritance is built. Those who accept Him receive the true cheleq; those who reject Him settle for polished river rocks.
commentary.application: This verse asks us to examine what we have accepted as our 'portion' and 'inheritance.' Have we traded the covenant inheritance YHWH offers—divine presence, exaltation, the fullness of His blessings—for the smooth stones of worldly comfort, social approval, material security, or intellectual sophistication? Are we pouring out our best offerings (time, energy, devotion, resources) on things that ultimately have no substance? The verse calls us to reclaim our true inheritance as covenant members and to redirect our offerings to the true altar. It challenges us to ask: Am I satisfied with polished stones, or am I reaching for the genuine covenants and promises of YHWH? The wordplay itself is a warning—we must listen carefully (chalqei sounds like cheleq) to detect when we are being lured into false inheritances masquerading as legitimate portions.

text_kjv: I create the fruit of the lips; Peace, peace to him that is far off, and to him that is near, saith the LORD; and I will heal him.

commentary.narrative:
This verse pivots Isaiah 57 from judgment to consolation, offering restoration to the exiled and the remnant. The phrase 'fruit of the lips' is not metaphorical praise arising from human piety—it is God actively creating the capacity for thanksgiving itself. This is theologically profound: the response of faith is not merely human achievement but divine gift. The doubled 'peace, peace' intensifies the promise, echoing Isaiah 26:3 where God guards those 'whose mind is stayed on thee.' The 'far off' and 'near' originally referred to those scattered in exile and those who remained in the land, but Paul's quotation in Ephesians 2:17 reveals a deeper Christological reading: Christ preaches peace to Gentiles (far off) and Jews (near), reconciling both through His blood.

The structure of this declaration—God speaking in first person ('I create'), then quoting Himself in direct speech ('Peace, peace')—creates an extraordinary rhetorical moment. God does not merely promise peace; He speaks it into reality. The 'healing' mentioned at the verse's end is not merely physical restoration but covenantal restoration, the mending of a broken relationship between God and His people. The Masoretic Text and the Dead Sea Scroll (1QIsaᵃ) preserve this reading identically, confirming that this promise was stable in Jewish tradition centuries before the Christian era.

For Isaiah's original audience, this verse would have felt like a reprieve in the midst of exile's despair. After chapters of warnings and descriptions of idolatrous corruption, the promise suddenly breaks through: God will heal. The doubling of 'peace' suggests not a tentative hope but an emphatic, unshakeable commitment. This is not peace on divine probation; it is peace declared and secured.

word_study.meaning: to create, to fashion, to bring into being from nothing. Root בָּרָא (bara), used primarily for divine creative action.
word_study.significance: God does not merely enable praise—He originates it. The fruit of the lips (thanksgiving, confession, worship) is divinely initiated. This echoes Genesis 1:1 (bara) and emphasizes that even the human response to grace is a divine work. The Covenant Rendering's emphasis on 'creating the fruit of the lips' underscores that gratitude itself is a spiritual gift, not earned human achievement.

word_study.meaning: literally, 'produce' or 'utterance' of the lips; the speech, confession, or praise that comes from the mouth. Niv (נִיב) can also mean 'branch' or 'sprout,' suggesting organic growth.
word_study.significance: This phrase appears in Hosea 14:2 (KJV) in a context of repentance: 'take with you words.' It denotes covenant language, testimony, and confession as the visible evidence of spiritual transformation. The metaphor of 'fruit' suggests that authentic worship grows naturally from a healed heart.

word_study.meaning: Peace is doubled for emphasis and intensity. Shalom carries semantic fullness: wholeness, health, safety, right relationship, prosperity, and completeness. The doubling intensifies each dimension.
word_study.significance: The TCR notes that this doubling echoes Isaiah 26:3 and extends healing to both 'the far and the near.' In Jewish rhetorical tradition, doubling emphasizes absoluteness and certainty (compare 'holy, holy, holy' in 6:3). This is not partial or conditional peace but total, covenantal restoration. Paul's quotation in Ephesians 2:17 identifies the cosmic scope: peace extends across the Jew-Gentile divide through Christ.

word_study.meaning: Distance and proximity. Originally, in exile context: those dispersed abroad vs. those remaining in the land. Ontologically: those far from God's presence vs. those near.
word_study.significance: This couplet carries multiple layers. Historically, it refers to diaspora and remnant. Theologically, it echoes Psalm 23 and Deuteronomy 30:11-14 (the word is 'nigh unto thee'). For NT readers (Ephesians 2:17), it becomes the paradigm for gentile inclusion and Jewish reconciliation through Christ. No one is too distant from God's healing.

word_study.meaning: To heal, to cure, to restore to wholeness. Can mean physical healing but more often covenantal restoration and spiritual wholeness.
word_study.significance: In Isaiah's context, healing is inseparable from covenant renewal. Exodus 15:26 associates healing with obedience to God's commandments. Isaiah 53:5 applies this term to the Servant's vicarious healing. The promise here is not merely medical but soteriological: restoration of the broken relationship.

cross_references.connection: Paul explicitly quotes Isaiah 57:19, applying 'peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near' to Christ's reconciliation of Jew and Gentile through His blood. This identifies Jesus as the one who creates the fruit of the lips and mediates all peace.
The doubled 'peace, peace' echoes this verse: 'Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee.' Both verses promise peace as a divine guard over the faithful remnant.

By his stripes we are healed' — this Suffering Servant passage applies healing (rafa) to the Messiah's vicarious atonement. Isaiah 57:19's healing promise is ultimately fulfilled in Christ's sacrifice.
Hosea uses 'fruit of the lips' (niv sefatayim) in the context of repentance and covenant renewal, establishing the phrase as language of spiritual return and confession.
God stills the storm and brings the troubled sea to calm, turning despair to peace. This echoes Isaiah's movement from the churning wicked (v. 20) to the peace offered to the repentant (v. 19).

commentary.historical_context: Isaiah 57:19 arrives at the climax of the exile's redemptive narrative. By the time this prophecy circulated in Judah (likely 6th century BCE, during or after Babylonian captivity), the community was fragmented: some deported, some remained, some fled to Egypt. The promise of 'peace to far and near' would have resonated powerfully as a reunification oracle—God's healing encompasses all branches of the scattered people. The language of 'creating fruit of the lips' reflects ancient Near Eastern understanding of divine speech-acts (dabar, the word that accomplishes what it declares). In Mesopotamian and Egyptian texts, divine utterance has creative force; Isaiah appropriates this cosmology for Israel's God, emphasizing that even human worship is a divinely spoken reality. The Dead Sea Scroll (1QIsaᵃ) preserves this reading identically with the Masoretic Text, confirming the verse's stability in Jewish textual tradition across a thousand-year span.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Book of Mormon prophets emphasize healing through covenant: 2 Nephi 25:23 ('it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do') echoes the idea that healing comes from God's initiative, though faith is required. Alma 7:10-12 describes Christ taking upon Himself the pains and infirmities of His people—the ultimate fulfillment of Isaiah 57:19's healing promise. 3 Nephi 17:7-9 shows Christ healing the sick among the Nephites, manifesting this peace and wholeness.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:1-2 ('I am the Lord your God...I give unto you a law...that ye might be sanctified by that law') echoes the covenant language of Isaiah 57:19. The Doctrine and Covenants consistently frames God's peace as a gift of sanctification and spiritual wholeness, not earned but received. D&C 19:23 ('I, the Lord, have suffered the pain of all men') applies Isaiah's healing promise directly to Christ in this dispensation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The promise of healing 'to the far and near' resonates with the temple theology of gathering and reconciliation. In Latter-day Saint thought, the temple is the place where dispersed Israel is reunited in covenant. The 'fruit of the lips' becomes the temple oath and testimony—the sanctified speech of those who enter God's house. The endowment narrative itself teaches the restoration and healing that Isaiah 57:19 promises.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 57:19 is explicitly Christological through Paul's quotation in Ephesians 2:14-17. Christ is the one who 'creates the fruit of the lips'—He authors the new covenant language of thanksgiving and praise. He is the peace-bringer to 'the far off' (Gentiles) and 'the near' (faithful Israelites). In Isaiah's Suffering Servant arc (chs. 50-57), this verse reveals the purpose of the Servant's work: not judgment, but healing and peace-making. The Servant's stripped, wounded, humiliated state (52:14, 53:2-3) leads to this restoration. Jesus Christ is the bearer of this peace and the one who makes the 'fruit of the lips' possible through His atonement.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 57:19 teaches that spiritual healing and peace are divine gifts, not achievements we earn through effort alone. The 'fruit of the lips'—our testimony, prayer, and praise—grows from ground that God prepares. When we feel distant from God through exile, doubt, or transgression ('far off'), this verse promises that distance is no barrier to healing. The doubled 'peace, peace' assures us that God's offer is absolute and unshakeable. Practically, this means we should speak and witness without shame—God creates the capacity for our testimony. It also means we should recognize doubt and distance not as disqualification but as the very condition to which this promise is addressed. The covenant of peace is inclusive and global; it reaches the exiled and the remnant alike. In our own era of dispersal—spiritual, geographical, familial—Isaiah 57:19 invites us to claim that peace through Christ, the one who makes us 'far and near' one people.

text_kjv: But the wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest, whose waters cast up mire and dirt.

commentary.narrative:
This verse provides the immediate counterpoint to verse 19's promise of peace. Where the righteous receive healing and shalom, the wicked experience endless turbulence. The sea image is one of ancient literature's most potent symbols of chaos, disorder, and moral instability. Unlike the Dead Sea's lifeless saltness or the Canaanite cosmic sea-dragon that required subduing (Psalm 74:13-14, Isaiah 51:9-10), this sea represents the self-generated turmoil of those who reject God's healing. The waters 'cast up mire and mud'—excrement and filth—suggesting that the wicked's own nature produces spiritual corruption. They are their own torment.

The theological contrast is stark and intentional. Verse 19 opens with God's creative word ('I create'). Verse 20 closes on the wicked's self-destruction ('cannot rest'). The Hebrew neg-rash (driven, churned) suggests violent, relentless agitation—not stasis but perpetual motion toward ruin. The mire and mud are not external obstacles but products of the waters themselves; the wicked generate their own desolation. This is not arbitrary punishment imposed from without but the inevitable consequence of rejecting God's shalom. In the context of Isaiah 57's preceding polemic against idolatry and covenant violation (vv. 3-13), this verse explains why the wicked cannot benefit from the healing offered in verse 19: their spiritual nature is fundamentally at odds with peace.

The Dead Sea Scroll variant is minor (yam vs. kayyam, 'a sea' vs. 'the sea'), but both readings preserve the image's force. Whether 'a sea' or 'the sea,' the turbulent waters symbolize the condition of those who remain unredeemed. This verse functions as Isaiah's version of interior punishment theology: you become what you love, and those who love disorder become disordered.

word_study.meaning: The wicked, the guilty, the morally corrupt. Plural of rasha (רָשָׁע), one who willfully transgresses covenant. In Hebrew moral vocabulary, distinct from 'fool' (kesil) or 'simple' (peti); the wicked are culpable, deliberate in their violation.
word_study.significance: Isaiah has identified the wicked throughout chapter 57: those who practice idolatry, feed on calves and horses, engage in cultic prostitution, make covenant with Molech. These are not accidentally astray but deliberately rebellious. The term carries judicial overtones; the wicked are under divine condemnation.

word_study.meaning: Like the sea that is driven, tossed, churned. Nigras (נִגְרָשׁ) is the Niphal passive of garas (גָּרַשׁ), meaning to drive out, to cast out, to agitate. The sea is relentlessly driven by internal and external forces.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering 'the churning sea' captures the continuous, violent agitation. In ancient cosmology, the sea is often chaos's dwelling; here, the sea's restlessness becomes the wicked's existential condition. Unlike Psalm 23's quiet waters, the wicked inhabit a realm of perpetual turbulence. The Covenant Rendering's choice of 'churning' emphasizes the internal fermentation and corruption.

word_study.meaning: Is unable to be quiet, unable to attain stillness. Sheket (שְׁקֵט) means quiet, stillness, rest, peace. Yukal (יוּכָל) is the Qal imperfect of yakol (יָכֹל), 'to be able, to have power.'
word_study.significance: The inability to rest is presented as a condition, not a choice. The wicked are trapped in perpetual agitation; shalom is inaccessible to them. This echoes Ecclesiastes 2:26 ('to the sinner he giveth travail'). It is the natural consequence of covenant violation: loss of rest, loss of peace, loss of wholeness.

word_study.meaning: Mire is mud or slime (refesh, רֶפֶשׁ); tiyt (טִיט) is mud or clay. Both terms connote impurity, filth, and corruption. In biblical language, being 'cast into mire' is humiliation and degradation (Psalm 69:2, Jeremiah 38:6).
word_study.significance: The sea casts up its own excrement. The imagery suggests that the wicked are immersed in the consequences of their own moral corruption. This is not external punishment but self-generated defilement. In Latter-day Saint theology, sin naturally darkens the spirit and removes one from the presence of God—not through arbitrary decree but through the nature of sin itself.

cross_references.connection: This identical refrain ('There is no peace, saith my God, unto the wicked') closes Isaiah 48, creating a structural and thematic bookend. Both instances mark the absolute exclusion of the wicked from divine peace.

The Psalms use similar sea imagery for the wicked: 'The wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest, whose waters cast up mire and dirt.' Isaiah likely echoes this psalm, deepening the tradition.
Jeremiah is cast into a dungeon of mire and mud as punishment—a visualization of Isaiah's metaphor. The mire becomes the wicked's literal and spiritual habitat.
To the wicked, God 'giveth travail, and sorrow'—a state of perpetual labor without rest, paralleling the sea's inability to be still. Both express the loss of shalom as a consequence of rebellion.

The lake of fire reserved for the wicked in John's vision embodies this same principle: the wicked are forever excluded from God's presence and peace. Isaiah 57:20 prefigures this eternal restlessness.

commentary.historical_context: The image of the wicked as a restless sea would resonate powerfully in a Jewish context. The Dead Sea itself was known for its deadness (no life, extreme salinity), yet Ezekiel's vision (47:8) prophesies that living waters will flow from the temple to heal even the Dead Sea. Isaiah's turbulent sea represents the opposite state: not dead but violently alive in its corruption, unable to find the healing and stillness that God offers. In the ancient Near East, the sea was often associated with primordial chaos (the Babylonian Tiamat); Isaiah appropriates this imagery to describe the moral chaos of those who reject covenant. The reference to waters 'casting up mire and mud' reflects observations of tidal action on the shores of the Mediterranean and Arabian seas, where silt and organic decay accumulate in shallow waters. For Isaiah's audience, both exiled and traumatized, this verse would have functioned as a clarification: the wicked's exclusion from peace is not a miscarriage of justice but a natural law operating within the moral order. The Dead Sea Scroll (1QIsaᵃ) preserves a minor variant (yam vs. kayyam), but both readings maintain identical theological content and force.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 12:34-37 describes the state of the wicked after judgment: they remain in darkness and are 'cast off...far from the presence of the Lord.' The inability to rest parallels Alma's depiction of the separated from God—a perpetual, inescapable condition of restlessness. Helaman 13:36-37 similarly describes the wicked as 'tormented within by the pains of a damned soul' because of their transgression.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 19:17 ('I, the Lord, have suffered the pain of all men...that they might not suffer if they would repent') implies that those who do not repent remain in their torment. D&C 76:103-106 describes the state of the sons of perdition—those who reject the gospel—as one of darkness and separation, unable to attain the peace promised to the righteous. The D&C frequently frames covenant violation as resulting in 'broken' or 'darkened' spiritual states.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple represents the place of rest and wholeness (shalom). Those who covenant there enter God's peace. Conversely, those outside the covenant remain in the 'churning sea' of worldly turbulence. The contrast between the temple's sacred stillness and the world's chaotic agitation embodies Isaiah 57:20's principle.

commentary.christological_typology: While verse 20 does not explicitly reference Christ, it establishes the contrast that makes His saving work necessary and efficacious. The wicked's inability to rest—their existential turbulence—is the condition Christ comes to heal. His peace ('the peace of God, which passeth all understanding,' Philippians 4:7) is the antidote to the wicked's churning. Christ's atonement is the mechanism by which the restless can attain rest. In Hebrews 4:9-10, the 'rest' of God becomes a type of salvation available through Christ. Isaiah 57:20 establishes the problem; Christ becomes the solution.
commentary.application: For modern readers, Isaiah 57:20 offers a penetrating diagnosis of unrepentant life. The 'churning sea' is not merely external circumstance but the inevitable interior state of those who reject God's healing. In our age of relentless information, social turbulence, and moral instability, the image of a sea that 'cannot rest' becomes haunting and clarifying. Addiction, unforgiveness, pride, lust—these become the wicked's churning waters, generating mire and mud from within. Conversely, the verse invites honest self-examination: Am I at peace? Or am I restlessly agitated, generating my own desolation? If the latter, Isaiah 57:19 offers the remedy—the peace of God is available to all who draw near. The verse also teaches compassion: the wicked in their turbulence are not to be scorned but pitied. Their condition is self-generated but not irreversible if they accept healing. In covenant community, we are called to model the peace (shalom) that is unavailable to those still churning in rebellion.

text_kjv: There is no peace, saith my God, unto the wicked.

commentary.narrative:
This verse serves as Isaiah's closing seal on chapter 57 and, more broadly, as a structural marker for the entire second half of Isaiah (chapters 40-66). The repetition of this refrain at Isaiah 48:22 creates a tripartite division of Isaiah's final 27 chapters: 40-48 (first nine chapters), 49-57 (second nine chapters), and 58-66 (third nine chapters). Each section closes with this solemn pronouncement: 'There is no peace...unto the wicked.' The repetition transforms the statement from a casual observation into a foundational principle of Isaiah's theology—not a temporary condition but an absolute, irreversible exclusion.

The shift in speaker—'saith my God' rather than 'saith the LORD'—personalizes the declaration. It is God Himself, speaking through the prophet, who delivers this judgment. The tone is neither angry nor vindictive but sorrowful and final. By verse 21, the reader has witnessed the complete trajectory of Isaiah 57: the righteous perish unnoticed but enter peace (vv. 1-2), the wicked practice idolatry and covenant betrayal (vv. 3-13), the contrite are comforted (vv. 14-18), and the righteous receive healing and the 'fruit of the lips' (v. 19). Yet the wicked, by their nature and choice, remain outside this circle of restoration. The Dead Sea Scroll (1QIsaᵃ) preserves this verse identically with the Masoretic Text, confirming its stability as a theological anchor in Jewish textual tradition.

For Isaiah's audience, this verse would have functioned as both warning and comfort: warning to those still entangled in idolatry and covenant violation; comfort to the faithful remnant that God's peace is real, protected, and assured. The finality of the declaration—'There is no peace'—is not arbitrary cruelty but a statement about the nature of reality itself: those who reject covenant with the God of peace cannot possess peace. Shalom and reshaim (peace and the wicked) are ontologically incompatible.

word_study.meaning: Peace, wholeness, completeness, health, safety, right relationship. The singular here (as opposed to the doubled 'peace, peace' of v. 19) gives weight and finality to the negation.
word_study.significance: By verse 21, shalom has been fully defined through its opposite (the churning sea) and its presence (healing to the far and near). Now the negation is absolute: shalom is not available to the wicked. This is the negative pole of covenant theology—those outside covenant lack the peace that defines covenant life.

word_study.meaning: The wicked, those who have deliberately violated covenant. Here, at the verse's climax, the term carries full weight of accumulated indictment from verses 3-13.
word_study.significance: By this point in the chapter, 'the wicked' is not an abstract category but has been concretely identified: those who practice idolatry ('kindle a fire,' v. 5), engage in sexual apostasy ('enlarging thy bed,' v. 8), serve other gods ('made a covenant with death,' v. 15). The term is specific, not generic, rooted in covenant language.

word_study.meaning: Says my God. Elohai (אֱלֹהַי) is the divine name used in direct, personal address—God in relationship to the prophet or people, not merely as abstract Creator (Elohim).
word_study.significance: The shift from 'the LORD' (YHWH, the covenant name) in verse 19 to 'my God' here is subtle but significant. It suggests intimacy, personal conviction, and the prophet's own assent to God's judgment. This is Isaiah speaking as the people's intercessor, affirming that even he acknowledges the finality of this verdict.

cross_references.connection: Identical refrain marking the end of the first section of Isaiah's latter half (chs. 40-48). The repetition at both 48:22 and 57:21 creates a structural template, suggesting a third occurrence frames 58-66.
Moses warns that those who turn to idolatry will experience divine wrath and severance from blessing. Isaiah's declaration echoes and fulfills this covenantal warning in the exile context.
Wisdom warns that the wicked who reject instruction will experience calamity and will not find peace when they call out. The principle is consistent across wisdom literature.

Paul quotes Isaiah and other prophets, noting that the wicked 'know not the way of peace.' Romans frames this as universal human condition—all have fallen short—but the principle echoes Isaiah's absolute statement.

Lehi teaches that humans are 'free to choose liberty and eternal life' or 'captivity and death.' Isaiah 57:21 expresses the reality of that latter choice: those who choose captivity (rejection of covenant) forfeit peace.

commentary.historical_context: In the context of the Babylonian exile (the likely historical setting for Isaiah 40-66), this verse would have been both threat and promise. For those still practicing idolatry in exile (syncretizing Babylonian and Hebrew worship, as archaeological evidence suggests), verse 21 was a warning: your gods cannot give you peace. For the faithful remnant maintaining covenant, it was an assurance: the wicked are not ultimately victorious; they remain excluded from the true peace of God. The tripartite structure (48:22, 57:21, and implicitly 66:24) creates a framework suggesting that Isaiah's final 27 chapters are organized around this theological principle: God's peace is real, protected, and ultimately unavailable to the wicked. The Dead Sea Scroll (1QIsaᵃ) preserves this verse without variant, confirming its textual stability across centuries. In Jewish tradition, this verse became part of the haftarah system (prophetic readings in synagogue), where it would be intoned as a solemn conclusion to Isaiah's promises and warnings.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 40:13-14 describes the state of the wicked after death—they are 'brought back into the presence of the Lord' but are 'cut off' and 'cannot dwell in the presence of God.' This is the Book of Mormon's expansion of Isaiah 57:21's principle into a doctrine of post-mortal separation. 2 Nephi 9:46 similarly states that 'the happiness of the righteous is upon their heads; and the wicked shall have cause to mourn.'
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:103-106 describes the sons of perdition—those who fully reject the covenant—as eternally separated from God's presence: 'from these shall be taken all things.' This is the D&C's fulfillment of Isaiah 57:21 in dispensational terms. D&C 130:10-11 further teaches that those who do not keep covenants are subject to the laws they themselves establish, and 'all kingdoms have a law given.' The wicked have set themselves outside the law of peace.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant explicitly binds the participant to seek 'the peace of God.' Those who break covenant (violate the oaths taken) become, in a real sense, the 'wicked' of whom Isaiah speaks. Conversely, the endowment teaches that faithful covenant-keepers inherit peace in this life and exaltation in the next. Isaiah 57:21 underscores why covenant fidelity is so central to Latter-day Saint theology: covenant is the mechanism of peace.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 57:21 establishes the necessity of Christ's mediatory work. If no peace is available to the wicked through their own effort or through external judgment, then only a transformation—a new birth, a new covenant written on the heart—can make peace possible. Christ's atonement in Isaiah's Suffering Servant narrative (chs. 50-53) is precisely this transformative work. Through Christ, the wicked can cease to be wicked; through His blood, those cut off can be redeemed. In this reading, verse 21 is not Christ's final word to the wicked but rather establishes the condition into which He enters to save. He comes for those 'outside the peace,' to make them 'inside.' The refrain's appearance at 48:22 and 57:21 (and implicitly 66:24, which closes the entire book with the image of the wicked's unending punishment) frames Christ's saving work as the sole means of escaping this verse's sentence.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 57:21 poses a searching question: Which side of this divide do we inhabit? The verse invites self-examination not in a spirit of self-condemnation but of clarity. Do we possess shalom—the peace of God that is more than the absence of conflict, but wholeness, right relationship, and spiritual security? If not, the chapter offers diagnosis and remedy. The wicked of Isaiah 57 are characterized by specific practices: idolatry, covenant betrayal, self-exaltation, sexual immorality, refusal of God's word. Those who turn from these toward repentance (v. 15: 'contrite and humble') find healing and peace (v. 18-19). Isaiah 57:21 thus becomes not a word of condemnation to those who are turning repentantly toward God but a word of solemn finality to those who harden their hearts. The application is one of covenant clarity: peace is not distributed by God's arbitrary will but follows naturally from covenant relationship. We are each choosing, day by day, whether to align ourselves with the peace-bringers of verses 19 or with the churning sea of verse 20. The verse calls us to choose wisely and to help others do the same—not through judgment but through witness to the peace we have been given.
